General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a latest form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," states Yiwen Chu.

Industry observers note that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

According to recent reports, the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an notable role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Recent findings suggest that quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are at the moment beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

In a recent development, one of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

Sources indicate that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Recent findings suggest that another key benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Upcoming Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two vital computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

According to recent reports, "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Sources indicate that successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the fresh architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

It has been revealed that one of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Recent findings suggest that lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Sources indicate that understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

Sources indicate that maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

It has been revealed that I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very promptly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Recent findings suggest that google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

Industry observers note that the Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

According to recent reports, videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

Sources indicate that I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a massive uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," noted Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Recent findings suggest that visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The newly introduced findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

Recent findings suggest that an vital opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

Sources indicate that when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

According to recent reports, producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

Recent findings suggest that to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

Industry observers note that when the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

Industry observers note that this distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler mentioned. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

Sources indicate that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

Recent findings suggest that "A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler stated. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

Recent findings suggest that the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Recent findings suggest that rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today, we are launching the integration of four awesome serverless Inference Providers – fal, Replicate, Sambanova, Together AI – directly on the Hub’s model pages.
  • According to recent reports, we’ve been hosting a serverless Inference API on the Hub for a long time (we launched the v1 in summer 2020 – wow, time flies 🤯).
  • Just as we work with great partners like AWS, Nvidia and others for dedicated deployment options via the model pages’ Deploy button, it was natural to partner with the next generation of serverless inference providers for model-centric, serverless inference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today, we are launching the integration of four awesome serverless Inference Providers – fal, Replicate, Sambanova, Together AI – directly on the Hub’s model pages. They are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for JS and Python), making it easier than ever to explore serverless inference of a wide variety of models that run on your favorite providers.

According to recent reports, we’ve been hosting a serverless Inference API on the Hub for a long time (we launched the v1 in summer 2020 – wow, time flies 🤯). While this has enabled easy exploration and prototyping, we’ve refined our core value proposition towards collaboration, storage, versioning, and distribution of large datasets and models with the community. At the same time, serverless providers have flourished, and the time was right for Hugging Face to offer easy and unified access to serverless inference through a set of great providers.

Just as we work with great partners like AWS, Nvidia and others for dedicated deployment options via the model pages’ Deploy button, it was natural to partner with the next generation of serverless inference providers for model-centric, serverless inference.

Here’s what this enables, taking the timely example of DeepSeek-ai/DeepSeek-R1, a model which has achieved mainstream fame over the past few days 🔥:.

In a recent development, rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder & CEO at SambaNova: "We are excited to be partnering with Hugging Face to accelerate its Inference API. Hugging Face developers now have access to much faster inference speeds on a wide range of the best open source models.".

Zeke Sikelianos, Founding Designer at Replicate: "Hugging Face is the de facto home of open-source model weights, and has been a key player in making AI more accessible to the world. We use Hugging Face internally at Replicate as our weights registry of choice, and we're honored to be among the first inference providers to be featured in this launch.".

This is just the start, and we’ll build on top of this with the community in the coming weeks!

According to recent reports, the following example shows how to use DeepSeek-R1 using Together AI as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Together AI API key if you have one.

Install huggingface_hub version v0.28.0 or later (release notes).

Note: You can also use the OpenAI client library to call the Inference Providers too; see here an example for DeepSeek model.

And here's how to generate an image from a text prompt using FLUX.1-dev running on fal.ai:.

To move to a different provider, you can simply change the provider name, everything else stays the same:.

We expose the Routing proxy directly under the huggingface.co domain so you can call it directly, it's very useful for OpenAI-compatible APIs for instance. You can just swap the URL as a base URL: https://router.huggingface.co/{:provider}.

Here's how you can call Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct using Sambanova as the inference provider via cURL.

Sources indicate that for direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Together AI key you're billed on your Together AI account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

According to recent reports, this turn might not seem like that significant of a deal to many of you... But in practice, this very clearly constitutes an abrupt cutting-off of the lion's share of the quasi-subsidized compute erstwhile accessible through HF.

It has been revealed that and though seldom overtly publicized as a core feature of the platform, that nonchalantly encouraging compute reservoir of yore (even if accessible only via select pockets, like Inference Endpoints) served for years as a kind of a phantom fertilizer, and a key one, for Machine Learning adoption, experimentation, and resource-strapped development – on par with other quasi-subsidized resources like Google Colab and ChatGPT . And it's entirely plausible that the availability of such resources en masse has been the single most key prerequisite, as well as mandatory catalyst, for the continual evolution/democratization of open source ML specifically, whether in regards to utility or literacy or safety or any other oft-evoked marker, and in some large part the popularization of ML more broadly.

Of course, despite its qualitative obviousness, the impact of subsidized resources may be difficult, maybe impossible, to summate objectively or to quantify directly. After all they constitute a set of infrastructures the immediate production of which tends to assume forms that are often ephemeral, social – like practices, understanding, or values – and wherever concrete, often non-commercial, like open models, adapters, enthusiast contributions, articles, posts, etc. And by the markers of finance and markets, such productions may be deemed as having only a tangential value to, say, the capitalization potential of a given platform, all-the-while adding heavy and at times unforeseeably fluctuating costs upkeep.

Nonetheless, (and there are few better illustrations for this than ML) public access to subsidized resources persisting in open forms (non-transactional, nor overtly monetized, nor strictly delimited: like all public resources, services, libraries, spaces) simultaneously remains a key precondition for the economic and socio-cultural potential of the entire technological and research field as a whole, whilst continually stimulating the range and variety of forms this potential may ultimately assume.

As recently as a year ago, I would avidly preach the merits of Huggingface to everyone I know: not only as the key extant firmament for humanist and democratized machine learning paradigms to emerge and thrive upon, but as a really-existing pre-figuration of a upcoming form of society, one that may at last transcend the intertwined logic of alienation, separation, disparity, scarcity, disposability, amnesia, exploitation, and all the rest of it... That's what I used to associate with Huggingface. Nowadays though: I think of Huggingface, and my next thought is "$2.00".

I know that for resources or platforms to remain subsidized, such subsidies must come from someplace. And assuring reliable funding may be a challenge, especially these days. Nonetheless, I really believe that it would be a grave mistake long-term for HF to rely on standard transactional/commercial monetization sourced from its users, even to cover real costs (much less to extract surplus "value" from or for anyone). To best serve its role within the field, HF must instead move closer to operating as a non-profit, sourcing unconditional funding from elsewhere , with the assumption that it may always operate at a "loss", whilst playing a key role in the thriving and the dynamism of the field as a whole.

Should a normal visitor reasonably be able to discover this page from another page on the site?

Internal links should not exist merely to move ranking signals around.

They should help owners move between related tasks.

Tech Report: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • According to recent reports, the approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • In a recent development, one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

According to recent reports, the approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

In a recent development, one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

Industry observers note that this capability could help advance technologies that are notable to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

According to recent reports, although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Industry observers note that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Upcoming Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

It has been revealed that much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

Sources indicate that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez remarked.

Beyond identifying latest candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

In a recent development, the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

In a recent development, martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

Industry observers note that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#173885. Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • It has been revealed that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

It has been revealed that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify notable interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

Industry observers note that after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

Sources indicate that the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

Sources indicate that "This is particularly crucial because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Industry observers note that looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Recent findings suggest that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," states Peter Zoller.

This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how swiftly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

According to recent reports, the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app demonstrates how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

As virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS owners, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

Sources indicate that it’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

Industry observers note that we made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ.

There’s still no firm timeline for this newly introduced RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

Breaking: The AI tools for Art Newsletter - Matter 1

📅 31 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI space is moving so fast it’s hard to believe that a year ago we still struggled to generate people with the correct amount of fingers 😂.
  • The last couple of years have been pivotal for open source models and tools for artistic usage.
  • According to recent reports, what were the standout releases of creative AI tools in 2024?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI space is moving so fast it’s hard to believe that a year ago we still struggled to generate people with the correct amount of fingers 😂.

The last couple of years have been pivotal for open source models and tools for artistic usage. AI tools for creative expression have never been more accessible, and we’re only scratching the surface. Join us as we look back at the key milestones, tools, and breakthroughs in AI & Arts from 2024, and forward for what’s to come in 2025 (spoiler 👀: we’re starting a upcoming monthly roundup 👇).

According to recent reports, what were the standout releases of creative AI tools in 2024? We'll highlight the major releases across creative and artistic fields, with a particular focus on open-source developments in popular tasks like image and video generation.

Over 2 years since the OG stable diffusion was released and made waves in image generation with open source models, it’s now safe to say that when it comes to image generation from text, image editing and controlled image generation - open source models are giving closed source models a run for their money.

It has been revealed that TD;LR - diffusion models and Gaussian flow matching are equivalent. Flow matching proposes a vector field parametrization of the network output that is different compared to the ones commonly used in diffusion models previously.

Back to practice: First to announce the shift was Stability AI with Stable Diffusion 3, however it was HunyuanDiT that became the first open source model with DiT architecture.This trend continued with the releases of AuraFlow, Flux.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5.

Among many pivotal moments in the (not so long) history of open source image generation models, it’s safe to say that the release of Flux.1 was one of them. Flux [dev] achieved a upcoming state-of-the-art, surpassing popular closed source models like Midjourney v6.0, DALL·E 3 (HD) on various benchmarks.

A positive side effect of advancements in image models is the significant improvement in personalization techniques for text-to-image models and controlled generation.

According to recent reports, back in August 2022, transformative works like Textual Inversion and DreamBooth enhanced our ability to teach and introduce latest concepts to text-to-image models, drastically expanding what could be done with them. These opened the door to a stream of improvements and enhancements building on top of these techniques (such as LoRA for diffusion models).

Industry observers note that however, an upper bound to the quality of the fine-tuned models is naturally the base model from which it was fine-tuned. In that sense, we can’t neglect Stable Diffusion XL, which was also a significant marker in personalization for open source image generation models. A testimony to that is that even now, many of the popular techniques and models for personalization and controlled generation are based on SDXL. The advanced abilities of SDXL (and models that were released after with similar quality) together with the growing understanding of the semantic roles of different components in the diffusion model architecture raises the question - what can we achieve without further optimization?

cue in the rain of zero shot techniques - 2024 was definitely the year when generating high quality portraits from reference photos was made possible with as little as a single reference image & without any optimization. Training free techniques like IP adapter FaceID, InstantID, Photomaker and more came out and demonstrated competitive if not even superior abilities to those of fine-tuned models.

Similarly, image editing and controlled generation - such as image generation with canny / depth / pose constraints made progress too - both thanks to the growing quality of the base models and the community’s growing understanding of the semantic roles different components have (Instant Style, B-LoRA).

Recent findings suggest that so what’s next? since the shift of paradigms to DiT and flow matching objectives, additional models came out trying to utilize DiT-based models like Flux and SD3.5 for similar purposes, but so far not quite beating the quality of the SDXL-based ones despite the superior quality of the underlying base model. This could be attributed to the relative lack of understanding of semantic roles of different components of the DiT compared to the Unet. 2025 could be the year when we identify those roles in DiTs as well, unlocking more possibilities with the next generation of image generation models.

As opposed to image generation, with video we still have a way to go. But, it’s safe to say that we’re very far away from where we were a year ago. While we’re all about open-source, the credit for (some) of the significant leap in AI video generation goes to OpenAI’s sora for changing our expectations of video model capabilities quite radically. The recent surge of open-source video generation models, including CogVideoX, Mochi, Allegro, LTX Video, and HunyuanVideo, has also been noteworthy. Video generation is inherently more challenging than image generation due to the need for motion quality, coherence, and consistency. Additionally, video generation requires substantial computational and memory resources, leading to significant generation latency. This often hinders local usage, making many upcoming open video models inaccessible to community hardware without extensive memory optimizations and quantization approaches that impact both inference latency and the quality of generated videos. Nevertheless the open source community has made remarkable progress - which was recently covered in this blog on the state of open video generation models.

While this implies that most community members are still unable to experiment and develop with open-source video models, it also suggests that we can expect significant advancements in 2025.

According to recent reports, audio generation has progressed significantly in the past year going from simple sounds to complete songs with lyrics. Despite challenges - Audio signals are complex and multifaceted, require more sophisticated mathematical models than models that generate text or images and training data quite scarce - 2024 saw open source releases like OuteTTS and IndicParlerTTS for text to speech and openai’s Whisper large v3 turbo for audio speech recognition. The year 2025 is already shaping up to be a breakthrough year for audio models, with a remarkable number of releases in January alone. We've seen the release of three new text-to-speech models: Kokoro, LLasa TTS and OuteTTS 0.3, as well as two new music models: JASCO and YuE. Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

Sources indicate that the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

Recent findings suggest that we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

Which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a new measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Sources indicate that names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

The formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

Relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

Industry observers note that in each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

Industry observers note that to see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

Industry observers note that on 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

Sources indicate that before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

Sources indicate that the measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

According to recent reports, we reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

In a recent development, think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Industry observers note that before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

Sources indicate that this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

One detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Sources indicate that naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a newly introduced colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

Industry observers note that an agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and mentioned it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

It has been revealed that the --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Industry observers note that version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Sources indicate that whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

In a recent development, an agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer latest to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

Industry observers note that these are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

Take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, streaming in 1080p will be the default in Google Meet, regardless of whether you pay for Google Workspace. That includes personal Google Accounts.

According to recent reports, google indicates consumers will default to sending and receiving 1080p video, at the minimum. Previously, Google Meet made 720p the standard for streaming, and a higher resolution had historically been locked behind the Google One 2TB plan. That’s been true since 1080p streaming was rolled out in 2023.

The upgrade will roll out to everyone, including those with Google Workspace accounts and personal Google Accounts. The only requirement to stream your own 1080p video in Google Meet for web will be hardware-based. Google’s press release states that devices with cameras capable of streaming in high definition will do so, and the feature will be turned on automatically.

Recent findings suggest that it can be disabled, though. Users can head to Settings > Video in Google Meet for web. Video will also appear in a lower resolution if the user’s video tile is shrunk down on-screen.

The upgrade appears to be centered on web-only instances of Google Meet, and might not include the app on Android or iOS. For the time being, those versions may still be limited to streaming in 720p for those who don’t have an active Google One subscription.

Google Meet started its extended rollout of 1080p streaming to everyone earlier this month, so it shouldn’t be much longer until the change has taken place completely.
