💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post was written by Philipp Schmid and orginially posted on philschmid.de code can found here.
  • The release of Deepseek R1 shocked the industry.
  • Industry observers note that in the paper they described an "aha moment" when using pure RL to train the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post was written by Philipp Schmid and orginially posted on philschmid.de code can found here.

The release of Deepseek R1 shocked the industry. Why? Well, DeepSeek-R1 is an open model that rivals OpenAI's o1 in complex reasoning tasks, introduced using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and RL-focused multi-stage training approach. They not only released the model, but also a research paper on how they did it.

Industry observers note that in the paper they described an "aha moment" when using pure RL to train the model. During this phase, DeepSeek-R1-Zero (the first test of DeepSeek-R1) learns to allocate more thinking time to a problem by reevaluating its initial approach without any human feedback or data describing how to do it. They describe this as an "aha moment" as:.

This behavior is not only a testament to the model’s growing reasoning abilities but also a captivating example of how reinforcement learning can lead to unexpected and sophisticated outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that in this blog post we want to recreate the small "aha moment" of DeepSeek-R1 using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and the Countdown Game. We will train an open model using reinforcement learning trying to teach it self-verification and search abilities all on its own to solve the Countdown Game. The Countdown game is a numbers puzzle where players use a set of randomly drawn numbers and basic arithmetic operations (+, -, ×, ÷) to reach or get as close as possible to a target number.

The blog post focuses on training distributed training using Deepspeed and vLLM. It was run on a 4x NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Note: This blog is inspired by Jiayi Pan who initially explored the idea and proofed it with a small model.

But Before we start, let's take a look at the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and understand how it works.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm to improve the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. It was introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper in the context of mathematical reasoning. GRPO modifies the traditional Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) by eliminating the need for a value function model. Instead, it estimates baselines from group scores, reducing memory usage and computational overhead. GRPO, now also used by the Qwen team, can be used with rule/binary-based Rewards as well as General Reward Models to improve models on helpfulness.

Our first step is to install Hugging Face Libraries and Pytorch, vllm, and trl, transformers and datasets. If you haven't heard of trl yet, don't worry. It is a fresh library on top of transformers and datasets, which makes it easier to fine-tune, rlhf, align open LLMs.

Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.

In a recent development, we are going to use the Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4 dataset, which contains samples with 3 to 4 numbers and solutions. As Model we are going to use Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct which is a 3B parameter instruction tuned model. This makes it easier to showcase the "aha moment" as it already can follow instructions. Jiayi-Pan explored that the model needs to have a certain quality to be able to learn the reasoning process, starting with > 1.5B parameters.

Industry observers note that TRL supports Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) through a dedicated GRPOTrainer for aligning LLMs from preference data, as described in DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. The GRPOTrainer is a subclass of the Trainer from the transformers library and supports all the same features, including logging, checkpointing, distributed training, and parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

Sources indicate that the GRPOTrainer supports generic Outcome Reward Models (ORM) and custom reward functions, that can be used to implement Rule-Based Reward Models. In the Deepseek R1 paper they implemented Rule-Based Reward Models to verify the correctness of the generated solutions. In our exmaple we are going to do a similar approach, where we will create 2 reward functions that:.

Note: Correct in our example includes the equation, for example 55 + 36 - 7 - 19.

It has been revealed that hugging Face TRL added support for distributed training with Deepspeed and using vLLM for faster generation. I preprared a run_r1_grpo.py script and a receipes/grpo-qwen-2.5-3b-deepseek-r1-countdown.yaml config file to run the training.

According to recent reports, this configuration is tested and validated on a Node with 4x H100 80GBs, where a single step takes around 45-60s, as we can leverage vLLM for generation and DeepSpeed for distributed training. Therefore we need to make sure we correctly set the num_processes to the number of GPUs you have - 1 as the last one will be used with vLLM for Generation. If you are using more GPUS you need to change the vllm_device in the config file to last index GPU, e.g. if you have 8 GPUs you need to set vllm_device=7 and your num_processes to 7.

According to recent reports, with the optimized distributed training a single step with 8 generations per sample on 4x H100 80GBs takes around 45-60s. The full training for 450 steps takes around 6 hours.

The script saves random completions to the completion_samples folder, which you can use to inspect the model's progress. It includes completion_samples.txt and success_completion_samples.txt. The completion_samples.txt includes all completions, while the success_completion_samples.txt which correctly solves the equation. Below you can find the interesating training obeserations on how the performance changes over time, as well as the Tensornoard logs and successfull reasoning samples.

The model with checkpoints for every 25th step can be found at philschmid/qwen-2.5-3b-r1-countdown.

Industry observers note that I started the experiment using the hyperparameters from the DeepSeekMath paper with a learning rate of 1e-6 and a beta (KL coefficient) of 0.04, which led to unstable training runs after around 150 steps. I ran some small ablations and decreased both the learning rate to 5e-7 and the beta to 0.001, based on a test from OpenRLHF. I coulnd't test how increasing the num_generations from 8 to 64 would affect the training. 64 is the generation value, which was used in the DeepSeekMath paper. All other parameters can be found in the grpo-qwen-2.5-3b-deepseek-r1-countdown.yaml config file.

I have 3 potential assumptions why the model shifts from "word reasoning" to "programmatic execution":.

The release of DeepSeek R1 and its research paper might be a breakpoint for open-science and open-source development. Just a week after the DeepSeek release, we've been able to reproduce a simple version of R1 learned "reasoning" using GRPO and the Countdown Game. While our implementation focuses on a specific task rather than general reasoning and convergence into a very specific "reasoning" format, it indicates that the method is working.

In a recent development, looking in to 2025, it's clear that we are on the cusp of even more significant progress. RL will become more accessible and user-friendly, more researchers and developers will explore its potential, but also require amount of more compute as before and compared to supervised fine-tuning.

I am excited for 2025. If you have any questions or ideas, feel free to reach out to me.

If this sounds interesting, we’d love your help! Whether it’s contributing code, joining discussions on Hugging Face.

#173873. Latest Update: China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes

Latest Update: China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors, as U.S.
  • More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers declared major expansion plans in the first half of 2026.
  • It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors, as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require.

More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers declared major expansion plans in the first half of 2026. Three recent reports from HSBC and J.P. Morgan suggest the shortages could extend to products as unglamorous as drill bits and copper foil. Having a plentiful and regular supply of those components in the manufacturing process is key because the tiny drill bit used to make the circuit boards inside AI servers could be worn out after drilling fewer than 200 holes, according to HSBC, compared with around 2,000 holes for older materials.

It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components.

It has been revealed that PCBs are built by layering copper and insulating material together, then drilling holes through them to connect their circuits. But the complexity of those boards is increasing as AI servers are designed to handle more data, including more layers than those seen in ordinary computers. HSBC estimates that a notebook PCB has four to eight layers, compared with more than 20 for Nvidia's H100 generation of GPUs.

But that’s just the beginning of the process. Analysts at the bank forecast that a backplane in Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra systems could contain 78 layers. Nor is the Rubin Ultra an outlier in that process: the bank also forecasts a 36% annual rise in the number of holes required per board between 2025 and 2028. The holes themselves are becoming more challenging to drill. According to a report by Taiwanese brokerage KGI Securities, the ratio between the depth of the hole and its diameter has increased from around 20:1 to 30:1 or 40:1. That requires pushing an extremely thin drill bit deeper into increasingly tough materials without bending or breaking it, or damaging the delicate circuitry, which can easily happen in such a sophisticated manufacturing process.

As well as the number of layers which have to be drilled through increasing in number, the materials involved are also adding complexity to the equation. Newly introduced grades of copper-clad laminate — the glass-fibre-and-resin material onto which copper is bonded — are becoming trickier for the tiny tungsten-carbide tools previously used in the process to cut. “AI PCBs are denser with thicker layers, requiring more holes drilled per PCB,” writes Helen Fang, head of Asia Pacific industrials research at HSBC. The increasingly common use of harder laminates is resulting in the bits being consumed more quickly.

That’s good news for those making drill bits: HSBC forecasts global demand growing 55% a year in the coming three years. And as with many parts of the AI revolution, the voracious appetite of the sector means that supplies can’t keep up. Even with manufacturers increasing production, the bank forecasts a 24% supply shortfall in PCB drill bits in 2027.

That could push the world towards Chinese suppliers, right as the west is trying to wean itself off a dependency on the country for rare earths and other elements necessary to make GPUs. Guangdong Dtech, based in China, is the world’s largest PCB drill bit maker by volume. Around three in every 10 drill bits made in 2025 come from the firm, with its monthly capacity potentially climbing from 160 million bits in June to more than 235 million by year-end. Japanese and Taiwanese manufacturers are still dominant at the premium end of the market, according to consultancy Frost & Sullivan, though Chinese manufacturers are trying to close that gap.

Sources indicate that in its 2026 interim results, Dtech reported that it had begun mass-producing drill bits with aspect ratios exceeding 40:1, while developing techniques for producing bits exceeding 60:1. Its newer diamond-coated tools for particularly tough M9+ board materials have also entered small-scale use.

It’s not just in drill bits that China has a chokehold. Another Chinese manufacturer, Defu Technology, has historically been a key supplier of copper foil for lithium-ion batteries, but is increasingly changing its manufacturing processes to try and capitalise on the AI boom. “AI server PCB/CCL upgrades require smoother HVLP copper foil to reduce high-speed signal loss,” writes Avery Chan, a JP Morgan analyst.

HVLP stands for hyper-very-low-profile copper foil, and its manufacturers must make the surface smooth enough to minimise signal loss while making sure it can still stick to the insulating material it is attached to.

The business has historically been dominated by suppliers outside mainland China, with Japan’s Mitsui Kinzoku and Furukawa Electric, and Taiwan’s Co-Tech, holding more than 60% of global HVLP supply in 2025. Defu is trying to break in to disrupt that, with the firm shipping around 700 tonnes of HVLP foil in September, including more than 180 tonnes of HVLP4. JP Morgan’s Chan forecasts a shortage of qualified HVLP4 supply of around 700 tonnes a month in 2026, rising to 1,200 tonnes in 2027. Defu plans to add 50,000 tonnes of annual high-end PCB foil capacity over 2027 and 2028. But all the foil it creates will have to get past stringent testing.

Even before finished chips reach a server, they must be tested using specialist probe cards and sockets, which themselves rely on sophisticated PCBs of a type not found in a server but just used to check whether the chips work. “PCB is becoming the bottleneck and the value-add in probe cards,” wrote JP Morgan analyst Jerry Tsai.

Industry observers note that because of that, China is focusing attention there, too. In September, its Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and National Development and Reform Commission published a five-year plan calling for advances in high-frequency, high-speed and densely layered PCBs, alongside copper-clad laminates, low-profile copper foil and specialist manufacturing equipment.

But China won’t see the benefits of building new factories immediately. Producing the most sophisticated PCBs requires experience, specialist equipment and the ability to manufacture complex designs consistently at scale. Tsai warned that “the learning curve is measured in years, rather than quarters.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It should serve both as an revision on the project and as a collection of interesting resources around DeepSeek-R1.
  • In a recent development, let’s start by looking at the progress we made on Open-R1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s been two weeks since the release of DeepSeek R1 and just a week since we started the open-r1 project to replicate the missing pieces, namely the training pipeline and the synthetic data. This post summarizes:.

It should serve both as an revision on the project and as a collection of interesting resources around DeepSeek-R1.

In a recent development, let’s start by looking at the progress we made on Open-R1. We started Open-R1 just one week ago and people across the teams as well as the community came together to work on it and we have some progress to report.

The first step in reproduction is to verify that we can match the evaluation scores. We are able to reproduce Deepseek's reported results on the MATH-500 Benchmark:.

You can find the instructions to run these evaluations in the open-r1 repository.

One observation we have made is the enormous size of the generations from the DeepSeek models, which makes even evaluating the model challenging. Here we show DeepSeek-R1 response lengths in the OpenThoughts dataset:.

Distribution of R1’s responses demonstrates that they are on average very long with the average response being 6,000 tokens long and some responses containing more than 20,000 tokens. Worth noting that the average page contains ~500 words and one token is on average slightly less than a word, which means the many reponses are over 10 pages long. (src: https://x.com/gui_penedo/status/1884953463051649052).

The length of responses will make GPRO training challenging, as we will have to generate long completions which will require a significant proportion of GPU memory to store the activations / gradients for the optimization step.

In order to share our progress publicly, we have created an open-r1 evaluation leaderboard, so the community can follow our reproduction efforts (space is here):.

According to recent reports, following the release of Open R1, GRPO (Grouped Relative Policy Optimization) was integrated into the latest TRL release (version 0.14). This integration enables training any model with one or multiple reward functions or models. The GRPO implementation integrates with DeepSpeed ZeRO 1/2/3 for parallelized training that scales to many GPUs, and uses vLLM for fast generation, which is the primary bottleneck in online training methods.

There are still some limitations relating to the use of high memory usage, and progress is being made to profile and reduce them.

One of the most exciting findings of the R1 report was that the main model can be used to generate synthetic reasoning traces and smaller models fine-tuned on this dataset see similar performance gains as the main model. So naturally we want to re-create the synthetic reasoning dataset as well such that the community can fine-tune other models on it.

Industry observers note that with a model as major as R1 the main challenge is scaling up generation efficiently and fast. We spent a week tinkering with various setups and configurations.

The model fits on two 8xH100 nodes so naturally we started experimenting with that setup and used vLLM as inference server. However, we promptly noticed that this configuration is not ideal: the throughput is sub-optimal and only allows for 8 parallel request, because the GPU KV cache fills up too quickly. What happens when the cache fills up ist that the requests which use a lot of cache are preempted and if the config uses PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE the requests are scheduled again later when more VRAM is available.

We then switched to a setup with 4x 8xH100 nodes, so 32 GPUs in total. This leaves enough spare VRAM for 32 requests running in parallel with barely any of them getting rescheduled due to 100% cache utilization.

Originally we started querying the vLLM servers with batches of requests but noticed promptly, that straggles in the batches would cause the GPU utiliziation to vary since a latest batch would only start processing once the last sample of the previous batch is done. Switching the batched inference to streaming helped stabilize the GPU utilization significantly:.

Industry observers note that it only required changing the code sending requests to the vLLM servers. The code for batched inference:.

The fresh code for streaming requests:.

We are generating at a fairly constant rate but might still explore a bit further if for example switching to the CPU cache is a better strategy when long queries get preempted.

The current inference code can be found here.

After a relatively calm first week post-release, the second week saw significant market reactions, prompting responses from multiple AI research labs:.

TL;DR the numbers seem generally in the right order of magnitude, as seen in these discussions:.

As many groups are working on reproducing the training pipeline, we’ll get more evidence on the possible training efficiency for the model.

Last week some speculations surfaced that DeepSeek might have been using OpenAI outputs to train its models. See for example the Financial Times. However, it is unclear at this point what the consequences of these allegations will be.

The open source community has been extremely active around DeepSeek-R1 and many people started building interesting projects around the model.

There have been a number of projects that try to reproduce the basic learning mechanics at smaller scale, so you can test the basic learning principles at home.

The community has been busy on a number of dataset efforts related to R1, some highlights include:.

This list only covers a small number of reasoning and problem solving related datasets on the Hub. We’re excited to see what other datasets the community build in the coming weeks.

Show, Don't Certify: How to Prepare for Your First Data Analyst Job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show.
  • Sources indicate that many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show. This strategy breaks preparation into eight skill areas, pairs each one with a learning option and a hands-on task, and gives you a simple test for knowing when to move on.

Sources indicate that many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews. Their CVs list SQL, Excel and Tableau, yet nothing on the page reveals those tools being used to answer a real question. Recruiters reading dozens of similar applications need something more concrete.

A course can give your learning a sensible order, but a completion badge says little about how you think. A small analysis that states its question, explains its method and admits its limits tells a hiring manager far more. This plan aims to collect that kind of proof while you learn, not after.

In a recent development, start by collecting ten to twenty entry-level postings in the industry you want to join, and tally the tools and tasks they mention. You will rapidly see a pattern. Some roles are built around Excel and routine reporting, while others want SQL, a BI platform and a bit of Python.

Industry observers note that the wider market follows a similar shape. Jobright’s 2026 analysis of data analyst hiring, which looked at 2025–2026 postings from LinkedIn, Indeed and Levels.fyi, found that more than 80% of data analyst jobs mention SQL, over 60% mention Excel or Google Sheets, and roughly half mention Python or R. Let your own tally decide the order you learn in, but expect SQL to sit near the top.

According to recent reports, as you work through each area below, finish with something you can show someone: a query, a tidied dataset, a chart, a one-page report or a portfolio project. Free material is often enough if you can stay disciplined. Pay for teaching only when it gives you something you cannot get alone, such as feedback, accountability or a fixed timetable.

Industry observers note that SQL is how analysts pull, join and summarise records from a database, and a tool like Tableau lets other people explore what you found. Treat them as one workflow rather than two subjects: frame a question, write the query, sanity-check the numbers and present the result so a non-technical reader can follow it.

SQLBolt offers free, bite-sized SQL lessons that run in the browser, and Tableau publishes free training videos on connecting to data and building dashboards. Used together, they are enough to produce a small end-to-end project.

If you learn better with a set schedule and an instructor checking your work, you could learn to analyse data with SQL and Tableau from scratch through a guided programme at Heicoders Academy in Singapore. Whichever route you take, compare what is covered, how feedback is given, when sessions run and the full cost against what free resources already offer.

Proof you can show: A working SQL query set and your first published dashboard.

Move on when: You can take a question from idea to dashboard on your own, without following a tutorial line by line.

According to recent reports, spreadsheets are still where much of a team’s day-to-day reporting lives, especially when colleagues don’t write SQL. Get comfortable with filtering, pivot tables, and lookup functions, and learn to spot quiet errors like dates saved as text or one category spelled three different ways.

The next step is automating the cleanup so it doesn’t have to be repeated by hand each month. Microsoft’s Power Query documentation demonstrates how to import and reshape data in recorded steps that refresh when newly introduced data arrives. The same ideas apply in other spreadsheet tools too.

Proof you can show: A messy export turned into a summary that refreshes itself.

Move on when: You can clean an untidy CSV and build a report that updates when the source file changes.

In a recent development, for most junior analyst roles, the technical interview is a SQL test. Basic SELECT statements won’t be enough; interviewers like to probe joins, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions, which answer everyday questions such as running totals or each customer’s first purchase.

Practise with timed problem sets and review your answers for correctness as well as speed.

Proof you can show: Confidence going into a live or take-home SQL test.

Move on when: You can solve intermediate problems in around 15 to 20 minutes each without looking up syntax.

Take-home assignments often come with data that has been made messy on purpose. Reviewers want to see how you deal with missing values, duplicates and inconsistent formats, and whether they can follow your reasoning afterwards.

Keep a short cleaning log as you work, noting each change and why you made it. A separate sheet tab or a list of comments in a notebook both work.

Proof you can show: A take-home submission a reviewer can audit step by step.

Move on when: Every change to your dataset is written down with a reason.

Case-study questions test whether you can read numbers sensibly, not just produce them. A working grasp of distributions, means and medians, spread, correlation and sampling will keep you away from the mistakes that undo otherwise good answers, such as quoting an average that a few extreme values have pulled out of shape.

Proof you can show: Clear, careful answers in case-study interviews.

Move on when: You can explain in everyday language why two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

Every chart should help someone answer a specific question. Learn where bars, lines, scatter plots and simple tables each work best, and how axis ranges, labels and colour can nudge a reader towards the wrong conclusion. On a dashboard, the most crucial finding should be the first thing people see.

According to recent reports, datawrapper’s guidance on picking chart types is a useful free reference. As practice, show the same result in two different chart types and decide which one represents the data more honestly.

Proof you can show: Portfolio charts that make a point, not just show off features.

Move on when: A person who has never seen your data can spot the main finding and its caveat at a glance.

What counts as a useful metric depends on the role. Marketing analysts focus on conversion and retention, operations analysts on delivery times and capacity, and finance analysts on margins and cash flow. Choose one sector and learn exactly how its key measures are defined.

Proof you can show: A project built around the questions your target industry actually asks.

Move on when: You can define several sector metrics and describe how a manager would use each one.

Your portfolio is where the other seven areas come together. Two or three deep, well-documented projects will say more about you than a long list of quick ones. Give each project a README that sets out the question, the data, your method, the findings and the limitations.

Proof you can show: A portfolio link and a write-up you can talk through in an interview.

Move on when: Every project clearly explains what it asked, how you answered it and what you found.

There is no need to finish all eight areas before you apply. Once you can use the tools your target roles mention, speak honestly about your work and point to two or three clearly explained projects, start sending applications and keep learning alongside them.

Industry observers note that adjust each application to the job. Lead with a reporting example for spreadsheet-heavy roles, a query that solved a real problem for SQL roles, and a chart that supported a decision for visualisation roles. Be upfront about which work you built independently and which came from guided exercises.

According to recent reports, do I really need eight courses? No. These are skill areas, not eight required qualifications. A single resource can cover several of them, and practice you do on your own counts as much as classroom learning.

Is it possible to prepare using only free material? Yes. Free tutorials, open textbooks, official documentation and public datasets cover the fundamentals well. The harder parts are sticking to a routine and finding people who will give you honest feedback.

Which should come first, SQL or spreadsheets? It depends on the jobs you want. Spreadsheets are an easy starting point for reporting roles, while SQL is expected wherever databases are involved. You will want both eventually, so start with whichever your target postings stress most.

How many portfolio projects should I have? Two or three solid ones are a good start. Each should show a clear question, steps someone else could repeat and an honest reading of the results, rather than several near-identical dashboards.

It has been revealed that do I need a certificate before I apply? Not usually. Some employers ask for one, but many judge skills through interviews, take-home tasks and tests instead. Go by what each posting actually requires.

#173869. DABStep: Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning

📅 04 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2355 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

DABStep: Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning

📅 04 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Language models are becoming increasingly capable and can solve tasks autonomously as agents.
  • To tackle this challenge, Adyen and Hugging Face built the Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (DABstep) together.
  • Our findings reveal that DABstep presents a significant challenge for current AI models, with the most capable reasoning-based agents achieving only 16% accuracy, highlighting significant progress to be made in the field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models are becoming increasingly capable and can solve tasks autonomously as agents. There are many exciting use cases, especially at the intersection of reasoning, code, and data. However, proper evaluation benchmarks on real-world problems are lacking and hinder progress in the field.

To tackle this challenge, Adyen and Hugging Face built the Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (DABstep) together. DABstep consists of over 450 data analysis tasks designed to evaluate the capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs and AI agents.

Our findings reveal that DABstep presents a significant challenge for current AI models, with the most capable reasoning-based agents achieving only 16% accuracy, highlighting significant progress to be made in the field.

In this blog post, we'll cover the design and construction of the benchmark, explore evaluation results, and discuss the significant gap between current models and the ability to solve complex data analysis tasks effectively.

According to recent reports, data analysis is both an art and a science that requires technical skill, domain knowledge and creativity, and thus, it’s rarely straightforward. Even seasoned data analysts face challenges like:.

According to recent reports, at companies like Adyen, analysts tackle a spectrum of problems, from routine queries to complex workflows requiring creativity, precision, and iterative reasoning. Access to a capable data analysis agent that can automate simple and repetitive tasks and assist with complex tasks would allow analysts to work faster, reduce mental strain, and focus on solving more impactful problems. That would be a pivotal moment for many industries that need data analysis and insights, such as finance.

Recent advancements in agentic workflows — where LLMs equipped with tools independently execute multi-step tasks — have shown tremendous promise across domains like coding, open QA, software engineering, and even Kaggle competitions. These systems aren’t just theoretical; they've been driving real-world productivity gains.

So, the question becomes: Can agentic workflows reshape the way we approach data analysis?

Progress in machine learning is fueled by high quality benchmarks that yield reliable progress signals. Thus, we are excited to introduce the Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (DABstep), a latest benchmark for evaluating and advancing agentic workflows in data analysis.

Here's what makes DABstep unique:.

Sources indicate that how does DABstep achieve all this and remain a simple to run benchmark? Let’s take a look at its design!

DABstep has been designed for low-barrier usage, quality evaluation and increasing difficulty levels. To this end, we are opening up the following items as part of DABstep: Datasets, Tasks, Evals, Real-time Leaderboard and Baselines.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges analysts must overcome, when working on real-world problems, is balancing domain knowledge and technical skills. To this end, DABstep contains both unstructured and structured data to measure domain knowledge and technical skills respectively.

Table 1 shows a snapshot of some of the dataset we are releasing with the benchmark.

Table 1: The benchmark is composed of various datasets across various tasks including the financial payments sector.

It has been revealed that some of the structured datasets include CSV and JSON files representing real-world data, such as transaction telemetry and business metadata (e.g., merchant category codes). Additionally, we have unstructured data such as documentation, lengthy manuals, and detailed handbooks that, for example, are issued by networks, regulators, and processors.

All of these datasets were extracted from real-world tasks at Adyen.

Based on the new datasets included in DABstep, we are releasing several tasks with increasing difficulty levels designed to test an AI agent’s accuracy.

Each task contains the following items:.

In a recent development, none of the tasks can be solved with 1-shot of code; in other words, they cannot be solved by reasoning alone, but rather, they require sequential steps of iterative problem-solving. For example, at the minimum, the agent must at least know what columns exist in the respective dataset to answer a question. This is contrasted with popular benchmarks like GAIA, MATH and SimpleQA, where it's possible to answer multiple questions with 1-shot of code correctly.

Two example tasks are shown in Figure 1, and an example human-made reference solution is shown in Figure 2.

Figure 1: On the left is an example Risk/Fraud question from the Easy Set. Solution requires referencing at least 2 data sources and 3-shots of code. On the right is an example Scheme Fees question from the Hard Set. The solution requires referencing at least 2 data sources and multiple shots of code. The included answers are just for demonstration purposes and are withheld from the dataset.

The benchmark consists of two difficulty levels:.

Industry observers note that as an example of a multi-step reasoning problem, The following code shows a snippet of the human-made reference solution to a Hard Level task. Overall, it is broken down into four(4) sequential steps including the development of various support macros. In order to code this solution, the agent would have to have specific domain knowledge and the ability to work in sequential steps of iterative reasoning.

Figure 2: The 220 line reference solution to a question in the Hard Set: “If the merchant {merchant} had switched its MCC code to {target_mcc} prior to the start of 2023, how much of a difference in fees would they have to pay for the year 2023?” The solution requires multiple steps of inductive reasoning difficult for 1 shot code generation.

Some quick comments on how we are hoping to encourage generalization with the benchmark.

Symbolic Reasoning: In the spirit of GSM-Symbolic, tasks have been exploded in cardinality using permutations of time ranges, merchant names, etc. The rationale is to remove the chance of “lucky guesses” and validate core reasoning (repeatability of reasoning) and generalization.

According to recent reports, hidden Test Set: We have opted not to divide the dataset into validation and test sets and are only releasing a heldout test set. This is because a data analyst agent should be able to generalize across various analysis tasks not per se captured in this benchmark version.

Dev Set: Given this hard generalization setting, the scale of the benchmark (450 questions), and in the spirit of developer friendliness, we have also released a dev set, which is a representative subset of the full test set, including answers. The spirit of this dev set is to allow researchers to configure their E2E submission pipeline locally, including evaluation and fast feedback loops, and then submit to the leaderboard proper.

In a recent development, to test broad generalization, DABstep should not be benchmarked alone, and it should be seen in combination with other benchmarks that test overall generalization and problem-solving (e.g. MMLU, SuperGlue, GPQA).

For simplicity, we have opted for a factoid-based answer evaluation system. This means that answers to benchmark questions should be simple words, numbers or multiple-choice combinations. This allows for unbiased, scaled and model-free evaluations. (This is as opposed to natural language answer submissions evaluated by a judge LLM).

It has been revealed that given that, we didn’t intend answer formatting to be the focus of the benchmark. To that end, we implemented a series of flexible evaluation methods that ensure that the focus remains on the accuracy of the answers rather than their formatting. As examples, we use adaptive tolerance to compare numerical values, allowing for variations in precision and formatting. Strings are normalized and compared using fuzzy matching with a similarity ratio threshold. Lists are evaluated element-wise after normalization.

In a recent development, DABstep features a real-time leaderboard hosted on Hugging Face, where participants can submit their answers to be graded instantly. You can see your standing against others around the globe with instant feedback.

Industry observers note that view of the leaderboard with the best ranked submissions. Link: DABstep Leaderboard.

We are providing a set of baseline evaluations across popular open and closed models.

Sources indicate that figure 3: Performance (on Hard set) across closed and open models/providers. * The Reasoning Models did not work well on the unified ReAct prompt we were using across all chat models, so we had to craft a special Reasoning Prompt. See baseline implementation and prompt details here. We benchmarked the commercial offering of DeepSeek-V3.

From Figure 3 we can see that there is a lot of progress to be made, even with the best agents available not crossing the 20% line.

Recent findings suggest that the best performing agents were based on the latest reasoning models with o3-mini coming out on top at 16% accuracy and R1 coming in at 13%**. The closest chat-based model was Claude Sonnet at 12% the open DeepSeek V3 coming in at 6%.

Industry observers note that one surprising finding was that while instruct models perform well out of the box with a ReAct prompt, reasoning models don’t and achieve 0% accuracy. Common failure modes include poor instruction following, invalid code syntax, closing code blocks (lack of), use tools (improper) and 1-turn dialogs (i.e., no sequential steps). It required multiple iterations on the prompt to get the reasoning models to perform well on this benchmark.

The baselines provided as part of the benchmark are standardized prompts across the chat and reasoning models, and thus, they should be considered non-optimized and a lower bound on performance.

*We had to design a special prompt for the reasoning models because our unified ReAct prompt, although performing excellently on chat models, performed exceptionally poorly on all the reasoning models.

** R1 performance is extrapolated from a sample due to the prolonged outage at the time of this publication.

Additionally, we tracked the cost to run the full benchmark for each commercial offering and compare them in Table 2 below:.

Table 2: Costs for commercial models. Due to subjectivity/variance, we did not include price analysis of open models. Cost/Perf % is explored in Figure 4.

We break down the economics in Figure 4 by looking at the Accuracy vs Cost tradeoff.

Figure 4: Curve w/ performance and cost tradeoff between commercial providers.

Arguably, the economics of DeepSeek R1 are ideal as there is essentially no tradeoff between performance and cost.

Now, let’s have a look at how you can run these benchmarks yourself and evaluate your own models.

We are mindful that doing agentic research by interacting with the benchmark requires an execution environment and involves costs. We are lowering the barrier by providing access to HuggingFace's Inference API and smolagents. With these tools, researchers get 1k free LLM requests daily and access to a secure local code execution environment.

For convenience, we provide an example notebook: a ready-to-go solution for submitting an entry at zero cost (quickstart.ipynb).

By eliminating friction, DABstep ensures that anyone, from seasoned researchers to curious newcomers, can contribute to advancing agentic workflows in data analysis.

We are really excited about the release of DABstep and think it will help test the state of data analysis agents today. However, this release marks just the first step and we plan to evolve the benchmark over time.

At the rate of progress in AI, we foresee that the benchmark will eventually be considered solved in its current state. However, the benchmark is designed to be valid for a longer time by increasing the difficulty in many dimensions. We will be building on the benchmark with full backwards compatibility. Below are some broad avenues on which we will improve the baseline.

Tasks: The current tasks are very narrow and limited in scope, encompassing mostly fraud and payment fees. This is a subset of the real world, as there are many other dimensions and variables at play. In the future, we will expand the same benchmark, including tasks in the area of approval rates (issuer refusals), authentication drop-offs, and real-time situations over a wider time span such as seasonal components. This would test the capacity of agents to balance several variables at the same time and execute trade-offs on multiple dimensions.

Domains: The benchmark at the moment revolves around tasks from the financial sector. However, we invite researchers and practitioners from other fields, such as health, biology, insurance, telecommunication etc. to contribute upcoming subsets to the benchmark so we can evaluate the performance across many domains.

It has been revealed that data scale: The structured data will eventually not be able to fit in memory. They will be analyzed with standard tooling, requiring the analysts to use distributed computing engines or scheduling workflows for later evaluation.

Documentation: The unstructured data that maps the domain knowledge will explode with more files containing time evolution (e.g., bulletins), different formats (e.g., PDF), and also different versions of similar but different logic that map each scheme, acquirer, or partner. The context will reach a step that will logically not fit the current and future token cardinality allowed in the context windows.

Multimodal: Agents should also become multimodal. To this end, we will enhance the benchmark with tasks that require extracting logic by interpreting and creating plots and graphs.

Existing benchmarks for evaluating AI in data analysis have advanced the field and DABstep is built on top of their foundations.

In a recent development, DS Bench evaluates 466 questions from Modeloff competitions, primarily designed for Excel-based workflows. While effective for small-scale tasks, Excel does not support the iterative, code-driven workflows common in real-world data analysis (e.g., Jupyter notebooks). Additionally, reliance on GPT-4 as an evaluator introduces bias and reduces generalizability.

According to recent reports, DS 1000 tests Python-based data analysis tasks sourced from StackOverflow, curated to avoid memorization. However, its tasks are short and single-shot, lacking real datasets and iterative reasoning. This limits its ability to evaluate end-to-end workflows or multimodal capabilities.

Acknowledgments: Harm de Vries (Graidd), Arjun Guha (Northeastern University), Hanna van der Vlis (Adyen).

[^1]: Tasks are realistic, the data has been generated synthetically. The business context (including merchant names, rates, volumes, transaction values, fraud rates, and fees) has been artificially generated and does not reflect the actual performance that businesses might exhibit. For example, fraud rates have been intentionally elevated for the purpose of this exercise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we have ported the first robotics foundation models to Hugging Face LeRobot! Both π0 and π0-FAST, developed by Physical Intelligence, are now available in the LeRobot repository, bringing generalist robotic intelligence to the Hugging Face ecosystem. If you are curious about how Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models differ from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and how actions are represented, dive into this blog post to find out!

Explore the model collection and the PyTorch Version of the model in our repository: Huggingface collection of Pi0 models | Huggingface collection of Pi0+FAST models | LeRobot repo.

Industry observers note that robert Heinlein suggests that a well-rounded person should be capable of handling a wide range of tasks—both intellectual and physical—rather than being narrowly specialized in one field. Drawing a parallel between a well-rounded person and machine intelligence: AI systems vary widely, but human intelligence excels in versatility—adapting to tasks, environments, and surprises. While large language and vision-language models (LLMs, VLMs) show promise, they lack interaction with the physical world. To bridge this gap, we need models trained on robotic data. Generalist robot models can enhance adaptability, using diverse data to improve generalization and robustness. Instead of training on isolated tasks, pre-training on varied robotic data—similar to LLMs—boosts efficiency and performance.

Developing generalist robot policies, or robot foundation models, presents three key challenges:.

The need for large-scale research to fully leverage pre-training benefits.

Designing model architectures that can integrate diverse data sources while capturing complex physical interactions. A key challenge in this regard is cross-embodiment training, where a model must learn from diverse robot types with varying configurations, control spaces, and action representations. Existing approaches tackle this by:.

Crafting an effective training recipe, as recent advances in NLP and vision have heavily relied on careful pre-training and post-training strategies.

In this post, we introduce π0 and π0-FAST, prototype models and learning frameworks developed by Physical Intelligence, designed to overcome these challenges.

π0 (Pi-Zero) is a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, developed by the Physical Intelligence team designed for generalist robot control. It builds upon large-scale pretraining and flow matching-based action generation, enabling robots to perform dexterous manipulation tasks across different embodiments.

π0 is trained on data from 7 robotic platforms and 68 unique tasks, demonstrating strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance on complex, real-world tasks such as laundry folding, table bussing, grocery bagging, box assembly, and object retrieval.

According to recent reports, unlike standard robotic policies, π0 employs flow matching to produce smooth, real-time action trajectories at 50Hz, making it highly efficient, precise, and adaptable for real-world deployment. Flow matching was used in continuous normalizing flows and improved generation quality in diffusion models. The denoising process π0 used works in the same way, starting with a random noise that progressively converges towards a sequence of motor actions that make sense.

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) share a common foundation: transformers. However, the key distinction lies in action representation. While VLMs process and generate multimodal representations (images and text), VLAs extend this by incorporating action and observation state tokens. With these additional tokens in place, the next challenge is understanding how attention is computed.

Let’s expand our vocabulary and introduce key terms:.

They are appended after the prefix portion (images + text), so the prefix serves as context (e.g., a scene image, language instructions like "be a good robot" or "transfer the cube"), while the suffix captures policy‐specific features.

However, efficiently handling attention in π0 comes with its own set of challenges. The unique shape of its attention mask influences how attention is computed—let’s dive into the details!

The resulting 2D causal mask exhibits strong block sparsity, but defining the boundaries of each block—especially in a batch of samples—is a bit tricky. We are used to causal masks with triangular structures for autoregressive modeling, but this is not one of those cases.

As you can see in this example below: the image (first element) has some padding tokens, representing empty cameras. Then, text tokens and state tokens are added. This "prefix" part forms a fully noncausal attention, as in PaliGemma. Then, the "suffix" (state + action/time tokens) has a causal-block structure. The eager naive implementation performs matrix multiplications and applies softmax across the entire input, making it highly inefficient.

Figure 1: The visualization of the VLA attention mask.

In a recent development, this looks like a FlexAttention job! It has a pure PyTorch interface, in which explored two options:.

The current implementation runs, and a WIP is to have it support torch.compile and leverage it to the fullest!

Industry observers note that now that we know actions are simply n-dimensional vectors that can be tokenized, we can explore the challenges of action representation in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The way actions are represented directly impacts efficiency, generalization, and execution fidelity.

Recent findings suggest that one approach is semantic action representation, where actions are described as high-level concepts like sub-tasks or keypoints. While this allows for few-shot and zero-shot learning, it often relies on hand-designed low-level controllers, limiting flexibility across different robots. In contrast, low-level control representations map actions directly to motor commands, enabling precise movements but making training less stable and harder to scale.

Most existing VLAs use discrete action tokenization, converting continuous actions into discrete tokens generated autoregressively. The most common method—per-dimension, per-timestep binning—struggles with high-frequency control tasks, leading to lossy representations and inefficient training. Alternatives like vector quantization (VQ) and time-series compression help, but VQ is sensitive to hyperparameters, making it less reliable for diverse robot designs.

It has been revealed that to address these issues, Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization (FAST) introduces a novel time-series compression approach using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). FAST reduces redundancy, improves efficiency, and enhances action fidelity.

With this, we present π0-FAST, faster and autoregressive version of π0 also available in Lerobot repo, an extension of π0, which leverages this fresh tokenizer for better action representation.

Paper | Jax Code | Our implementation in Lerobot.

π0-FAST is an autoregressive version of π0, introducing **FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization)**—a new tokenization scheme that enhances efficiency and performance.

🔗 The π0-FAST tokenizer can be accessed here: FAST Tokenizer.

🔗 Pretrained weights can be accessed here: Pi0+FAST.

FAST uses the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to compress continuous action sequences into discrete tokens. The process, illustrated in Figure 2, begins with normalizing raw robot actions, mapping the 1st and 99th quantiles of each action dimension to the range [-1,1]. This normalization is used to ensure consistency across different robotic systems and improve robustness against outliers.

Each action dimension is then transformed independently using DCT, converting the time-domain signal into the frequency domain. To reduce redundancy, insignificant coefficients are removed through a scale-and-round operation, where a hyperparameter balances compression rate and reconstruction accuracy. The resulting DCT coefficient matrix, often sparse, is flattened into a one-dimensional sequence of integers, interleaving low-frequency components first across dimensions to preserve critical information.

To further compress the sequence, Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is applied. As usual, BPE merges frequently occurring patterns across dimensions while maintaining a fixed-size vocabulary.

Figure 2: The FAST action tokenization pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that since all operations are invertible, actions can be reconstructed efficiently and losslessly from tokens. The tokenization pipeline has only two hyperparameters: the scaling coefficient applied before rounding and the BPE vocabulary size. Both parameters remain robust across different datasets.

According to recent reports, additionally, a universal version of FAST, called FAST+, has been trained on one million action sequences from single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation robots, making it applicable across diverse robotic setups. FAST+ is available as a Hugging Face AutoProcessor, allowing people to tokenize action sequences with just a few lines of code.

For optimal compression, input actions should be quantile-normalized to [-1,1] before tokenization. With the AutoProcessor module, the consumers can train a custom FAST tokenizer on their own datasets.

🔗 Code for the usage and training custom action tokenizers in the official FAST Repo.

FAST is integrated into Hugging Face Transformers and can be easily used for encoding and decoding robot action sequences.

Industry observers note that with π0 and π0-FAST, we take a significant step towards generalist robot intelligence, bringing scalable, efficient, and versatile Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to LeRobot. By leveraging FAST tokenization, we enhance action representation, enabling robots to perform a diverse range of tasks with higher efficiency and adaptability. These steps open the door for future multi-embodiment, real-time robotic policies, pushing the boundaries of what robots can achieve in the real world. 🚀.

It has been revealed that your accessibility check in CI is green. axe-core ran, zero violations, and the badge in the README looks great. Your site can still fail WCAG 2.2.

Industry observers note that that isn't a bug in axe. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. It added nine success criteria and dropped one (4.1.1 Parsing), and most of the latest ones can't be judged by reading the DOM. Deque mentioned as much when it shipped the first WCAG 2.2 support in axe-core 4.5: the target-size rule would probably be the only new-criterion rule they added, because the others can't be automated without a lot of false positives.

So the rest is on you. This article covers the one criterion axe can check and three it can't (focus not obscured, dragging movements, accessible authentication), with Playwright tests you can drop into a project. I ran all of them against a small test page that fails every criterion on purpose, and against a fixed version of the same page. If you want a plain-language rundown of every change first, WCAG 2.2 vs 2.1 goes through them. Here I only care about what you can put in a pipeline.

Sources indicate that level A and AA are what most contracts and laws point at, so those are the ones that matter first. The AAA criteria are still worth knowing about.

That's four AA criteria with something you can script, one of which axe already handles. The rest of this article goes through those four.

Industry observers note that the AA rule is smaller than most people expect: a pointer target should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or sit far enough from its neighbours that a 24px circle centred on it wouldn't overlap another target or that target's own circle. There are exceptions, including inline links in a sentence, and targets whose size the browser controls.

axe-core has a target-size rule for this. One catch: it isn't part of a default run. In my setup (axe-core 4.14.1 through @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0), a plain analyze() on the broken page reported nothing at all. The rule only demonstrated up once I asked for it:.

Industry observers note that on the broken page this lists the three 16px toolbar buttons by selector. On the fixed page, with 32px buttons, it passes. If you've been running axe for years and never seen a target-size result, this is why.

Some context on how common the problem is. In the scan data behind my last SitePoint article, 34.5% of the 1,025 sites had controls below a stricter 44px threshold. That is a tougher standard than the 24px that AA asks for, so don't read it as "a third of sites fail 2.5.8". Plenty of those would pass. But it does show how many production sites ship tiny controls.

If you'd like a quick look at one page before wiring anything up, browser tools such as axe DevTools, WAVE, or a WCAG checker will show the same thing.

axe can't test it, because you have to press Tab and look at where the browser scrolled. Two details caught me out building this:.

Recent findings suggest that the check below samples a grid of points inside the visible part of the focused element and asks the browser what's on top at each one. If none of the points land on the element or its children, it's covered.

On my broken page it reported nine hits: links hidden behind the footer going forward ("Section 4 link", "Section 10 link", "Section 16 link") and the toolbar buttons and a few links hidden behind the header coming back. The output names the element and the key, which is what you want when you're staring at a failed build.

The fix is one CSS rule, sized to your sticky elements:.

That tells the browser to leave room when it scrolls a focused element into view. With it in place the same test passes.

In a recent development, be aware of what this can't see: a modal that opens over the page, or a chat widget that only appears after a delay, will not show up unless your test opens or waits for them. Adrian Roselli's piece on 2.4.11 and adversarial conformance is worth reading for the awkward cases.

Sources indicate that anything you can do by dragging needs a way to do it with a single click or tap, unless dragging is essential. Sortable lists, sliders, kanban cards, file reorderers: all of them.

You can't prove a drag alternative works from a script. But you can catch the obvious mistake, which is a draggable item with no button anywhere near it:.

The limit is real. It only recognises the native draggable attribute. Libraries built on pointer events, such as dnd-kit, don't set it, so this test will walk right past them. If you use one of those, replace the selector with whatever your component renders, or add a test per drag component. Treat it as a tripwire for the common case, not a verdict.

The fix, in the fixed page, is a pair of "Move up" and "Move down" buttons on each item, each with an accessible name that indicates which item it moves.

This dispatches a synthetic paste event and checks whether anything called preventDefault() on it. It catches the old onpaste="return false" trick, and it catches script-based blockers too. It does not tell you whether your login has a CAPTCHA that needs an alternative, or an emailed one-time code you must retype. Those need a person.

On a pull request, a plain GitHub Actions job is enough:.

Point PAGE_URL at a running preview, and run the tests against the pages that matter most: sign-in, checkout, anything with a sticky element. Don't try to crawl everything on the first pass. A test that fails for reasons nobody owns gets deleted within a month.

Four things I haven't tried to automate, and wouldn't:.

According to recent reports, automation will keep the regressions out. It won't tell you the work is finished. A green build and a conformant site are different things, and WCAG 2.2 widened the gap between them.

The tests and both test pages are small enough to read in one sitting. Copy what's useful, change the selectors, and keep the broken page around: it's a handy way to check that a test fails when it should.

#173861. How to protect your retirement savings if the AI bubble bursts

How to protect your retirement savings if the AI bubble bursts

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that after stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov.
  • After stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov.
  • While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks. Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Here are some basic facts to guide your planning. Many Americans are saving on autopilot Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund, which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s notable to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund. About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion. Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices: U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund, who expect to retire imminently. Tech volatility is forcing new questions That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers, Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4%. Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement initiative on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds have significant tech exposure Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold. And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500, according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund, with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a major impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average. What to check now if you own a target-date fund In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone. The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. But a saver still needs to check three things. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. What to do if you hold other funds About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly. For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund, and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. But the pattern can flip quickly: International stocks gained about 29% in 2025, far ahead of the S&P 500’s 16%. Align your savings to your timeline How much this month’s news matters depends on when you’ll need the money. If you’re decades from retirement, a downturn can work in your favor, because every paycheck contribution buys shares at lower prices. Keep contributing and capture your full employer match. My own research with a colleague has found that accounts on systematic investment plans akin to 401(k)s earned better market-adjusted returns than accounts funded with lump sums. If you’re within 5-10 years of retirement, the bigger danger is what planners call sequence-of-returns risk: A large loss right before or just after you start withdrawing can permanently shrink what your savings can support. A good defense is to hold several years of expected withdrawals in lower-risk assets, such as bonds or money market funds, so you’re never forced to sell stocks after a drop. For retirees, Morningstar’s Christine Benz suggests one to two years of withdrawals in cash and five to eight more in bonds. What not to do The costliest mistake is usually the most tempting: selling everything and waiting for the dust to settle. During the 2008-09 financial crisis, about 117,000 Fidelity 401(k) participants moved entirely out of stocks. Those who stayed out saw their balances grow just 2% by mid-2011, while those who kept some stock exposure saw balances rise 50% on average. Other moves to avoid include stopping your own 401(k) contributions, chasing whatever theme looks safe this month, and pulling money out early, which can mean taxes, penalties and a locked-in loss. Last, don’t hand the decision to a chatbot. It will likely give you sound general guidance, such as diversifying and not panic-selling, and that consensus advice is where AI is reliable. But it is weakest on high-stakes questions that turn on your own situation.
