According to recent reports, AI companions are the most demanding consumer use of large language models right now. A coding assistant can forget your last message and still be useful. A companion that forgets your name, your running story, or the blueprint you made last Tuesday has failed at its one job. On top of that, customers now expect voice calls that feel like a phone conversation, not a walkie-talkie exchange with a five-second pause.

Three engineering problems decide whether a companion app works: how much of the conversation fits in the model's context window, what the app remembers once the window fills up, and how fast the voice pipeline answers. Here is how consumer companions handle each one, with real tier and pricing examples, and what developers can take from their designs for their own products.

Recent findings suggest that most LLM products are judged on single answers. Companions are judged on continuity. That creates pressure in three places at once:.

Every consumer companion is a different set of trade-offs across those three constraints, and the trade-offs are increasingly how the apps are priced.

Industry observers note that the context window is the total number of tokens the model can see when it writes the next reply. In a companion app, that budget is spent before the user notes anything:.

According to recent reports, when the chat log outgrows what is left, the oldest messages fall out. The user experiences this as the companion "forgetting" mid-conversation. This is why context size is now a headline spec in the category, and a paid feature. SpicyChat AI, for example, gives free accounts a 4K context window, then scales memory to 8K on its $19.95/mo tier and 32K on its $29.95/mo tier. Janitor AI runs about 9K of context on its own JanitorLLM. Independent uncensored AI chat benchmarks record these context sizes alongside refusal behavior and pricing, because context length predicts how long a roleplay stays coherent better than any marketing claim.

According to recent reports, some apps sell memory in messages rather than tokens. Fantasy GF's pricing page lists a 60-message base "smart memory" and 5x that, 300 messages, on its Ultra plan. Others sell it as a memory multiplier on higher subscription tiers. The pattern is consistent across the category: memory depth is the upgrade lever, not the model itself.

In a recent development, no consumer app keeps an entire relationship in the prompt. Persistent memory is a separate system that writes to storage and reads back into the context window on each turn. In practice it has three layers:.

The differences users notice are usually retention policies, not algorithms. Crushon AI's own subscription docs say free-strategy chat history is deleted after 7 days of inactivity, while paid intends keep it for the membership period. Paid tiers across the category commonly promise that memories never expire. There is also a security angle worth stating plainly: companion chat logs are among the most sensitive data a consumer product can hold. A 2024 breach at Muah.ai, first reported by 404 Media, exposed roughly 1.9 million users' email addresses together with their private prompts. Any app that builds persistent memory is also building a liability, and developers copying the pattern should treat the memory store as the most protected part of the system.

It has been revealed that A voice call in a companion app is three models chained together: speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech. Run them strictly in sequence and a single reply can take several seconds, which reads as dead air. The apps that feel fast attack each stage the same way:.

Industry observers note that with every stage streaming, time-to-first-audio can land close to a second on a good connection, which is roughly the threshold where a conversation stops feeling laggy. Voice is also expensive to run - three model calls instead of one, plus audio bandwidth - which is why it is metered harder than text. Fantasy GF charges 8 tokens per minute for voice calls (4 on Ultra), which turns the 100 monthly tokens on its entry plan into about 12 minutes of call time. SpicyChat, for its part, only adds text-to-speech at its top tier. Latency engineering and unit economics are the same problem here: faster pipelines cost less per call, and cheaper calls are what make voice viable below the top plan.

Tier details below come from each app's own pricing or documentation pages, checked November 16, 2026, and cross-checked against il.ly's AI companion testing guide, which hands-tests 15 companion apps across memory, media, and voice.

It has been revealed that two takeaways from the table. First, nobody sells a bigger base model - they sell a bigger window into the same one. Second, the free tiers are deliberately memory-poor: limited context and short retention are the upgrade prompt.

Even if you never build a companion, these apps are a useful reference architecture for any stateful LLM product:.

Consumer AI companions have turned three hard infrastructure problems - bounded context, durable memory, and real-time voice - into their pricing pages. Context size, memory depth, and voice access are the tiers. If you are building anything stateful on an LLM, this category is worth watching closely: it is solving continuity and latency problems at consumer scale, in public, one subscription tier at a time.

It is the total amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider when writing its next reply. The character definition, stored memories, recent chat, and the fresh message all share that budget. When the conversation exceeds it, the oldest content drops out and the companion appears to forget.

Recent findings suggest that yes, through a memory system separate from the context window. Apps summarize older chats, extract stable facts about you into a profile, and retrieve relevant past moments into the prompt. Retention varies: some free tiers delete chat history after as little as 7 days of inactivity, while paid aims typically keep memory for the membership period.

A voice turn runs three models - speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech - instead of one, plus audio transfer. Providers pass that cost on through per-minute token charges or by locking voice behind higher tiers.

For casual chat, 4K to 9K tokens works. For long-running roleplay or a companion expected to hold plot threads for weeks, 32K and up, or a well-built memory layer on top of a smaller window, makes the visible difference.

Tech Report: Open R1: Update #2

📅 10 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are now two weeks into the Open R1 project which aims to reconstruct the missing pieces of DeepSeek R1—specifically, the training pipeline and synthetic data.
  • In this post, we are happy to share the construction of OpenR1-Math-220k: our first large-scale dataset for mathematical reasoning!
  • We also take a look at some exciting developments from the community towards curating small, high-quality datasets for fine-tuning, along with insights into how to control the length of the chain-of-thought from reasoning models at both train-time and inference-time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are now two weeks into the Open R1 project which aims to reconstruct the missing pieces of DeepSeek R1—specifically, the training pipeline and synthetic data.

In this post, we are happy to share the construction of OpenR1-Math-220k: our first large-scale dataset for mathematical reasoning!

We also take a look at some exciting developments from the community towards curating small, high-quality datasets for fine-tuning, along with insights into how to control the length of the chain-of-thought from reasoning models at both train-time and inference-time.

One of the key advantages of DeepSeek R1 is its ability to transfer advanced reasoning capabilities to smaller models through distillation. The DeepSeek team demonstrated this by generating 600k reasoning traces and fine-tuning a series of Qwen and Llama models, showing that direct distillation from R1 can achieve competitive reasoning performance without reinforcement learning. Notably, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B achieved 55.5% on AIME 2024, surpassing larger models like QwQ-32B-Preview.

Recent findings suggest that however, the reasoning traces used for distillation have not been released publicly, prompting the community to independently recreate similar datasets. So far, multiple open datasets have been released by the community, including OpenThoughts-114k, Bespoke-Stratos-17k, Dolphin-R1, and LIMO.

🐳  Introducing OpenR1-Math-220k, a large-scale math reasoning dataset generated locally on 512 H100s, with multiple answers per problem. To create OpenR1-Math-220k, we collaborated with Numina who have developed a brand upcoming version of their popular NuminaMath-CoT dataset.

What’s latest in OpenR1 dataset compared to existing datasets:.

By demonstrating scalable, high-quality reasoning data generation, we hope this pipeline can be extended beyond math to domains like code generation.

To build OpenR1-220k, we prompt DeepSeek R1 to generate solutions for 400k problems from NuminaMath 1.5. We follow the model card’s recommended parameters and prepend the following instruction to the user prompt:.

"Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.".

In a recent development, we set a 16k token limit per generation, as our analysis revealed that only 75% of problems could be solved in under 8k tokens, and most of the remaining problems required the full 16k tokens. Initially, we used vLLM for inference, achieving a throughput of 15 generations per hour per H100, and shared our generation scripts in previous updates and on the OpenR1 repo. Recently, we started experimenting with SGLang and we were able to generate 25 solutions per hour per H100 (almost 2x speedup!), enabling us to generate 300k problem solutions per day on 512 H100s. This allowed us to produce 800k reasoning traces in just a few days.

We generate two solutions per problem—and in some cases, four—to provide flexibility in filtering and training. This approach allows for rejection sampling, similar to DeepSeek R1’s methodology, and also makes the dataset suitable for preference optimisation methods like DPO.

The scripts for the data generation are available here: https://github.com/huggingface/open-r1/tree/main/slurm.

The unfiltered dataset is available here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-r1/OpenR1-Math-Raw.

According to recent reports, to retain only high-quality, correct reasoning traces, we leverage Math Verify, a robust mathematical expression evaluation system designed to assess LLM-generated answers. We extract the final answers from model generations and compare them against ground truth answers in the dataset.

Sources indicate that we find that 55% of problems have at least one correct answer. However, some ground truth answers in NuminaMath 1.5 were empty or not in a verifiable format, making automatic validation challenging. While we have improved Math-Verify to more accurately handle these more uncommon output formats (see Math-Verify improvements below), we also explored an alternative method to recover valid solutions from rejected samples: using Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct as a judge on a subset of rejected problems. Before running this verification step, we filter out samples that are incomplete or that contain an empty ground truth answer, ensuring that only well-formed responses with a clearly boxed final answer are considered. This process successfully retrieves 28,000 of previously rejected problems.

We prompt Llama3.3-70B-Instruct as follows:.

By combining rule-based verification (Math Verify) with LLM-based evaluation, we improve dataset quality while maintaining scale. The final dataset consists of 220k problems with verified reasoning traces, making it a valuable resource for training reasoning models. Providing multiple solutions per problem gives the community flexibility to filter for better generations and apply more targeted refinements based on NuminaMath data sources and problem types.

The dataset is available in two splits:.

For rows with multiple correct answers, we also tried applying a Reward Model (RM) as a final filter to select the best response. For each row with multiple correct generations by R1, we extracted the final answer by removing the thinking tokens (…), and then pass the problem + the extracted answer to Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-RM-72B served using vLLM to get an score. Using these scores, we built a ranking for each row containing more than one correct response. The top-1 correct generations were selected and included in the training dataset, but sadly the training ablations demonstrated that this approach doesn’t help to improve model performance with respect to selecting one random correct generation. A possible improvement could be to include the reasoning trace rather than just the final answer when scoring with the RM.

It has been revealed that we fine-tune Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct for 3 epochs on the default split of the dataset using a learning rate of 5e-5. To extend the context length from 4k to 32k, we increase RoPE frequency to 300k. The training follows a linear learning rate schedule with a 10% warmup phase. The table below compares the performance of OpenR1-Qwen-7B to DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B and OpenThinker-7B using lighteval.

This dataset represents an initial version, providing a foundation for further refinement. The community can explore additional filtering strategies to improve performance, such as rejection sampling, which was used in DeepSeek R1 to enhance quality.

We identified several failure cases in Math-Verify during our inspection of the verification results. To address these challenges, we implemented significant improvements and fixes. We strongly recommend updating to the latest version (0.5.2) to benefit from these enhancements:.

The following is the summary of the most important improvements:.

This week saw the community explore GRPO from many different angles, while multiple research labs have shown that only ~1000 high quality training samples may be sufficient to elicit reasoning in existing open models.

The first part of the AIME 2025 was released this week, which consists of 15 difficult math problems that are used to train high school students for the International Math Olympiad. In the past year, AIME 2024 has stood as the main benchmark to probe the mathematical capabilities of LLMs and the community was excited to see how well models performs on a new set of unseen problems:.

Industry observers note that an interesting upcoming research paper demonstrates that by using a recurrent language model, it is possible to scale test-time compute by implicitly reasoning in latent space. This resembles Meta’s Coconut work to train language models in latent space, but now adapted to reasoning tasks. The advantage of these methods is that they are far more compute efficient: by exploring the latent, one does not need to generate huge amounts of “thinking” tokens to obtain high performance.

While DeepSeek R1 leveraged 600k reasoning traces for distillation, recent work suggests that complex reasoning can emerge in language models not through massive-scale training, but through a small number of carefully curated samples.

One example of this approach is the s1K dataset. It consists of 1,000 carefully selected math questions with distilled reasoning traces from Gemini Flash. The selection approach focuses on difficulty, diversity, and quality. The authors fine-tune Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on s1K and manage to exceed OpenAI’s o1-preview on competition math benchmarks by up to 27%.

It has been revealed that another dataset, LIMO, pushes this idea further, achieving strong performance on AIME and MATH benchmarks using only 817 training samples. The authors hypothesize that when a model has already acquired extensive domain knowledge during pre-training, only a small number of well-structured examples may be needed to unlock advanced reasoning capabilities.

One crucial ingredient allowing the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model from s1K to reach such strong performance is budget forcing, a test-time compute technique that either extends or truncates reasoning by appending “Wait” or an end-of-thinking token delimiter to the model’s generation, respectively. This tool allowed the authors to vary thinking time and conclude that their model exhibits test-time scaling: as thinking time increases, so does accuracy on different math benchmarks.

According to recent reports, similarly, Demystifying Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs (Yeo et al.) also studies the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) length on model performance. They introduce the Cosine Reward — a novel reward function that they use to incentivize shorter CoTs for correct generations and longer CoTs for wrong generations — which stabilizes RL training, particularly when the model has relatively limited max context size and average response length could explode. Repetition penalty is also employed when the model starts to show signs of reward hacking on hard questions, by artificially increasing CoT length through repetition instead of attempting to solve the problem.

In a recent development, now that GRPO is humming in TRL, we are running an extensive set of experiments to understand which hyperparameters and reward functions have the greatest impact on training. You can follow our progress in the community tab and will write up our findings in the next upgrade!

If you want to contribute check out the open-r1 repository on GitHub or follow the Hugging Face open-r1 org.

Built around an aluminium case with squared edges and a cool metallic finish, Ear (note) introduces machined metal and brutalist forms into Nothing’s transparent design language. Clear windows are inspired by the contours of topographic maps, revealing depth and dimensionality within the case. The TALK button and a new RECORD button draw on the controls on a retro Walkman, both positioned to be easy to reach and to provide tactile feedback when activated.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Nothing has confirmed that its new AI product is “Ear (note).” This builds on a pair of earbuds by turning the charging case into an AI-powered recorder.

The case has a “Talk” button, like Ear (3), which can be used to record your own voice, where a record button enables the ability to “record and transcribe conversations.” Ear (3a)’s ability to record audio from the earbuds will also carry over to Ear (note), giving the product the ability to record both conversations in person and over the phone.

Nothing is entering a crowded market here with products from Plaud, Amazon, and countless others already offering AI recording/transcribing products, but building in earbuds is indeed a unique selling point.

According to recent reports, nothing Ear (note) is launching on December 8, though pricing is unclear. Pei’s comments suggest a subscription will be used in some capacity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tooling for image generation datasets is well established, with img2dataset being a fundamental tool used for large scale dataset preparation, and complemented with various community guides, scripts and UIs that cover smaller scale initiatives.
  • Our ambition is to make tooling for video generation datasets equally established, by creating open video dataset scripts suited for small scale, and leveraging video2dataset for large scale use cases.
  • “If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(This post was authored by hlky and Sayak).

Tooling for image generation datasets is well established, with img2dataset being a fundamental tool used for large scale dataset preparation, and complemented with various community guides, scripts and UIs that cover smaller scale initiatives.

Our ambition is to make tooling for video generation datasets equally established, by creating open video dataset scripts suited for small scale, and leveraging video2dataset for large scale use cases.

“If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants”.

Industry observers note that in this post, we provide an overview of the tooling we are developing to make it easy for the community to build their own datasets for fine-tuning video generation models. If you cannot wait to get started already, we welcome you to check out the codebase here.

Typically, video generation is conditioned on natural language text prompts such as: "A cat walks on the grass, realistic style". Then in a video, there are a number of qualitative aspects for controllability and filtering, like so:.

Sources indicate that video generation models are only as good as the data they are trained on. Therefore, these aspects become crucial when curating the datasets for training/fine-tuning.

Our 3 stage pipeline draws inspiration from works like Stable Video Diffusion, LTX-Video, and their data pipelines.

Like video2dataset we opt to use yt-dlp for downloading videos.

We create a script Video to Scenes to split long videos into short clips.

In a recent development, florence-2 microsoft/Florence-2-large to run Florence-2 tasks , , and on extracted frames. This provides different captions, object recognition and OCR that can be used for filtering in various ways.

Sources indicate that we can bring in any other captioner in this regard. We can also caption the entire video (e.g., with a model like Qwen2.5) as opposed to captioning individual frames.

In a recent development, in the dataset for the model finetrainers/crush-smol-v0, we opted for captions from Qwen2VL and we filtered on pwatermark < 0.1 and aesthetic > 5.5. This highly restrictive filtering resulted in 47 videos out of 1493 total.

Let's review the example frames from pwatermark -.

Two with text have scores of 0.69 and 0.61.

The "toy car with a bunch of mice in it" scores 0.60 then 0.17 as the toy car is crushed.

All example frames were filtered by pwatermark < 0.1. pwatermark is effective at detecting text/watermarks however the score gives no indication whether it is a text overlay or a toy car's license plate. Our filtering required all scores to be below the threshold, an average across frames would be a more effective strategy for pwatermark with a threshold of around 0.2 - 0.3.

Let's review the example frames from aesthetic scores -.

The pink castle initially scores 5.5 then 4.44 as it is crushed.

The action figure scores lower at 4.99 dropping to 4.84 as it is crushed.

The shard of glass scores low at 4.04.

In our filtering we required all scores to be below the threshold, in this case using the aesthetic score from the first frame only would be a more effective strategy.

Industry observers note that if we review finetrainers/crush-smol we can notice that many of the objects being crushed are round or rectangular and colorful which is similar to our findings in the example frames. Aesthetic scores can be useful yet have a bias that will potentially filter out good data when used with extreme thresholds like > 5.5. It may be more effective as a filter for bad content than good with a minimum threshold of around 4.25 - 4.5.

Here we provide some visual examples for each filter as well as the captions from Florence-2.

We have created various datasets with the tooling in an attempt to generate cool video effects, similar to the Pika Effects:.

In a recent development, we then used these datasets to fine-tune the CogVideoX-5B model using finetrainers. Below is an example output from finetrainers/crush-smol-v0:.

It has been revealed that we hope this tooling gives you a headstart to create small and high-quality video datasets for your own custom applications. We will continue to add more useful filters to the repository, so, please keep an eye out. Your contributions are also more than welcome 🤗.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • When one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run. On one RTX 3090 with the same model file, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp wrote text within about 10 percent of each other, because all three run llama.cpp underneath. That changes when your app sends several requests at once. With four requests, the best setup produced more than three times as much text as the worst, and the cause was a default setting, not the engine. With 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times as much text as the best llama.cpp setup I tested.

This article puts those numbers side by side and highlights which setting to change for your app.

According to recent reports, I ran every test on one machine. The full write-ups, with every command and the raw results, are on homebrewserver.club.

Every server got the same requests:.

Recent findings suggest that ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp loaded the exact same GGUF files, checked by SHA-256. vLLM cannot run GGUF files well, so it loaded a 4-bit AWQ file of the same model (9.1 GB). Answer quality was not compared.

According to recent reports, the tests ran between 8 and 16 November 2026, and speeds on this machine varied by a few percent from one day to the next. Treat a gap under about 5% as a tie. All of this is one consumer GPU and one model family, so read the numbers as a guide to how the servers behave, not as a ranking for your hardware.

This is the short prompt with a 512-token answer.

Ollama and LM Studio both start llama.cpp's llama-server program for each model they load. Ollama has done this since version 0.30, and a comment in its source code notes so. On Linux, LM Studio's CUDA runtime is a folder with llama.cpp libraries and a llama-server binary.

Ollama logs the command it starts when you set OLLAMA_DEBUG=1. When llama.cpp was started by hand with that exact command, in a run next to Ollama, its speed matched Ollama's within 1%. So Ollama adds no speed cost of its own. LM Studio was 5 to 10% slower in this test. The test did not separate whether that came from its llama.cpp build or its other start options.

For one user, the gap between Ollama and LM Studio was about 0.4 s on a 512-token answer from the 9B model. You would notice it in long answers, and hardly in a chat window.

A web app rarely sends one request at a time. A chat page, a background summary job and an agent can all call the same model at the same moment. The next test sent four requests at once, each asking for 256 tokens, and measured the total output per second.

A slot is one request that the server works on at the same time as others. llama-server sets the number of slots with -np (short for --parallel), and Ollama and LM Studio pass their own setting through to it.

With one slot, the server answers the four requests one after another, so the total stays at the speed of a single request. That is Ollama's default. With four slots, the server puts the four requests through the model together, and the total rose to more than twice that of one slot. That is the default in LM Studio and llama.cpp. vLLM was the fastest at four requests, but it was tested only with the 9B model. Its lead grows with more requests, as the section after next reveals.

For your app, this means that the fourth user of a default Ollama server waits for the first three answers to finish before their own answer starts.

The obvious fix is OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4. It worked for the 9B model, though in one of three rounds Ollama still answered at the speed of a single request. With the 27B model, it made Ollama slower than its default.

Recent findings suggest that the cause is how each server sizes the context, the memory that holds each request's prompt and answer. Ollama picks the context from the GPU's memory: 32,768 tokens on a 24 GB card, according to its docs. With four slots, it gives each slot its own 32,768 tokens, so it started llama-server with a 131,072-token context. The Ollama FAQ says the memory needed grows with the number of parallel requests multiplied by the context length.

In a recent development, that context did not fit next to the 27B model in 24 GB. ollama ps highlighted 16% of the model on the CPU, and the total speed fell to 33.1 tokens per second.

LM Studio and llama.cpp handle it differently. Their four slots share one pool of context:.

The price of LM Studio's default is a short context. Four requests sharing 8,192 tokens leave little room for long documents or a long chat history. If your app sends long prompts, load the model with a larger context.

It has been revealed that in Ollama, setting a smaller context with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH next to OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL should avoid the spill to the CPU. The test did not try this, so measure it on your own card.

Recent findings suggest that the last test went further, from 1 to 32 requests at once, with the 9B model. It compared vLLM, a server built to serve one model to many users, with llama.cpp at its defaults and with more slots. Ollama and LM Studio were tested only up to four requests, so they are not in this table.

All figures are total tokens per second.

Sources indicate that with its defaults, llama-server chose four slots by itself, so it worked on four requests and queued the rest. Its total stayed near 330 tokens per second from 4 requests to 32. Setting -np 16 or -np 32 roughly doubled the total at 16 requests.

Industry observers note that vLLM's lead came from each request running faster inside a large batch. At 32 requests, each vLLM request generated about 61 tokens per second, against about 27 on llama.cpp with 32 slots. vLLM's README names the two techniques behind this: PagedAttention, which stores each request's working memory in small blocks, and continuous batching, which adds new requests to the batch the GPU is already working on.

Total output tells you how much work the server does. The wait for the first word tells you how the app feels to the user behind the last request:.

For a web app, that is 22.5 seconds of spinner before any text appears. Long prompts make every wait longer, on both servers. With eight requests of about 4,120 tokens each, the last request waited 7.9 s on vLLM and 8.8 s on llama.cpp with 32 slots.

If you set the slots yourself, the llama-server README lists three options that work together:.

If you run an older llama.cpp, update first. Four requests at once ran 14 to 22% faster on v1.0.0 than on the build from five days earlier, while one request stayed the same. The most likely reason is a new CUDA kernel in v1.0 for steps of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards.

vLLM's throughput comes with two costs that matter on a shared machine.

Recent findings suggest that it reserves most of the GPU. By default, vLLM takes 92% of the card's memory before it loads anything, and fills what the model does not need with cache. With a desktop and a browser holding about 2 GiB, vLLM refused to start:.

Sources indicate that setting --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 alone was not enough with this model, because the default limit of 256 sequences needed more cache than fit. Adding --max-num-seqs 32 fixed it. With both settings, vLLM held 12.7 GiB and kept the same speeds. llama.cpp works the other way: it sizes its cache from -c and -np and never asked for more than 15.1 GiB in this test.

It starts slowly. llama-server answered requests 2 to 5 s after its container started. vLLM compiles the model before it serves anything. That took 72 s with its compile cache already on disk, and 173 s on the first start without it. Changing a vLLM argument triggered a fresh compile.

According to recent reports, it also needs a different model file. vLLM loads Hugging Face safetensors, so a 4-bit model is a separate AWQ or GPTQ upload. The AWQ file here was 9.1 GB against 5.7 GB for the GGUF, because its recipe leaves some layers unquantized. Check the file size, not only "4-bit", when you size a model for your card.

Industry observers note that all four servers have an OpenAI-compatible API under /v1, so the same client code works with each one. You change the base URL and the model name. These are the ports used in the tests:.

In a recent development, in Node.js with the openai package, that looks like the sketch below. The measurements came from a Python test client, and this snippet was not part of them:.

Qwen3.5 thinks before it answers unless you turn it off. The tests sent "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to vLLM and llama.cpp.

None of the servers asked for a password in these tests. llama-server also warned at start-up that its CORS rule allowed all origins. Bind the port to 127.0.0.1, as in the table, and set --api-key on llama.cpp or vLLM if anything else on your network can reach it.

Recent findings suggest that before you choose, count how many requests your app really sends at the same moment. Log the timestamps for a day, or count the parallel calls your agent makes per user action. If that number is one, any of these servers will do. If it is four or more, the slot setting will change your users' wait more than the choice of engine.

Not for one request with the same settings. Ollama runs llama.cpp's own server, and the two were within 1% when started with the same command. llama.cpp was faster with four requests at once, because it starts four slots by default and Ollama starts one.

Ollama gives each parallel request its own full context. With four slots on a 24 GB card, that was 131,072 tokens, which pushed 16% of a 27B model onto the CPU. A smaller context may avoid that, but this test did not measure it.

It has been revealed that when many requests arrive together. At 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times the output of llama.cpp with 32 slots and kept every first-word wait under a second. For one request at a time, llama.cpp was 5% faster and started in seconds instead of more than a minute.

In a recent development, usually not. All four serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, so you change the base URL and the model name.

Industry observers note that if you are looking for a reliable, everyday handset without spending flagship money, Samsung’s mid-range lineup is usually a safe bet. Right now, the Samsung Galaxy A56 has dropped to just $299 on Amazon, which makes a sizable $200 dent in its original $499 retail price.

Sources indicate that at under $300, the biggest selling point here isn’t just the upfront savings; it is the longevity. Samsung committed to six years of OS and security updates for the Galaxy A56, meaning this device will stay current and secure well into 2032. For a budget-tier purchase, getting that kind of software runway is hard to beat and only matched by Google with the Pixel 10a.

Hardware-wise, the A56 punches above this sale price. You get a crisp 6.7-inch 120Hz Super AMOLED display, an IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating, and a 5,000mAh battery with 45W wired charging, matching the charging speeds of Samsung’s flagship models. The triple-camera array, led by a 50MP main sensor with OIS, won’t win any photography awards against Ultra-tier phones, though it is plenty capable for casual snaps. Plus, One UI brings plenty of handy Samsung ecosystem features and baked-in AI tools like Object Eraser.

Of course, the Google Pixel 10a is the obvious rival in this space. If you can catch the Pixel 10a on sale around the $350 mark, its cleaner Android experience, seven-year enhancement promise, and superior computational photography make it a very tempting alternative.

That said, it hasn’t been available at that price point for a while and can only be picked up for $400 if you buy renewed. Which annoyingly means the Pixel is sitting closer to its $499 MSRP and has last years specs anyway, so in many ways that makes the Galaxy A56 potentially a smarter buy for your wallet despite being a year older.

In my opinion, for first-time smartphone owners, kids, or anyone who just wants a large, smooth screen and years of updates on a budget, $299 is tough to argue with.

#173832. From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

📅 12 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

📅 12 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository.
  • If we focused solely on maximizing deduplication, the design would call for the smallest possible chunk size.
  • Sources indicate that on Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository. The idea is straightforward: break each file’s data into chunks, store only unique ones, reap the benefits.

In practice, it's more complex. If we focused solely on maximizing deduplication, the design would call for the smallest possible chunk size. By doing that, we’d create significant overheads for the infrastructure and the builders on the Hub.

Sources indicate that on Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases). Our guiding principle is simple: enable rapid experimentation and collaboration for teams building and iterating on models and datasets. This means focusing on more than just deduplication; we’re optimizing how data moves across the network, how it’s stored, and the entire development experience.

Imagine uploading a 200GB repository to the Hub. Today, there are a number of ways to do this, but all use a file-centric approach. To bring faster file transfers to the Hub, we've open-sourced xet-core and hf_xet, an integration with huggingface_hub which uses a chunk-based approach written in Rust.

It has been revealed that if you consider a 200GB repository with unique chunks, that's 3 million entries (at ~64KB per chunk) in the content-addressed store (CAS) backing all repositories. If a newly introduced version of a model is uploaded or a branch in the repository is created with different data, more unique chunks are added, driving up the entries in the CAS.

Recent findings suggest that with nearly 45PB across 2 million model, dataset, and space repositories on the Hub, a purely chunk-based approach could incur 690 billion chunks. Managing this volume of content using only chunks is simply not viable due to:.

In short, network requests balloon, databases struggle to manage the metadata, and the cost of orchestrating each chunk skyrockets all while you wait for your files to transfer.

These challenges lead to a key realization:.

Deduplication is a performance optimization, not the final goal.

The final goal is to improve the experience of builders iterating and collaborating on models and datasets. The system components from the client to the storage layer do not need to guarantee deduplication. Instead, they leverage deduplication as one tool among many to aid in this.

By loosening the deduplication constraint, we naturally arrive at a second design principle:.

Avoid communication or storage strategies that scale 1:1 with the number of chunks.

What does this mean? We scale with aggregation.

Aggregation takes chunks and groups them, referencing them intelligently in ways that provide clever (and practical) benefits:.

It has been revealed that together, blocks and shards unlock significant benefits. However, when someone uploads a newly introduced file, how do we know if a chunk has been uploaded before so we can eliminate an unnecessary request? Performing a network query for every chunk is not scalable and goes against the “no 1:1” principle we mentioned above.

According to recent reports, the solution is key chunks which are a 0.1% subset of all chunks selected with a simple modulo condition based on the chunk hash. We provide a global index over these key chunks and the shards they are found in, so that when the chunk is queried, the related shard is returned to provide local deduplication. This allows us to leverage the principles of spatial locality. If a key chunk is referenced in a shard, it’s likely that other similar chunk references are available in the same shard. This further improves deduplication and reduces network and database requests.

The Hub currently stores over 3.5PB of .gguf files, most of which are quantized versions of other models on the Hub. Quantized models represent an interesting opportunity for deduplication due to the nature of quantization where values are restricted to a smaller integer range and scaled. This restricts the range of values in the weight matrices, naturally leading to more repetition. Additionally, many repositories of quantized models store multiple different variants (e.g., Q4_K, Q3_K, Q5_K) with a great deal of overlap.

Industry observers note that A good example of this in practice is bartowski/gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF which contains 29 quantizations of google/gemma-2-9b-it totalling 191GB. To upload, we use hf_xet integrated with huggingface_hub to perform chunk-level deduplication locally then aggregate and store data at the block level.

Industry observers note that once uploaded, we can start to see some cool patterns! We’ve included a visualization that indicates the deduplication ratio for each block. The darker the block, the more frequently parts of it are referenced across model versions. If you go to the Space hosting this visualization, hovering over any heatmap cell highlights all references to the block in orange across all models while clicking on a cell will select all other files that share blocks:.

Recent findings suggest that A single block of deduplication might only represent a few MB of savings, but as you can see there are many overlapping blocks! With this many blocks that swiftly adds up. Instead of uploading 191GB, the Xet-backed version of the gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF repository stores 1515 unique blocks for a total of approximately 97GB to our test CAS environment (a savings of ~94GB).

In a recent development, while the storage improvements are significant, the real benefit is what this means for contributors to the Hub. At 50MB/s, the deduplication optimizations amount to a four hour difference in upload time; a speedup of nearly 2x:.

Recent findings suggest that similarly, local chunk caching significantly speeds up downloads. If a file is changed or a latest quantization is added that has significant overlap with the local chunk cache, you won’t have to re-download any chunks that are unchanged. This contrasts to the file-based approach where the entirety of the new or updated file must be downloaded.

Taken together, this demonstrates how local chunk-level deduplication paired with block-level aggregation dramatically streamlines not just storage, but developing on the Hub. By providing this level of efficiency in file transfers, AI builders can move faster, iterate swiftly, and worry less about hitting infrastructure bottlenecks. For anyone pushing large files to the Hub (whether you're pushing a fresh model quantization or an updated version of a training set) this helps you shift focus to building and sharing, rather than waiting and troubleshooting.

We’re fast at work, rolling out the first Xet-backed repositories in the coming weeks and months! As we do that, we will be releasing more updates to bring these speeds to every builder on the Hub to make file transfers feel invisible.

Follow us on the Hub to learn more about our progress!

Sources indicate that how can we find the chunk content using chunk hash? The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

Recent findings suggest that what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash"?

How can we find the chunk content using chunk hash?

Chunk hash is calculated via content-defined chunking (CDC), which means that if two chunks have the same content they will share the same hash. CDC removes the need to store the mapping between chunk hash -> chunk content because we know if two chunks share the same hash, they will have identical content.

The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

Industry observers note that this is explained in the "key chunks" section in the blog post above. Essentially we only store a tiny subset of chunk -> block by leveraging spatial locality in the file. Trying to store every mapping of chunk -> block can get impractical very rapidly.

According to recent reports, what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash".

You can think of the shards as storing mappings between file (identified via file hash) to list of chunks that make up the file.

I hope this help explains our underlying tech better!

Industry observers note that if we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file. For example if a model does not have a key chunk, the shard info only contains "file hash -> list of chunks", the CAS only has "block hash -> block content", how can we know which block is needed ?

For example if a model does not have a key chunk.

Two points of clarification might be in order concerning the above point:.

If we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file.

Sources indicate that when downloading a model file, a request is made to our services with the file hash. This is mapped to a list of block subranges. Logically these are chunks, but by storing the offsets we save on the metadata storage and ultimately many offsets will share boundaries inside a block (allowing us to group them together in a response) providing benefits when sending the content back to the client.

#173827. 5 Things Most Developers Get Wrong When Turning Images into HTML

5 Things Most Developers Get Wrong When Turning Images into HTML

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.

You have a picture (a mockup, a screenshot, a Figma export), and your job is to turn it into working HTML in a browser.

But here is the catch. A design image is static, while a webpage is dynamic and responsive across different screen sizes and devices. A webpage needs to load rapidly, adapt perfectly to different screen sizes, and allow touch interactions on mobile devices.

Most mistakes in this process happen when the conversion is treated as copying a picture instead of rebuilding it.

This section walks you through the mistakes developers often make, and more importantly, how to fix each of them.

Recent findings suggest that whether you are slicing a client mockup or converting a screenshot into code, avoiding these mistakes can save you from hours of rework. Let’s get into the details.

According to recent reports, A screenshot reflects how a page appears at a particular display. But it doesn’t show how the layout will behave when the content changes or the screen gets smaller.

Sources indicate that developers sometimes try to copy the exact positions and dimensions of every element. To match the screenshot, they may use fixed widths, large margins, and absolute positioning.

This can work at one screen size, but the layout may break on smaller screens or when a heading wraps onto an extra line.

The better approach is identifying the layout rules behind the design. CSS Grid can arrange the cards in columns. Flexbox can help align elements within each card. And media queries can adjust the layout for smaller screens.

Pixel-level comparison can be useful in some cases, but it should not come at the cost of a flexible layout.

When developers recreate a design, it’s easier for them to focus on shapes and spacing rather than the purpose of each element. So, they may use generic elements for headings, buttons, navigation areas, and content sections instead of choosing elements that reflect each element's purpose.

This may produce the right appearance, but it often makes the code harder to maintain and understand. And when developers fail to use the right HTML elements, it can also create accessibility problems later.

Industry observers note that so don’t put everything inside several unnamed containers. Instead, use a clear structure with appropriate headings, meaningful alt text for informative images, and real buttons for actions.

Semantic elements (e.g., header, nav, main, section, and footer) can also help organize a large page when they match the content’s purpose.

A design image may have headings, descriptions, prices, labels, or button text.

In a recent development, reusing the entire image to reproduce the original design feels quick. But it can create problems when that text has to work as part of a responsive web page.

It has been revealed that for example, there’s a promotional banner that contains a heading, a short description, and a CTA button. If you use the entire banner as one image, you can’t easily change the heading, translate the text, or make the button work as a real element.

So, don’t treat the image like that. Instead, use the original image where appropriate and recreate the text and button in HTML. CSS can control their position, size, color, and spacing.

Make sure you distinguish between visual elements that should remain images and text that should be recreated as HTML.

Not every part of turning images into HTML needs to be done manually.

Developers sometimes spend too much time on recreating basic elements when there are free online conversion tools available. These tools can help them get an initial version much faster.

An online conversion tool may be helpful when you need to extract text or generate a rough starting layout from a design image.

For example, you can upload a design image into an online image to html converter to get a starting point (rather than starting from a blank file). Review the tool’s output. Identify the parts you can reuse (as they are) and tweak the parts that need adjustments.

Keep in mind that the first result generated by the tool isn’t the final code. You may need to reorganize the HTML, refine the CSS, and adjust the layout to make it responsive.

Use automation where it saves time and your own judgement where it matters.

Sources indicate that A screenshot demonstrates just one view of a page. It doesn’t show how the layout may change on a phone or how people using a keyboard/screen reader can interact with it.

So, developers who focus only on the desktop design may end up with:.

buttons that are difficult to use.

content that becomes too small on mobile devices.

There’s also a chance of accessibility problems when images lack suitable alt text/interactive elements.

Sources indicate that let’s say a page has three cards in a row. On the desktop, this arrangement may work well. But on a phone, you may need to stack the cards vertically so their content remains readable.

That’s why accessibility should be considered during the same process. Use meaningful headings and provide appropriate alt text for images. Also, maintain sufficient text contrast and make sure interactive elements can be operated with a keyboard.

Lastly, don’t forget to test the page on both desktop and mobile screen sizes before finalizing it.

HTML and CSS handle the structure and appearance of a webpage, but JavaScript makes it possible to add interactive features.

For example, a design image may contain a navigation menu with a button. When recreating this design, developers should make sure the button performs an actual action rather than simply looking like a clickable element.

You can use JavaScript's event listeners to handle these interactions.

Now, add JavaScript to make the menu functional:.

In a recent development, in this example, clicking the button opens or closes the navigation menu. The aria-expanded attribute also communicates the menu's current state to assistive technologies.

According to recent reports, this is a simple example of why converting a design image into HTML involves more than matching its appearance. Developers also need to recreate the behavior of interactive elements using appropriate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The process of turning an image into HTML feels easy when you treat it the right way.

Start by identifying the main sections, text, images, and interactive elements. Then create meaningful HTML and build the layout with CSS. Make the necessary adjustments to ensure it works across different screen sizes.

Industry observers note that use a conversion tool when it can really save time. But don’t forget to review the generated output of the tool thoroughly before using it.

A screenshot is a visual reference, not a complete set of development instructions. And the best result for you isn’t simply a page that looks like the image.

It is a page that also works well, adapts well, and stays easy to maintain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve optimized your model. Your pipeline is running smoothly. But now, your cloud bill has skyrocketed. Running 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day isn’t just a technical challenge—it’s a financial one. How do you process at this scale without blowing your budget? Whether you're running large-scale document classification or bulk embedding pipelines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), you need cost-efficient, high-throughput inference to make it feasible, and you get that from having a well optimized configuration.

According to recent reports, these tasks often use encoder models, which are much smaller than modern LLMs, but at the 1B+ inference request scale it's still quite a non-trivial task. Just to be clear, that's English Wikipedia 144x over. I haven’t seen much information on how to approach this with cost in mind and I want to tackle that. This blog breaks down HOW to calculate cost and latency for large scale classification and embedding. We’ll analyze different model architectures, benchmark costs across hardware choices, and give you a clear framework for optimizing your own setup. Additionally we should be able to build some intuition if you don't feel like going through the process yourself.

You might have a couple questions:.

Here is the code to make it happen: https://github.com/datavistics/encoder-analysis.

tl;I'm not gonna reproduce this, tell me what you found;dr.

To evaluate cost and latency we need 4 key components:.

I’ll be leveraging Inference Endpoints for my Hardware Options, as it allows me to choose from a wide range of hardware choices. Do note you can replace that with your GPUs of choice/consideration. For the Deployment Facilitator I'll be using the ever so useful Hugging Face Hub Library which allows me to programmatically deploy models easily.

For the Inference Server I’ll also be using Infinity which is an amazing library for serving encoder based models (and more now!). I’ve already written about TEI, which is another amazing library. You should definitely consider TEI when approaching your use-case, though this blog focuses on methodology rather than framework comparisons. Infinity has a number of key strengths, like serving multimodal embeddings, targeting different hardware (AMD, Nvidia, CPU and Inferentia) and running any upcoming models that contain remote code that have not been integrated into huggingface’s transformer library. The most key of these to me is that most models are compatible by default.

It has been revealed that for Load Testing I'll be using k6 from Grafana which is an open-source load testing tool written in go with a javascript interface. It’s easily configurable, has high performance, and has low overhead. It has a lot of built-in executors that are super useful. It also pre-allocates Virtual Owners (VUs), which can be much more realistic than throwing some testing together yourself.

I'll go through 3 use-cases that should cover a variety of interesting points:.

Sources indicate that optimization is a tricky issue, as there is a lot to consider. At a high level, I want to sweep across vital load testing parameters and find what works best for a single GPU, as most encoder models will fit in a single GPU. Once we have a baseline of cost for a single GPU, the number of GPUs and throughput can be scaled horizontally by increasing the number of replica GPUs.

For each use-case this is the high-level flow I’ll use:.

Since you have the code, feel free to adjust any part of this to your:.

It has been revealed that VUs and Batch Size are crucial because these influence how well we take advantage of all the compute available in the GPU. A large enough Batch Size makes sure we are fully utilizing the Streaming Multiprocessors and VRAM. There are scenarios where we have VRAM left over but there is a bandwidth cost that prevents throughput from increasing. So experimentation can help us. VUs allow us to make sure we are fully utilizing the batch size we have available.These are the main parameters I'll be testing:.

Depending on your model you might want to consider:.

In a recent development, K6 is great because it allows you to pre-allocate VUs and prevent some insidious bugs. It's quite flexible in how you are sending requests. I decided to use it in a specific way.

When I'm calling a k6 experiment, I mainly want to know what the throughput and average latency is for the requests, and have a few sanity checks for the load testing parameters I have chosen. I also want to do a sweep which means many experiments.

Industry observers note that I use the shared-iterations executor (docs) which means K6 shares iterations between the number of VUs. The test ends once k6 executes all iterations. This allows me to have a reasonable time-out, but also put through enough requests to have a decent confidence that I can discriminate between load testing parameters choices in my sweep. In contrast to other executors, this allows me to be confident that I'm simulating the client working as hard as possible per VU which should show me what the cheapest option is.

Sources indicate that I use 10_000 requests† and have a max experiment time of 1 min. So if 10_000 requests aren’t finished by 1 minute, then that experiment is over.

Sources indicate that † I use less max requests for the Vision Embeddings given that the throughput is much lower and images are heavy.†† P95 means that 95% of requests complete within this time. It represents the worst-case latency for most owners.

You can find the 3 notebooks that put the optimization workflow together here:.

The main purpose was to get my experiments defined, launch the correct Inference Endpoint with the right parameters, and launch k6 with the right parameters to test the endpoint.

I made a couple design choices which you may want to think through to see if they work for you:.

Text Classification can have a variety of use-cases at scale, like Email Filtering, Toxicity Detection in pre-training datasets, etc. The OG classic architecture was BERT, and quickly many other architectures came about. Do note that in contrast to popular decoder models, these need to be fine-tuned on your task before using them. Today I think the following architectures† are the most notable:.

† Do note that for these models, you typically need to fine-tune this on your data to perform well†† I'm using “Engineering performance” to denote anticipated latency/throughput.

According to recent reports, I chose DistilBERT to focus on as it’s a great lightweight choice for many applications. I compared 2 GPUs, nvidia-t4 and nvidia-l4 as well as 2 Infinity Docker Images.

It has been revealed that you can see the results in an interactive format here or in the space embedded below in the Analysis section. This is the cheapest configuration across the experiments I ran:.

It has been revealed that text Embeddings are a loose way of describing the task of taking a text input and projecting it into a semantic space where close points are similar in meaning and distant ones are dissimilar (example below). This is used heavily in RAG and is an important part of AI search (which some are fans of).

There are a large number of architectures which are compatible, and you can see the most performant ones in the MTEB Leaderboard.

According to recent reports, modernBERT is the most exciting encoder release since DeBERTa back in 2020. It has all the ahem modern tricks built into an old and familiar architecture. It makes for an attractive model to experiment with as it's much less explored than other architectures and has a lot more potential. There are a number of improvements in speed and performance, but the most notable for a user is likely the 8k context window. Do check out this blog for a more thorough understanding.

In a recent development, it's notable to note that Flash Attention 2 will only work with more modern GPUs due to the compute capability requirement, so I opted to skip the T4 in favor of the L4. An H100 would also work really well here for the heavy hitters category.

According to recent reports, you can see the results in an interactive format here. This is the cheapest configuration across the experiments I ran:.

Recent findings suggest that colQwen2 is a Visual Retriever which is based on the Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and uses ColBERT style multi-vector representations of both text and images. We can see that it has a complex architecture compared to the encoders we explored above.

There are a number of use-cases which might benefit from this at large scale like, e-commerce search, multi-modal recommendations, enterprise multi-modal RAG, etc.

ColBERT style is different than our previous embedding use-case since it breaks the input into multiple tokens and returns a vector for each instead of 1 vector for the input. You can find an excellent tutorial from Jina AI here.This can lead to superior semantic encoding and better retrieval, but is also slower, and more expensive.

I'm excited for this experiment as it explores 2 lesser known concepts, vision embeddings and ColBERT style embeddings†. There are a few things to note about ColQwen2/VLMs:.

†Do check out this more detailed blog if this is new and interesting to you.

I wanted to try a small and modern GPU like the nvidia-l4 since it should be able to fit the 2B param model but also scale well since it's cheap. Like the other embedding model, I'm varying batch_size and vus.

Scaling to 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day is a non-trivial challenge, but with the right optimizations, it can be made cost-effective. From my experiments, a few key patterns emerged:.

In a recent development, your data, hardware, models, etc might differ, but I hope you find some use in the approach and code provided. The best way to get an estimate is to run this on your own task with your own configurations. Let's get exploring!

In a recent development, special thanks to andrewrreed/auto-bench for some inspiration, Michael Feil for creating Infinity. Also thanks to Pedro Cuenca, Erik Kaunismaki, and Tom Aarsen for helping me review.

Sources indicate that it's crucial to scale sanity checks as your complexity scales. Since we are using subprocess and jinja to then call k6 I felt far from the actual testing so I put a few checks in place.

The goal of task performance is that for a specific configuration we are performing similarly to what we expect. Task Performance will have different meanings across tasks. For classification I chose accuracy, and for embeddings I skipped it. We could look at average similarity and other similar metrics. It gets a bit more complex with ColBERT style since we are getting many vectors per request.

Sources indicate that even though 58% isn't bad for some 3 class classification tasks, it's irrelevant. The goal is to make sure that we are getting the expected task performance. If we see a significant change (increase or decrease) we should be suspicious and try to understand why.

Below is a great example from the classification use-case since we can see an extremely tight distribution and one outlier. Upon further investigation the outlier is due to a low amount of requests sent.

You can see the interactive results visualized by nbviewer here:.

In a recent development, we should expect to see no failed requests as Inference Endpoints has a queue to handle extra requests. This is relevant for all 3 use-cases: Classification, Embedding, and Vision Embedding.

sum(df.total_requests - df.successful_requests) allows us to see if we had any failed requests.

Industry observers note that as described above we are using a nice strategy of using exponential increases and then a binary search to find the best number of VUs. But how do we know that we tried enough VUs? What if we tried a higher amount of VUs and throughput kept increasing? If that's the case then we would see a monotonically increasing relationship between VUs and Throughput and we would need to run more tests.

You can see the interactive results visualized by nbviewer here:.

We are using a ColBERT style model for Vision Embedding which means we should be getting multiple vectors per image. It's interesting to see the distribution of these as it allows us to check for anything unexpected and to get to know our data. To do so I stored the min_num_vectors, avg_num_vectors, max_num_vectors, in the experiments.

We should expect to see some variance in all 3, but it’s ok that min_num_vectors and max_num_vectors have the same value across experiments.

Here is a short description, but you can get a more detailed interactive experience in the space: derek-thomas/classification-analysis.

For the classification use-case we looked at 2 different Infinity Images, default and trt-onnx. Which one was better? It's best if we can compare these across the same settings (GPU, batch_size, VUs). We can simply group our results by those settings and then see which one was cheaper.

According to recent reports, this is a key chart as for many use-cases there is a maximum latency that a user can experience. Usually if we allow the latency to increase we can increase throughput creating a trade-off scenario. That's true in all the use-cases I've looked at here. Having a pareto curve is great to help visualize where that tradeoff is.

In a recent development, lastly it's crucial to build intuition on what is happening when we try these different settings. Do we get beautiful idealized charts? Do we see unexpected gradients? Do we need more exploration in a region? Could we have issues in our setup like not having an isolated environment? All of these are good questions and some can be tricky to answer.

It has been revealed that we've shown you our selection of gaming laptops and PCs, but the sounds of explosions and dulcet tones of soundtracks deserve a lot better than some dollar-store earbuds you've had since you were a kid. Additionally, when you want some quiet time for yourself, those earbuds won't do you much good. To properly enjoy some aural bliss along with peace and quiet, we suggest the Sony WH-1000XM5 wireless headset, which can be obtained for only $169.99 from Best Buy, or 23% off its regular $219.99.

According to recent reports, the Sony XM line of headsets is known for its top-notch active noise cancellation (ANC), and I can attest to that as the proud owner of the XM4s. This later model has a much slimmer headband and improved noise control. As with other ANC sets, it's an over-ear, closed-back design that insulates you from the world outside. The driver units have 30-mm drivers backed by light and efficient neodymium magnets, with a carbon fiber composite dome.

The Sony XM line of headsets is known for its top-notch active noise cancellation (ANC), and the WH-1000XM5s deliver on front, along with top-notch audio quality, support for lossless codecs, and a hardware equalizer.

Sony says that the frequency response is an oddly wide 4 Hz to 44 kHz, though from personal experience I have no trouble believing they cover pretty much the entire range of human hearing (20 Hz to 20 kHz), judging by how deep the bass can go in my XM4s.

It has been revealed that the onboard equalizer is hardware-based, meaning your EQ settings will be kept in the headphones and apply if you connect them to another device, or through the 3.5-mm jack — something even some super-expensive headsets fail at, cough AirPod Max cough. The noise cancellation is configurable, and there's an air pressure optimizer good for plane travel, as well as speak-to-chat functionality that lets ambient sound through on request if you need to talk to someone.

In a recent development, as befits any audiophile-grade bit of kit, the headset supports high-end audio codecs, up to LDAC lossless. In wired operation, the impedance is 48 Ohm, low enough for a phone to drive them to high volume levels if needed. The ANC also works in wired mode, too. The onboard battery lasts 30 hours, or 40 if you forego ANC.

Google has a fresh “Priority Notifications” feature in the works for Pixel phones with the ability to pull your most important information to the top of the screen and even highlight it with a bit of color.

Google Pixel phones already have tools to manage your notifications, but an upcoming enhancement seems to be building on that functionality. The folks at Android Authority flipped the switch on some work-in-progress changes that reveal “Priority Notifications.”.

This is a newly introduced feature that Google describes as “highlighting urgrent messages” and “time-critical updates” by adding color to the notification and placing it at the top of the stock. Android’s notifications list already tries to place messages at the top, but it sounds like this AI-powered feature will further emphasize that. It’s also mentioned that this is powered by on-device AI.

Google’s early blurb describes:.

Highlight urgent messages, deliveries, and time-critical updates with hints of color at the top of your notifications.

Sources indicate that priority notifications use Al on your device, which may sometimes make mistakes. Your notifications are never sent to Google.

The feature would also integrate with HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro series and the feature allows users to exclude certain apps. Google also seems to be shuffling the branding, turning “Notification intelligence” into “Notification organizer,” and the existing organizer section into “Notification bundles.”.

Exactly when this might land on Pixel phones is unknown. It’s not mentioned what build this feature was found hiding in, but it seems likely it was in the ongoing QPR3 beta. QPR3’s stable release will arrive around March 2027, but there’s no guarentee it’ll bring this upcoming feature with it.
