Sources indicate that online payments are an essential part of modern web applications. E-commerce platforms, subscription services, and online marketplaces all depend on payment gateways to process transactions and manage customer orders.

However, integrating a payment gateway involves more than adding a payment button or displaying a checkout form. Developers must ensure that payment requests are sent to legitimate providers, transaction information is validated correctly, and payment confirmations cannot be manipulated.

According to recent reports, fake payment gateways introduce another challenge. They can imitate legitimate payment interfaces, use copied checkout templates, and redirect customers to fraudulent websites. Even when a checkout page looks professional, its underlying implementation may not be trustworthy.

It has been revealed that for developers, understanding these risks is notable when designing payment workflows. This article explores common payment integration vulnerabilities and practical techniques for building secure checkout systems using JavaScript and Node.js.

A payment gateway connects an application with a payment processing service. It handles transaction requests and communicates payment results to the merchant's application.

A typical checkout process involves several components:.

A frontend checkout interface where customers review their orders.

A backend application that creates payment requests.

A payment provider that processes transactions.

A webhook endpoint that receives payment notifications.

A database that stores order and transaction information.

Attackers can target different parts of this process.

For example, a fraudulent website may copy the appearance of a legitimate checkout page while sending submitted information to an unauthorized server. Another approach involves manipulating payment requests or creating fake confirmation pages that make an unsuccessful transaction appear complete.

These techniques are also relevant to marketplace fraud. An eBay scam can involve fraudulent payment requests and misleading transaction links, illustrating why developers need to consider payment security beyond the appearance of a checkout page.

The notable distinction is that a legitimate-looking interface does not establish that the payment request is reaching an authorized provider.

One of the first steps in reviewing a payment integration is checking where the application sends its payment requests.

Sources indicate that developers should inspect network requests using browser developer tools. The Network tab can reveal which domains receive requests when a customer opens the checkout page or submits a payment form.

Look for unexpected requests, unfamiliar domains, and scripts loaded from sources that are not part of the approved integration.

For example, a checkout application might load a payment script like this:.

The URL above is illustrative, not an actual payment provider.

Developers should compare the script URL and integration method with the provider's official documentation rather than trusting a URL simply because it appears familiar.

Reviewing external JavaScript dependencies.

Checking whether payment forms submit data to approved endpoints.

Inspecting redirects during checkout.

Confirming that HTTPS is used throughout the payment process.

Reviewing changes to payment-related scripts during development.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) can also restrict which domains are allowed to load scripts and receive certain types of requests.

These example domains must be replaced with the actual domains documented by the selected payment provider.

A carefully configured policy can reduce the risk of unauthorized scripts and unexpected form submissions.

A common mistake in payment development is trusting values submitted directly from the browser.

Consider an application where the frontend sends an order ID and payment amount to the backend.

Sources indicate that an attacker could modify the amount before submitting the request. If the backend accepts that value without checking the original order, the application may create a payment session for an incorrect amount.

The safer approach is to retrieve the order from the database and calculate the amount on the server.

Here is a simplified Node.js example:.

Here, payment Gateway create Checkout Session() represents a provider-specific server-side SDK method.

The key part is that the backend retrieves the amount from its own database rather than accepting a price supplied by the customer.

Developers should also validate product IDs, quantities, discounts, currency, and order ownership before creating a payment session.

This prevents frontend manipulation from directly determining the final transaction amount.

Developers should avoid building payment processing around unverified scripts, copied templates, or unknown third-party services.

Instead, use official APIs and SDKs provided by established payment processors.

Recent findings suggest that A hosted checkout integration is one common option. The merchant's backend creates a payment session through the provider's API, and the customer is redirected to the provider's hosted checkout page.

This approach can reduce the amount of sensitive card information handled by the merchant's application.

However, developers still need to configure the integration correctly.

Store secret API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager.

Never expose private credentials in frontend JavaScript.

Use the provider's official SDK where available.

Validate checkout session creation on the backend.

Restrict success and cancellation URLs to approved destinations.

Use HTTPS for application and payment communication.

According to recent reports, developers should also understand the difference between public and secret API credentials. Public keys may be designed for browser use, while secret keys must remain on the server.

The OWASP Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration Cheat Sheet provides additional guidance on securing payment requests, validating transaction details, and handling payment callbacks.

Payment providers often use webhooks to notify applications when transactions are completed, failed, or refunded.

However, webhook endpoints are publicly accessible URLs in many integrations. Without proper verification, an attacker may send a fabricated HTTP request that looks like a successful payment notification.

Developers should verify webhook signatures using the payment provider's official SDK.

Consider this simplified Node.js example:.

The verify Webhook() method represents the signature verification functionality of a payment provider's SDK. It is not a universal Node.js method.

The example also assumes that the provider's event contains the relevant order and transaction details. Developers should follow the provider's actual event schema and retrieve the authoritative payment status when required.

The application should never mark an order as paid simply because a customer has reached a success URL.

Instead, payment confirmation should depend on an authenticated provider notification or a server-side verification request.

Another key concern in payment development is duplicate processing.

Imagine a customer clicks the payment button twice because the first request takes too long. The application may create two payment sessions or attempt to charge the customer more than once.

Network interruptions and automatic retries can create similar situations.

Idempotency helps prevent these problems by ensuring that repeated requests with the same idempotency key do not create duplicate operations.

A simplified example using Node.js might look like this:.

The example uses a provider-specific idempotency option. Actual SDK syntax and key requirements vary between providers.

In a production application, developers should also store payment attempts in the database and enforce appropriate uniqueness constraints.

This helps maintain consistent transaction records even when requests are repeated or interrupted.

A payment integration should be tested beyond the normal successful checkout process.

Most established payment providers offer sandbox environments that allow developers to simulate transactions without charging real customers.

These environments are useful for testing different transaction scenarios.

A practical testing checklist includes:.

Missing or invalid webhook signatures.

Duplicate webhook notifications.

Network interruptions during checkout.

Incorrect order and transaction IDs.

Developers should also test whether the application handles provider downtime correctly.

For example, if the payment provider becomes temporarily unavailable, the application should not mark an order as completed or assume that the transaction succeeded.

Automated integration tests can help verify these scenarios before deployment. Monitoring payment failures, unexpected status changes, and repeated webhook errors can also help developers identify problems after release.

Security does not end when a payment integration goes live.

Developers should implement monitoring to identify unusual transaction patterns and unexpected changes in payment behavior.

Useful monitoring activities include:.

Recording payment attempts and transaction IDs.

Tracking failed payment requests.

Monitoring webhook signature verification failures.

Detecting repeated requests for the same order.

Alerting on unexpected order status changes.

Reviewing payment provider API errors.

However, logging must be implemented carefully.

Applications should never store card verification codes or expose secret API keys in application logs. Sensitive information should be excluded from debugging output, and access to transaction records should be restricted.

Developers should also follow the payment provider's security requirements and applicable PCI DSS obligations when handling payment data.

Detecting fake payment gateways and building secure checkout integrations requires more than checking whether a payment page looks legitimate.

Developers need to examine the complete transaction flow, validate payment information on the server, use official payment APIs, verify webhook signatures, and prevent duplicate transactions.

JavaScript and Node.js provide useful tools for implementing these security controls, but the reliability of a payment system ultimately depends on how its frontend, backend, database, and payment provider communicate.

Sources indicate that A well-designed checkout integration should verify every notable transaction before fulfilling an order. By following these development practices, teams can build payment systems that are easier to maintain, more reliable, and better protected against common payment manipulation techniques.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 3 weeks ago, we indicated how hard it is to correctly evaluate LLM performance on math problems, and introduced Math-Verify, a better solution to validate models on math (read more in the announcement)!
  • Today, we’re thrilled to share that we’ve used Math-Verify to thoroughly re-evaluate all 3,751 models ever submitted to the Open LLM Leaderboard, for even fairer and more robust model comparisons!
  • It has been revealed that the Open LLM Leaderboard is the most used leaderboard on the Hugging Face Hub: it compares open Large Language Models (LLM) performance across various tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

3 weeks ago, we indicated how hard it is to correctly evaluate LLM performance on math problems, and introduced Math-Verify, a better solution to validate models on math (read more in the announcement)!

Today, we’re thrilled to share that we’ve used Math-Verify to thoroughly re-evaluate all 3,751 models ever submitted to the Open LLM Leaderboard, for even fairer and more robust model comparisons!

It has been revealed that the Open LLM Leaderboard is the most used leaderboard on the Hugging Face Hub: it compares open Large Language Models (LLM) performance across various tasks. One of these tasks, called MATH-Hard, is specifically about math problems: it evaluates how well LLMs solve high-school and university-level math problems. It uses 1,324 highest difficulty problems (Level 5) from the Hendrycks MATH dataset spread across 7 topics (precalculus, prealgebra, algebra, intermediate algebra, counting/probability and number theory), using a 5-shot approach (the model is provided with 5 examples in the prompt to showcase how it should answer).

A typical question looks like this:.

In the leaderboard, models would have to end their answers with a very specific string (following the Minerva-Math paper):.

The leaderboard would then try to parse [ANSWER] with SymPy to convert it to a symbolic representation (and simplify the values if needed), before finally comparing it to the gold target.

However, customers reported a number of challenges with the above.

It has been revealed that to start, a recurring issue was the inability of some models to follow the expected answer format from the examples: they outputted other sentences instead to introduce their answers. Since the format was not followed, answers were marked as wrong even if they were actually correct! (Which is an issue if what you’re interested in is “how good the model is at math” specifically).

The next step, converting [ANSWER] to the symbolic representation also presented some problems, this time linked to the SymPy parsing:.

On the final step, when comparing the extracted answer with the target expression, a number of complications also occurred:.

All of these complications are now completely fixed with the new Math-Verify parser!

As all these issues tend to accumulate, some models deeply suffered from this, and their performance was strongly underestimated… so we removed the previous evaluator and added Math-Verify, which was as simple as changing only 3 lines of code! (You can try it too on your math evals!).

This therefore meant re-evaluating all submitted models since June… and it completely overhauled the top 20 models on the MATH subset of the leaderboard.

On average, models solved 61 more problems across the board, equating to a 4.66-point increase across the board!

The two subsets that demonstrated the most significant improvement were both algebra-related (Algebra and Prealgebra) with gains of 8.27 and 6.93, respectively. In extreme cases, some models demonstrated improvements of nearly 90 points on these subsets. We believe these subsets saw the greatest improvement because they frequently involve answers presented as sets (due to questions with multiple solutions) and matrices. The Math-Verify has enhanced its handling of both answer types, contributing to these notable gains.

In a recent development, we initially discovered the math evaluation concerns when inspecting Qwen models, which had unusually low scores compared to the self-reported performance. After the Math-Verify introduction, the scores more than doubled for these models, showcasing previous severe underestimation of performance.

But Qwen models aren’t alone. Another major family affected is DeepSeek. After switching to Math-Verify, DeepSeek models almost tripled their scores! This is because their answers are typically wrapped in boxed (\boxed{}) notations which the old evaluator couldn’t extract.

Sources indicate that as mentioned at the beginning, the Top 20 rankings have undergone a significant shift, with Nvidia’s AceMath models now dominating the MATH-Hard leaderboard. Other major beneficiaries of this change are the Qwen derivatives, which are now almost exclusively the only models ranking right below AceMath. Following is the complete table comparing the old and new Top 20 leaderboard rankings:.

Finally, we examined how the overall Leaderboard results have evolved. While the top four positions remain unchanged, the rest have undergone significant shifts. Due to the rise of multiple Qwen derivatives in the MATH subset, the presence of Qwen models among the top 20 has grown-derived models grown even further at the Overall results.

It has been revealed that many other models also completely jumped in the rankings, gaining 200 places or more! You can check out the results in more detail at the Open LLM Leaderboard.

The introduction of Math-Verify has significantly improved the accuracy and fairness of our evaluations on the Open LLM Leaderboard. This has led to a reshuffling of the leaderboard, with many models showing substantial improvements in their scores.

Sources indicate that we encourage all developers and researchers to adopt Math-Verify for their own math evaluations. By doing so, you can ensure that your models are evaluated with more reliable results. Additionally, we invite you to explore the updated rankings and see how your favorite models have changed in performance.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored.
  • By this point, you don’t need me to tell you that this is a familiar design.
  • I hoped that the maximum brightness bug would have been resolved by now with the screen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored.

By this point, you don’t need me to tell you that this is a familiar design. It’s turning into a comfortable pair of slippers at this point in time. Nothing is wrong, and nothing particularly stands out. A safe but samey design that is inoffensive.

I hoped that the maximum brightness bug would have been resolved by now with the screen. It creates a shadow around the edges of the display after a minute or so when in direct sunlight. Somewhat like blooming on a cheap LCD screen. It does diminish what is otherwise a great display.

Recent findings suggest that the thickness has started to feel like a relic of the 2023 design that feels a little dated now. I have been using the Pixel 11 without a case most of the time, which mitigates it, but throw a case on and it’s a chunky boi. The added thickness would probably have been acceptable had the extra space been filled with more battery, but it feels like that boat has set sail a long time ago. A slimmer profile probably would have helped differentiate without deviating too much from last year’s phone.

Sources indicate that after months of using the Pixel 11, the move of the NFC module to the top edge has been huge for me because my car uses an NFC terminal to lock and unlock when you’re without a set of car keys. With the Pixel 10, it worked but not quite as smoothly. It’s one of those inconsequential changes that makes a real-world difference.

Gemini Intelligence has been something I’ve started to rely on quite heavily. I love that I get a prompt to add an appointment to my calendar, and all of the important details have been taken care of, like the location, extra contact details, the works.

It has been revealed that I’m not sure what the hold-up is for adding wider functionality. It’s actively hurting things, in my opinion. Google Messages is great, but some of the automation functions locked in there mean I haven’t been saving any time with Gemini’s prowess at doing the legwork of keeping my life up to date.

I’ve tried using Pause Point, but found it’s just easier to leave my phone face down rather than use an app to try and stop using my phone…maybe if we all did that, so many of the world’s ills wouldn’t be so pronounced. Just a thought.

Sources indicate that the November Pixel Drop has also made some notable changes to the Pixel 11 experience that I can’t believe were held back since launch. If you waited and bought in the last few weeks with the substantial discounts kicking around, you objectively get a better phone today than at launch.

The improvements don’t overhaul things, just enhance or heighten the fluidity and experience above what was available in the months post-launch. More cohesive theming, little tweaks to the UI; it’s not reinventing the Pixel 11, just augmenting it in ways that would have been nice back in August.

In a recent development, I don’t really have much to complain about with the Pixel 11 lifespan even after months of charging. Yes, charging is still slow, but you only need to charge once per day. If we were talking about a phone with bad battery life and slow charging, I’d have more to complain about. However, it’s still solid and dependable.

The camera continues to impress without really improving drastically. I can’t help but feel that every couple of generations, the Pro camera setup should be passed on to the base Pixel, then we get a newer, improved system on that specific Pro model. It’d allow for quicker improvements and maybe, dare I say it, make the camera system cheaper as parts get reused. If anything, it would help Google’s supposed environmental pledges by preventing camera components from hitting landfill.

According to recent reports, A lot of people will tell you the best camera is the one you have with you, and this hasn’t ever been a problem for a recent Pixel. I can count on one hand the frustrations I have felt with the Pixel 11 camera since it landed on my desk on launch day. I am happier than a year ago with the base Pixel 10 than the 11, which is to say this is a bigger leap or a return to form.

Having the ability to tune Camera Looks was something I have loved, but you might just fall into using one tuned look that fits your own personal style. There is an element of this that might change the perception of the Pixel 11 camera consistency versus its predecessors. What I mean is that while it does still excel at point-and-shoot, the fact that Looks are baked into the JPEG could be a problem. There are times when I’ve thought that an image might have been better using default settings.

That stated, I have stuck to “Shadows” with Contrast set to -5, Highlights to -5, Shadows to -5.5, warmth to 0.5, and Grain to “Strong.” That is a recipe I’ll probably stick with for a long time to come. It’s still weird that we can do all this at the camera level with a Pixel. Whether “normies” even use the options or just stick to the out-of-the-box default settings is another discussion for another day.

At $699, the Pixel 11 becomes a decent buy for a lot of people. For others, the distinct lack of power is something that can’t ever be overcome. I would buy this for a relative because it’ll do everything they could ever want and more. For a friend who cares about having the cutting edge in their pocket? Probably not.

A lot of the problems over the past few years on Pixel phones have come from the price tag.

Even with the discounts in and around Black Friday, the fact that you can get a device like the Galaxy S25 Ultra that’ll have better specs and lots of valuable features for around the same price. The last few generations of the Pixel have been harder to recommend because of the drawbacks versus the cost and the competition.

I mentioned a few months ago that there is a good phone under the price hikes, and that remains unchanged. However, there are better products from the year prior that won’t compromise and are even cheaper. In a silo, you’re getting a 7/10 product at a 3/10 price. Just how that changes depends on forthcoming updates. One saving grace is that no Pixel is ever quite the same months after it rolls off the production line. A few Pixel Drops, even more discounts, and maybe a true seal of approval might be easier.

It has been revealed that to put it into context, this was never a $900 phone and arguably never should have been. That’s somewhat a failing on Google’s part in more ways than one. At least it’s down to a palatable price that should be the Pixel baseline.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The most powerful CPU on the market, AMD's Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, is down to its lowest price ever of $759 this Black Friday. By the numbers, it's the best CPU for gaming, and the fastest in multithreaded workloads. It's also the first processor AMD has ever created that uses its 3D V-Cache across both CCDs.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has an MSRP of $900, but it introduced at $1,000 before settling back down to $900. Although we've occasionally seen $50 off the CPU here and there, this is the first time we've seen this steep of a discount. The processor is on sale for $799 at most retailers, knocking $100 off its list price. On Amazon, however, an on-page coupon knocks off an additional $40, bringing the price down to $759.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 is AMD's first dual-CCD CPU with 3D V-Cache. It sports 16 cores and 192 MB of L3 cache, and it can boost up to 5.6 GHz.

In a recent development, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D features 128MB of L3 cache, which enables it to claim the title of the fastest gaming chip on the market. It features 16 Zen 5 cores and 32 threads of computing power, reaching a peak clock speed of 5.7 GHz.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D, which features the stacked cache on a single CCD, is also on sale for $115 off, bringing its list price of $699 down to $583.55. For most people, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D is the better buy. Outside of a few niche applications, it performs identically to the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 across games and productivity workloads.

In a recent development, you can see that reflected in the charts above, which we gathered during our Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 review. Regardless of which processor you go with, you're getting top-shelf gaming performance. The Ryzen 7 9850X3D is a touch faster, but realistically, this is identical gaming performance in practice.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has a small 4% advantage over the Ryzen 9 9950X3D in multithreaded workloads, and the two perform identically in single-threaded workloads, falling short of Intel's latest Core Ultra 7 270K Plus.

Sources indicate that we recommend the Ryzen 9 9950X3D for most people, but if you want the best of the best, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 at $759 is an excellent deal. Make sure to pair it with a quality CPU cooler (ideally an AIO), as well as a midrange to high-end B850E or X870 motherboard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and big-budget blockbusters.

Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and massive-budget blockbusters.

One of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux. It’s a moody, black-and-white title with obtuse puzzles and a main character that constantly narrates to himself with dramatic language. Its credits attribute pretty much everything to a developer named Johannes Zuch. It’s generated a lot of discussion for seemingly mocking games like Jonathan Blow’s The Witness or The Chinese Room’s Dear Esther. It’s also a game that only exists inside of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Developer Rockstar Games has stuffed a lot of satirical media inside of GTA VI, including TV highlights you can watch, books you can read, and radio shows you can listen to. It’s all in service of making the world feel like a funhouse-mirror version of our current reality — Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis plays a right-wing radio host, for example. There are more games you can play inside GTA VI in addition to Tenebrae Lux, including a zombie-themed roguelike. But Tenebrae Lux, which you have to see as part of GTA VI’s main story, is the one that has struck a chord, including with indie developers like Sam Barlow and Robert Yang.

“I have to admit it’s kind of funny for the biggest blockbuster game of all time to go after arthouse indie,” Yang tells The Verge, noting that it’s “like a fighter jet getting obsessed with an ant, petty in a funny way.” (Given that GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day, the gulf between Rockstar and indie game studios that are struggling to get by is vast.).

It has been revealed that but Yang suggested that Rockstar developers are probably well versed in the types of games they’re lampooning in GTA VI. “I don’t think gamers understand how much indie experimental stuff any decent AAA dev plays,” Yang said, pointing out that Rockstar’s environmental artists and level designers “all probably love Dear Esther,” the influential first-person game that helped popularize the “walking sim” concept when it rolled out in 2012.

“I was mostly taken with what it meant that the millions of people playing the game were having to sit down and play through an extended gag about indie games,” Barlow tells The Verge. “That made me feel like we were part of larger culture.” He added that he hopes some of these players might “seek out what these arty indie games might be.”.

Recent findings suggest that rockstar is self-aware enough to use its video games to poke fun at the medium itself. As part of a long conversation between protagonist Jason Duval and his friend Cal Hampton before they start playing Tenebrae Lux, Cal hypes the game by saying that none of it is “just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking.” Initially, you only play Tenebrae Lux for a few minutes, which is enough time to get stumped on the initial puzzles, before the game cuts back to Jason being bored. “Got anything else, a little less, uh… y’know?” he asks. They play the zombie game, titled Street Trash 3 Dezombifier, right after. (You can go back and play the entirety of Tenebrae Lux later if you want.).

Barlow said that the cut “felt very true to the character and story. I gather there is more to the game, but it felt natural to me to hit a wall with the pretentious puzzle design and then move on!”.

Industry observers note that yang also pointed out that from a design perspective, GTA VI has more in common with Tenebrae Lux than Street Trash 3 Dezombifier. GTA VI is “basically a walking sim where you walk around Florida and listen to people talk,” Yang stated. “What’s the difference? Well, just like a billion dollars I guess.”.

Most Android bugs are not exotic. They are a button hidden behind a keyboard, a screen that breaks on a smaller display, a permission prompt nobody tested, or an install that fails on an older version of the system. You can catch many of these problems without owning a single test phone, as long as you set up your Windows PC properly and test with a initiative.

This guide covers how to prepare Windows, how to choose and configure an emulator, how to install and verify APK files with Android Debug Bridge (ADB), what a good test session checks, and where virtual devices stop being trustworthy. It includes a small Python helper that explains install failures and reads launch times from ADB output, with tests. Tool versions and menu names change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

According to recent reports, ● Emulators find the large, repeatable problems fast. Use them for functional checks, layouts and install testing, and confirm hardware behavior on real devices.

● Prepare Windows first. Enable hardware virtualization and the Windows Hypervisor Platform, and check the result with the emulator’s own acceleration check.

In a recent development, ● Match the virtual device to real customers. Test the oldest and newest Android versions you support, a small screen and a modest memory profile.

● Learn ADB. It makes installs, data resets and evidence capture scriptable and repeatable.

● Do not trust emulator performance numbers. Your PC is usually faster than your owners’ phones.

Recent findings suggest that testing on a desktop gives you speed and control that physical phones rarely match. A fresh install takes seconds. You can wipe app data, change the screen size, switch the Android version and try again without hunting for a charger. When a tester finds a bug, they can record the screen, copy the log and attach both to a report from the same machine.

According to recent reports, it also opens testing to people who are not developers. Product managers, support staff, designers and content reviewers can open a build, follow a script and report what they see with a full-size screen, a keyboard and a mouse. That alone shortens the feedback loop on most teams.

Recent findings suggest that the tradeoff is realism, which this guide returns to later. For now, the point is that an emulator is the fastest way to find the large, obvious, repeatable problems, which is exactly what you want to clear out before involving real devices.

There are two broad families of tools, and they suit different work.

The first is the official Android Emulator that comes with Android Studio. It simulates hardware in detail, supports a wide range of device profiles and connects directly to debugging and profiling tools. It is the right choice when you are tracing a crash, profiling memory or testing against a specific system image. It is also heavier to install and configure.

The second family is general-purpose emulators built for speed and convenience. A good android emulator such as LDPlayer installs swiftly, runs on ordinary hardware, can open several instances side by side, and makes it easy to drop in an APK, map keyboard controls and record the screen. Other examples include BlueStacks and Genymotion, the latter aimed at developers and test automation. Many of these tools are designed first for gaming or for general app use, so check whether they expose the Android versions, system images and debugging features your testing needs.

Many teams use both: the official tools for debugging, and a lighter emulator for broad functional testing. When you compare options, ask a few practical questions:.

Preparing Windows Before You Install Anything.

Ten minutes of preparation prevents most early frustration.

Turn on hardware virtualization. Emulators run dramatically faster when virtualization is enabled in your BIOS or UEFI. The setting is usually called Intel Virtualization Technology (VT-x) or SVM Mode on AMD systems. If your emulator feels slow for no clear reason, check this first.

Recent findings suggest that enable the Windows Hypervisor Platform. The Android documentation recommends the Windows Hypervisor Platform (WHPX) for Windows acceleration, and notes that you can turn it on under “Turn Windows features on or off”, then restart. Its older Android Emulator hypervisor driver is being phased out, so check the current emulator acceleration guide for your setup. Also note that a hardware-accelerated emulator cannot run inside another virtual machine.

Sources indicate that verify it. The emulator includes a check that reports whether acceleration is usable:.

In a recent development, revision your graphics drivers. Android interfaces rely on graphics acceleration. Outdated drivers cause black screens, flickering and random crashes that testers wrongly blame on the app.

It has been revealed that check memory and storage. As a rule of thumb, 8 GB of RAM is workable for a single virtual device and 16 GB is more comfortable for several. Leave several gigabytes of free disk space, because every virtual device stores its own system image and data.

Close heavy background programs. Browsers with dozens of tabs and other virtual machines compete for the same resources and make performance results misleading.

Recent findings suggest that the default configuration is rarely the one your audience uses. Spend a few minutes matching it to reality.

Industry observers note that pick a screen size and density similar to a popular mid-range phone rather than a very large display, because layout problems tend to appear on smaller screens first. Assign a sensible number of CPU cores and memory, enough to be smooth but not so much that you hide performance problems your customers on modest phones will feel.

Industry observers note that choose the Android version carefully. If your app supports several versions, test at least the oldest and the newest. Behavior changes significantly between releases, especially around permissions, notifications, background activity and gesture navigation. For example, Android 13 (API level 33) introduced a runtime notification permission, so a flow that works on an older version can silently differ on a newer one.

With the Android Emulator, you can list and start saved devices from the command line, which helps when you keep several profiles:.

Finally, confirm the network works by loading a web page in the virtual browser. A surprising number of reported app bugs turn out to be a virtual device with no connection.

Industry observers note that an APK is the package file Android uses to install an app. Installing one on a virtual device is easy, but doing it carefully makes your results more reliable.

It has been revealed that use trusted files only. Take builds from your own team, your continuous integration system or the developer’s official release page. An APK from a random download site can be modified or carry malware, and testing it proves nothing about the real product.

Install it. Most emulators accept a dragged APK file or have an install option. If you use the command line, Android Debug Bridge (ADB) installs a package with a single command and is the better route when you want to automate repeated installs. These are the commands you will use most:.

adb devices                          # confirm the emulator is connected.

adb install -r app-debug.apk         # install, replacing an existing copy.

adb shell pm clear com.example.app   # wipe app data for a fresh start.

adb shell am start -W -n com.example.app/.MainActivity   # launch and print timing.

adb logcat -d > session.log          # save the log for a bug report.

adb exec-out screencap -p > shot.png # take a screenshot.

Recent findings suggest that know the common install failures. If the install fails, the message usually explains why. A package built for a newer Android version than your device runs is rejected, a build compiled only for a different processor architecture may not install or may crash on launch, and an upgrade signed with a different key than the installed version is refused, in which case you uninstall the old version first. The helper below turns raw ADB output into a one-line explanation and also reads the launch time that am start -W prints:.

"""Small helpers for reading adb output during APK testing.""".

"INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK": "The app needs a newer Android version than this device runs.",.

"INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS": "The app has no native code for this device's CPU architecture.",.

"INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE": "Signed with a different key than the installed copy. Uninstall first.",.

"INSTALL_FAILED_VERSION_DOWNGRADE": "The installed copy has a higher version code. Uninstall first.",.

Recent findings suggest that "INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE": "The virtual device is out of storage. Wipe data or enlarge the disk.",.

def explain_install_failure(output: str) -> str:.

"""Turn raw adb install output into a one-line explanation.""".

m = re.search(r"(INSTALL_[A-Z_]+)", output).

Industry observers note that return "Unknown failure. Read the full adb message.".

return f"{code}: " + INSTALL_HINTS.get(code, "No hint recorded for this code.").

def launch_time_ms(output: str):.

"""Read TotalTime from adb shell am start -W output, or None if the launch failed.""".

m = re.search(r"TotalTime:\s*(\d+)", output).

return int(m.group(1)) if m else None.

The tests feed it realistic ADB output, including a successful install, three common failures, an unknown code, a successful launch and a failed one:.

from adbtools import explain_install_failure, launch_time_ms.

assert explain_install_failure("Performing Streamed Install\nSuccess") == "Installed.".

older = "adb: failed to install app.apk: Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK]".

assert "newer Android" in explain_install_failure(older).

abi = "Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS: Failed to extract native libraries, res=-113]".

assert "architecture" in explain_install_failure(abi).

sig = "Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE: Package com.example signatures do not match]".

assert "Uninstall first" in explain_install_failure(sig).

assert explain_install_failure("Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_SOMETHING_NEW]").endswith("No hint recorded for this code.").

assert explain_install_failure("error: device offline").startswith("Unknown failure").

good = "Starting: Intent { cmp=com.example/.MainActivity }\nStatus: ok\nActivity: com.example/.MainActivity\nTotalTime: 523\nWaitTime: 530\nComplete".

assert launch_time_ms(good) == 523.

assert launch_time_ms("Error type 3\nError: Activity class does not exist.") is None.

In a recent development, understand split packages. Many modern apps ship as bundles made of several files instead of one APK. If you are given a bundle format, you may need a tool that installs all the parts together, or a universal APK generated for testing.

Sources indicate that test the right build. Debug builds and release builds do not always behave the same. Release builds often apply code shrinking and optimization that can break features that worked in debug. Before sign-off, run your main flows on a release build, not only the one developers use daily.

Recent findings suggest that wandering through an app and tapping things will find some problems. A structured pass finds far more. Work through these areas on each build.

Capture evidence as you go. A short screen recording with the exact steps, plus the saved log, is worth far more to a developer than a paragraph of description.

A very common mistake is testing everything on one virtual device and assuming the result applies everywhere. Android is a fragmented platform, and your audience is spread across many versions, screen sizes and memory limits.

Create a small set of profiles and rotate through them. A low-memory profile reveals how the app behaves on budget hardware. A small screen exposes cramped layouts. An older Android version reveals compatibility gaps. A different language and region setting reveals text-length problems, date and number formatting issues and right-to-left layout errors.

In a recent development, because tools such as the Android Emulator and several third-party emulators let you keep multiple saved devices, you can keep these profiles ready and compare behavior across them. This is where testing on Windows becomes efficient, turning a long list of devices you would have to buy into a handful of saved configurations.

Being honest about the limits protects you from false confidence.

● Hardware features. Camera quality, fingerprint sensors, Bluetooth accessories, NFC, precise GPS behavior and motion sensors are hard to reproduce faithfully. You can simulate basic values, but real hardware behaves differently.

● Real performance. Speed on an emulator depends on your PC. A strong computer can make an app feel faster than it will on a typical phone, so never use emulator results as proof of smooth performance for users.

● Manufacturer customizations. Phone makers modify Android with their own battery management, notification handling and interface layers. An app can work on a clean system and fail on one brand’s modified version, particularly around background tasks and push notifications.

Sources indicate that ● Real networks. A home network is stable. Mobile networks have weak signal, handoffs between towers and restrictions that an emulator will not recreate.

● Apps that block virtual devices. Some apps, particularly in banking, security and competitive gaming, detect virtual environments and refuse to run. That is a deliberate choice by the developer, and testers should respect it instead of attempting to bypass it.

In a recent development, the sensible approach is to let emulators handle the broad middle of your testing, then confirm anything involving hardware, payments or notifications on a few real devices before release. The script above also only interprets a handful of ADB messages, so it is a convenience for triage, not a replacement for reading the full output.

If you want something simple to adopt, use this sequence on every build.

Start with a clean virtual device matching a common phone.

Install the new build and run a quick smoke test, a fast pass over the main features to confirm nothing is fundamentally broken.

Test the specific areas that changed in this version in more depth.

Repeat the most key flows on a second profile with a different Android version and screen size.

Log every problem with exact steps, the build number, the device profile and a screenshot or recording.

Before release, verify camera, location, notifications and payments on at least one physical phone.

Sources indicate that write this down as a short checklist and share it. Consistent steps make results comparable between testers and between builds, which is how you notice regressions instead of rediscovering the same bugs.

Industry observers note that do I need Android Studio to test an APK on Windows? Not necessarily. Many emulators accept an APK directly, and ADB can be installed on its own as part of the Android platform tools. Android Studio becomes useful when you need to debug or profile.

It has been revealed that why is my emulator slow? The usual causes are virtualization or the Windows Hypervisor Platform being off, outdated graphics drivers, too little memory and heavy background programs. Run the acceleration check first.

Can an emulator replace a real test phone? No. It covers the broad middle of testing, but hardware, true performance, manufacturer behavior and real networks need a few physical devices.

Is it safe to install APKs from the internet? Only from trusted sources, such as your own team, your build system or an official release page. Files from random sites can be modified or carry malware.

According to recent reports, testing Android apps on Windows is practical, affordable and flexible when you treat the emulator as a tool with a clear purpose. It gives you fast installs, repeatable conditions and easy access to many device profiles, which makes it well suited to functional checks, layout reviews and APK testing. It does not replace real hardware for sensors, true performance and manufacturer-specific behavior, so keep a few physical devices for the final confirmation.

Industry observers note that prepare your PC, choose a tool that fits your workflow, configure devices that resemble real owners, follow a consistent checklist and vary your environments. Do that consistently and you will catch most problems long before they reach your users.

Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.

Industry observers note that game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.

According to recent reports, leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.

Sources indicate that portWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.

According to recent reports, at this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

Sources indicate that last December, Google released PaliGemma 2: a new family of pre-trained (pt) PaliGemma vision language models (VLMs) based on SigLIP and Gemma 2. The models come in three different sizes (3B, 10B, 28B) and three different resolutions (224x224, 448x448, 896x896).

Today, Google is releasing PaliGemma 2 mix: fine-tuned on a mix of vision language tasks, including OCR, long and short captioning and more.

Sources indicate that paliGemma 2 pretrained (pt) variants are great vision language models to transfer on a given task at hand. All pt checkpoints are meant to be fine-tuned on a downstream task and were released for that purpose.

Industry observers note that the mix models give a quick idea of the performance one would get when fine-tuning the pre-trained checkpoints on a downstream task. The main purpose of the PaliGemma model family is to provide pretrained models that can learn better on a downstream task, instead of providing a versatile chat model. Mix models give a good signal of how pt models perform when fine-tuned on a mix of academic datasets.

You can read more about PaliGemma 2 in this blog post.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.
  • Sources indicate that in most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

Sources indicate that in most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll. It could be Los Santos or a twisted take on Manhattan, but the idea is that the main story is just one part of the experience. After that’s done, there are usually still places you haven’t explored or side missions you left lingering. But Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t work quite the same way. Because of its storyline, which involves a couple trying to get out of the criminal life for good, that kind of ending didn’t really fit.

“In this one it didn’t make sense,” Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North, told me ahead of the game’s launch. “Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”.

This story contains light spoilers for the ending of Grand Theft Auto VI, along with a key plot point from chapter 1.

To be clear, you can still play GTA VI after the main storyline wraps up. But in order for that to happen, you have to zip back in time to a moment before a pivotal decision — I won’t spoil it for you — that alters the lives of main characters Jason and Lucia, along with their young son Tomás, who they’re attempting to get custody of. Nelson claims the team tried “all sorts of things” but soon realized that “in no way did it make sense” to have the game end like a traditional GTA experience.

“Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”.

Sources indicate that “You go back and have this open time again where you have the best single-player safehouse you’ve ever had in a GTA, with a garage full of supercars, a helipad, a gym, and all of the stuff you could ever want,” he indicates of the solution the studio landed on. “And you can spend as long as you want there. But you don’t have Tommy. So the characters don’t have the one thing that they wanted at the start. There’s the tension where you have to spend some extra time grinding to make some more money without knowing what it’s going to get you, and it plays out differently if you get that money.”.

One advantage of this structure is that it lets you try out different endings. GTA VI’s story can wrap up in multiple ways based on a variety of factors: how much money you have saved up, what kind of criminal you were throughout the game, and some key decisions you’re forced to make in the final moments. The new postgame structure creates an opportunity to see some of the alternate ways the story can go. “There’s a large number of potential outcomes based on how you played it,” Nelson indicates.

The tools split into two families.

Recent findings suggest that performance transfer is great for animation, but someone has to record a latest take for every change. If your promise is “fix the reaction in the footage you already have,” direct editing fits better.

Sources indicate that DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, users upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid plans. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

In a recent development, for developers, SyncMonster publishes public API documentation for DRAMA. Here is what those docs state, as checked on November 10, 2026:.

In a recent development, A few things to note honestly. The same generate endpoint also serves other SyncMonster features behind their own flags, so read the parameter table carefully. In the version we checked, the parameter table marks an audio input as required on generate, and the drama-only example includes one, so blueprint for that in your request builder. The emotion values exposed in the API are the four core emotions, and the extra app presets did not appear in the API docs. The docs describe polling only, with no webhooks mentioned, and they do not publish rate limits, an SDK, or a numeric maximum video duration (an error code exists for exceeding a duration limit).

Industry observers note that runway exposes Act-Two through its developer API as the character_performance endpoint. You send a character (image or video) and a driving performance video, and Act-Two transfers facial expression, and optionally body and hand motion, onto the character. Output is 24fps.

Sources indicate that runway’s API pricing guide lists Act-Two at 5 credits per second of output, with credits priced at $0.01 each, so $0.05 per second. Earlier documentation mentioned a 15-credit minimum per generation, and the current pricing page does not list one, so check for minimums before you budget short clips. The documentation also exposes an expression intensity setting to control how strongly the performance is applied.

Industry observers note that the catch is the input requirement: every edit needs someone to act the latest reaction. That suits character animation, but it is a heavy ask for a user who wants a slightly warmer smile in an interview clip. It also drives one character per generation.

Recent findings suggest that livePortrait is an open-source portrait animation framework from Kuaishou’s KwaiVGI group. It animates a source image or video using a driving video or a saved motion template, supports video-to-video portrait editing, and offers retargeting controls for eyes and lips.

In a recent development, the README sets up a Python 3.10 conda environment and expects Git and FFmpeg, with an NVIDIA GPU recommended. It also notes that Apple Silicon runs roughly 20x slower than an RTX 4090, and that Humans mode needs PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 on a Mac. That matters if you were hoping to prototype on a MacBook and ship the same setup. A basic run adapted from the README looks like this:.

Also read the repository’s license file before you plan any commercial use.

According to recent reports, the Hugging Face Spaces demo is handy for experiments, but production means owning GPU provisioning, queueing, model updates and quality review. You still steer with a driving input rather than a “happier by 30%” control.

Rule of thumb: if expression editing is a feature rather than your product, buy. If you need on-prem processing or model-level changes, build on LivePortrait and budget for ops.

SmolVLM2: Bringing Video Understanding to Every Device

📅 20 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SmolVLM2 represents a fundamental shift in how we think about video understanding - moving from massive models that require substantial computing resources to efficient models that can run anywhere.
  • Industry observers note that we are releasing models in three sizes (2.2B, 500M and 256M), MLX ready (Python and Swift APIs) from day zero.
  • Check out our interactive chat interface where you can test visual and video understanding capabilities of SmolVLM2 2.2B through a simple, intuitive interface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SmolVLM2 represents a fundamental shift in how we think about video understanding - moving from massive models that require substantial computing resources to efficient models that can run anywhere. Our goal is simple: make video understanding accessible across all devices and use cases, from phones to servers.

Industry observers note that we are releasing models in three sizes (2.2B, 500M and 256M), MLX ready (Python and Swift APIs) from day zero. We've made all models and demos available in this collection.

Want to try SmolVLM2 right away? Check out our interactive chat interface where you can test visual and video understanding capabilities of SmolVLM2 2.2B through a simple, intuitive interface.

We are introducing three latest models with 256M, 500M and 2.2B parameters. The 2.2B model is the go-to choice for vision and video tasks, while the 500M and 256M models represent the smallest video language models ever released.

In a recent development, while they're small in size, they outperform any existing models per memory consumption. Looking at Video-MME (the go-to scientific benchmark in video), SmolVLM2 joins frontier model families on the 2B range and we lead the pack in the even smaller space.

Video-MME stands out as a comprehensive benchmark due to its extensive coverage across diverse video types, varying durations (11 seconds to 1 hour), multiple data modalities (including subtitles and audio), and high-quality expert annotations spanning 900 videos totaling 254 hours. Learn more here.

Sources indicate that compared with the previous SmolVLM family, our fresh 2.2B model got better at solving math problems with images, reading text in photos, understanding complex diagrams, and tackling scientific visual questions. This shows in the model performance across different benchmarks:.

In a recent development, when it comes to video tasks, 2.2B is a good bang for the buck. Across the various scientific benchmarks we evaluated it on, we want to highlight its performance on Video-MME where it outperforms all existing 2B models.

We were able to achieve a good balance on video/image performance thanks to the data mixture learnings published in Apollo: An Exploration of Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models.

It’s so memory efficient, that you can run it even in a free Google Colab.

Nobody dared to release such small video models until today.

Our newly introduced SmolVLM2-500M-Video-Instruct model has video capabilities very close to SmolVLM 2.2B, but at a fraction of the size: we're getting the same video understanding capabilities with less than a quarter of the parameters 🤯.

According to recent reports, and then there's our little experiment, the SmolVLM2-256M-Video-Instruct. Think of it as our "what if" project - what if we could push the boundaries of small models even further? Taking inspiration from what IBM achieved with our base SmolVLM-256M-Instruct a few weeks ago, we wanted to see how far we could go with video understanding. While it's more of an experimental release, we're hoping it'll inspire some creative applications and specialized fine-tuning projects.

To demonstrate our vision in small video models, we've built three practical applications that showcase the versatility of these models.

We make SmolVLM2 available to use with transformers and MLX from day zero. In this section, you can find different inference alternatives and tutorials for video and multiple images.

The easiest way to run inference with the SmolVLM2 models is through the conversational API – applying the chat template takes care of preparing all inputs automatically.

Breaking: This gaming mouse should be a Logitech-killer, but it has one major flaw

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿.

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

It has been revealed that when Keychron revealed its $90 G6 HE gaming mouse, I immediately thought, “Cool! A cheaper alternative to the pricey $180 Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike.” Logitech’s innovation with the Superstrike is using magnetic Hall effect switches for a user-adjustable mouse click depth, with haptic vibrations mimicking the tactile click feel. The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it.

Recent findings suggest that the mouse’s shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily customizable (through a browser-based app, no less). But the clicks? The clicks are all wrong.

According to recent reports, the left and right mouse buttons on the G6 HE use Keychron’s MagOptic switches, which are both magnetic Hall effect and optical. They click just like any standard mouse, regardless of where you set the actuation point. There are no fancy haptics on the Keychron. If you set the buttons to a shallow hair-trigger depth, you’ll register a press before you actually feel or hear any click. Set the depth for a very heavy press, and the mouse clicks before it actually registers. That… kind of defeats the purpose here.

Sources indicate that there’s not much point in tuning the actuation depth of the G6 HE’s buttons if the click feel doesn’t match it. I suppose it’s still nice to have a hair-trigger-like setting for taking faster single shots in an FPS, but not feeling anything when you shoot is weird. And it gets frustrating when using the G6 HE as a regular mouse for productivity — like you’re getting phantom clicks as you mouse around your computer. At least I can feel my accidental clicks when using a Logitech Superstrike with the action set too high, and I know I’m to blame for leaving the mouse on my try-hard settings.

I reached out to Keychron for the reasoning behind the G6 HE’s magnetic-but-not-haptic setup, and cofounder Fab Chan noted, “There are two reasons for this design. First, many consumers still prefer the feel of a traditional click over haptics. Second, a haptic motor adds weight, and for this model we prioritized a lighter design. That said, we’re planning a model with haptic feedback. It will be slightly heavier than the G6 HE, and we’ll share more details soon.”.

Recent findings suggest that the G6 HE is a lightweight mouse. It’s only 49g with its battery, or 40g in wired mode with the battery removed. The Logitech X2 Superstrike is 60g, and the newer X3 Superstrike is 59g — each still pretty light. If you ignore all the Hall effect stuff and just use the G6 HE as a regular mouse, it has some things going for it over the Superstrikes. In addition to its lighter build and much lower price, it feels a tiny bit comfier in my hand, thanks to its side walls that curve slightly inward at the bottom.

Recent findings suggest that one of its best features is hot-swappable batteries. From my time testing Angry Miao’s AM Infinity Mouse, I know that once you can pop out a magnetic battery pack and quickly swap it, you never want to go back to plugging in your mouse to charge. You can also get the G6 HE in black with a standard built-in rechargeable battery for $15 less, but I don’t think that’s enough savings to forgo the convenience of hot-swap batteries.

Sources indicate that the G6 HE’s charging base doubles as the wireless receiver, and of course it’s lit up with customizable RGB lighting. It has four programmable buttons for on-the-fly changes to things like DPI, lighting, mouse profiles, or just about anything else you want to program. The browser-based Keychron Launcher software is robust and makes tinkering with the G6 HE or its base very easy. And for some reason, the receiver / charging base is designed like a vacuum tube, which is fun, but it means you’re unscrewing its clear housing to access the battery — a little tedious.

I can’t shake my disappointment with the G6 HE’s lackadaisical magnetic switch implementation. Keychron seems proud of the fancy MagOptic Switch it put into the G6 HE, even going so far as to call it “next gen,” but this mouse seems a jack of all trades and master of none. The G6 HE is cheaper than most other mice with hot-swap batteries — which can still make it worthwhile if you don’t care about all the Hall effect stuff — but that is its lone saving grace.

Industry observers note that we’ll have to wait and see if Keychron’s follow-up model with haptics can properly compete with the Superstrike mice and their hallmark feature. I’m excited to see where Hall effect tech goes in mice, and how more companies can evolve it, but the G6 HE is a half-measure.

In a recent development, like other Google apps, Messages for Android A/B tests many features. It can take the RCS/SMS client a rather long time to actually launch fresh functionality in stable. From various reports, Google announcements, and devices we’ve checked, this is the current state of Messages.

These are Messages features that Google confirmed or have been spotted in the wild by beta customers.

In the US, Google Messages now lets you “Text with Gemini” using the “Channels” feature introduced in November. This uses RCS Business Messaging and Gemini “tasks” (previously Spark) for a more proactive experience that also lets you direct the agent to accomplish actions from the Messages app. Use the chat with the four-color Gemini logo after setting up via gemini.google.com/channels.

Instead of pinned chats appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is elevating them above all conversations as circular contact photos.

You now access “Search” — which has a redesigned page — from a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside “Start chat.”.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image.

Read receipts are now placed in a circle at the bottom-right corner of message bubbles and images. You swipe left to see timestamps and the encryption lock, while you can swipe right to reply. This first started appearing in August of 2024, but is now seeing wide beta and stable availability.

Enhanced Protection adds “Advanced detection to prevent spam and scams” across three features. Go to Google Messages settings > Protection & safety.

To see timestamps and the RCS encryption lock, you can now swipe left anywhere in a conversation. To reply to a message, you have to swipe right on the bubble. Tapping a message still shows the read receipts.

Recent findings suggest that instead of a top toolbar, long-pressing on a message or image opens a floating menu as the background blurs. Another press lets you copy just a part of the chat. Previously, you had to copy the entire message.

With iOS 27’s September launch, Android-iPhone conversations over RCS gain support for inline replies that include quotes, as well as photo reactions with the actual emoji instead of just the text description.

Jfc what is so hard about adding categories for conversations?

The new Google Keep integration lets you swiftly create and share notes inside chats. If you don’t see a contextual suggestion to “Create list,” open the ‘plus’ menu for a new “Keep Notes” tile.

In a recent development, this will slide up a sheet that shows your list of notes and the “Create a note” button. Upon selecting or starting a note, you’ll see a send button in the bottom-right corner. Afterward, there’s a live preview in the conversation thread.

Usually, buying a monitor involves some sort of compromise: maybe it's not the brightest, or the refresh rate is low, or the text is blurry, etc. How about one that is essentially pitch-perfect? The Alienware AW3226Q, a 32" 4K OLED display with a 165 Hz refresh rate, RGB subpixel layout, and DisplayHDR 400 True Black and Dolby Vision certifications, can be yours for only $549.99 from the Dell store, or $150 off its regular price.

If you're keeping track of features and thinking that this monitor looks about perfect, you're absolutely correct. A resolution of 3840x2160 at 32" is about perfect for a balance between perceptual sharpness and graphics card load in gaming — plus, while ultra-wide displays are excellent for gaming, their curved nature doesn't quite lend itself as well to productivity tasks.

The Alienware is a sharp, colorful OLED display with 4K resolution, 165 Hz refresh rate, and Dolby Vision support.

Make no mistake, though: this isn't a "work monitor." First off, the 165 Hz refresh rate is supported by Nvidia G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro compatibility for smooth motion in games, and the peak HDR brightness is 1000 nits, letting you enjoy gorgeous vistas with natural highlights and sun — like, say, in STALKER 2, at least before a mutant chews your face off. As with most any OLED panel, the pixel response time is effectively zero, making for a blur-free experience, and the color gamut covers 99% of the DCI-P3 color space.

According to recent reports, the pure RGB subpixel layout is worth expanding on, with good reason — most forms of anti-aliasing, namely but not only for text in Windows, assume left-to-right RGB for each color component. Until relatively recently, OLED monitors had acceptable-to-poor text rendering, because they used unorthodox layouts like RGWB or RGBW pixel arrangements. Meanwhile, this one? Our reviewer called it "easily on par with the best professional displays [he's] reviewed.".

The thin frames, height-, tilt-, and swivel-adjustable stand, and built-in USB hub with USB-C power delivery round out the main specifications. Grab the Alienware AW3226Q OLED monitor for only $549.99 at Dell's store.

Industry observers note that pose detection in the browser is a solved problem. You can load a model, point it at a webcam, and get a skeleton tracking a human body in real time, on a laptop, with no server involved.

And then you have a skeleton that follows someone around the screen, which is a toy.

In a recent development, the gap between that toy and a feature someone would pay for is smaller than most developers expect, and it isn't made of machine learning. It's made of trigonometry you already know. This article builds a working bicep-curl rep counter to show exactly where that line falls — and more importantly, which side of it your bugs live on.

In a recent development, I'm using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker from Google AI Edge, which is Apache-2.0 licensed and runs entirely in the tab. Here's the whole setup:.

Point that at a element carrying a camera stream and call detectForVideo. What comes back, per frame, is this:.

Industry observers note that thirty-three points. Each one is a normalised coordinate — x and y run 0 to 1 across the frame, z is a relative depth estimate — plus a visibility score saying how confident the model is that it can actually see that joint.

That's the entire output. Coordinates and confidences.

Recent findings suggest that the model has no concept of exercise. It doesn't know what an arm is for. It has never heard of a bicep curl. It reports where it thinks your joints are, thirty-odd times a second, and stops.

Everything that turns that into a product is yours, and it's ordinary code.

According to recent reports, A bicep curl is a change in the angle at the elbow. The elbow angle is defined by three of those 33 points: shoulder, elbow, wrist. In MediaPipe's pose topology those are indices 11, 13 and 15 on the left side, 12, 14 and 16 on the right.

Getting the angle is two vectors and a dot product:.

According to recent reports, this is the same maths you'd use to point a game character in a direction. Nothing about it is machine learning, and that matters for a reason I'll come back to.

According to recent reports, one thing to notice: I'm ignoring z entirely. The depth estimate is relative, not metric — it's good enough for working out which parts of a body are nearer the camera, and not good enough to measure anything. For a 2D elbow angle, using it adds noise and buys nothing.

Here's where almost everyone's first attempt breaks.

The naive version looks at the angle and counts whenever the arm is up:.

It has been revealed that run that at 30 frames a second and one slow curl gives you about twenty reps. You haven't counted repetitions. You've counted frames in which the arm happened to be bent.

A rep isn't a state. It's a transition between states:.

Industry observers note that fifteen lines, and that's the feature. The counter increments exactly once per cycle, on the edge, because the guard on phase makes every other frame in that cycle a no-op.

Recent findings suggest that if you used a single threshold — say, 100 degrees — you'd get a counter that fires repeatedly whenever someone holds their arm near 100 degrees and the estimate jitters by a degree either side. Every tiny fluctuation across the line is a transition, and every transition is a rep.

Sources indicate that two widely separated thresholds give you hysteresis. Once the arm is "up," it has to travel all the way past 150 degrees before the counter will consider another rep. Noise of a few degrees can't produce a count because no amount of jitter near 55 crosses 150.

According to recent reports, this is the same trick a thermostat uses to avoid switching the heating on and off every few seconds, and it's the single most useful pattern in this whole category of work. Any time you turn a continuous signal into discrete events, you want two thresholds, not one.

visibility is the field people skip, and skipping it is how you get phantom reps.

When a joint goes out of frame or gets occluded, the model still returns a coordinate for it. It is obliged to return 33 points. What it does is return a guess, with a low visibility score attached — and a guessed wrist position can swing wildly between frames, which looks exactly like a very fast curl.

Returning null and having update bail out means an occluded frame holds the current state rather than corrupting it. The arm stays "up" until the model can actually see it come down.

Industry observers note that if you want to be stricter, smooth the angle over the last three or four frames with a rolling median before it reaches the state machine. A median rejects single-frame outliers in a way a mean doesn't.

Once you've written one of these, you start recognising the shape everywhere:.

In a recent development, none of those require a different model. They're the same 33 coordinates with different geometry sitting on top, and the geometry is a few dozen lines each.

Here's why I keep insisting on the distinction between coordinates and meaning.

It has been revealed that when my rep counter miscounts, I don't retrain anything. I don't collect a dataset, I don't label examples, I don't spin up a training job. I look at two things: my thresholds, and my state machine. One of them is wrong.

That's a normal bug in normal code, and you already know how to find it. You can log the angle. You can set a breakpoint on the transition. You can write a unit test that feeds a synthetic sequence of angles through update and asserts the count — no camera, no model, no fixtures:.

Sources indicate that the hard part of this problem — turning pixels into joint positions — was solved by a research team and shipped to you as a file you can download. The part that's left is the part you're already good at.

In a recent development, you are not blocked on machine learning knowledge. You were blocked on nobody telling you this was available.

Recent findings suggest that I set delegate: 'GPU' above without comment, and it deserves one. MediaPipe Tasks lets you choose between a CPU path and a GPU path, and availability of the GPU path varies by browser, platform and graphics driver.

The practical consequence is that you have to test the CPU path, because for some meaningful share of your customers it isn't a fallback — it's the only path they will ever take. If you develop on a machine where the GPU delegate works and never exercise the CPU one, you have shipped something you've never run.

According to recent reports, that, and the question of how often you should run the model at all, is a bigger subject than this article. It's the next one.
