💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are pleased to announce our partnership with JFrog, creators of the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.
  • Sources indicate that we have decided to add JFrog's scanner to our platform to continue improving security on the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are pleased to announce our partnership with JFrog, creators of the JFrog Software Supply Chain Platform, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.

Sources indicate that we have decided to add JFrog's scanner to our platform to continue improving security on the Hugging Face Hub. JFrog's scanner brings upcoming functionality to scanning, aimed at reducing false positives on the Hub. Indeed, what we right now observe is that model weights can contain code that is executed upon deserialization and sometimes at inference time, depending on the format. This code is oftentimes a non harmful practicality for the developer. As our picklescan scanner only performs pattern matching on module names, we cannot always confirm that usage of a given function or module is malicious. JFrog goes a step deeper and will parse and analyze code it finds in models weights to check for potential malicious usage.

Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub? Please get in touch with us over at security@huggingface.co.

To share models, we serialize weights, configs and other data structures we use to interact with the models, in order to facilitate storage and transport. Some serialization formats are vulnerable to nasty exploits, such as arbitrary code execution (looking at you pickle), making shared models that use those formats potentially dangerous.

As Hugging Face has become a popular platform for model sharing, we’d like to help protect the community from this, hence why we have developed tools like picklescan and why we are integrating JFrog in our scanner suite.

It has been revealed that pickle is not the only exploitable format out there, see for reference how one can exploit Keras Lambda layers to achieve arbitrary code execution. The good news is that JFrog catches both of these exploits and more in additional file formats – see their Model Threats page for up to date scanner information.

Read all our documentation on security here: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security 🔥.

Sources indicate that there's nothing you have to do to benefit from this! All public model repositories will be scanned by JFrog automatically as soon as you push your files to the Hub. Here is an example repository you can check out to see the feature in action: mcpotato/42-eicar-street.

Note that you might not see a scan for your model as of today, as we have millions of model repos. It may take us some time to catch up 😅.

In total, we have already scanned hundreds of millions of files, because we believe that empowering the community to share models in a safe and frictionless manner will lead to growth for the whole field.

Latest Update: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (316 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images.
  • To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench.
  • Recent findings suggest that gemini 4 Argon and Carbon demonstrated that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability.

Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.

To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.

Recent findings suggest that gemini 4 Argon and Carbon demonstrated that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it aims the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.

Hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.

When running LLMs on mobile devices, size matters significantly:.

When selecting a model, consider both the parameter count and the quantization level. For example, a 7B model with Q2_K quantization might run better than a 2B model with Q8_0 quantization. So if you can fit a small model comfortably on your device try to use a bigger quantized model instead, it might have a better performance.

The HF_TO_GGUF object maps user-friendly model names to their corresponding Hugging Face repository paths. For example:.

Next, let's create a way to fetch and display available GGUF model files from the hub for our selected model format.

According to recent reports, when a user selects a model format, we make an API call to Hugging Face using the repository path we mapped in our HF_TO_GGUF object. We're specifically looking for files that end with '.gguf' extension, which are our quantized model files.

Once we receive the response, we extract just the filenames of these GGUF files and store them in our availableGGUFs state using setAvailableGGUFs. This allows us to show owners a list of available GGUF model variants they can download.

This callback is triggered during the download process to update the progress. Before downloading we need to have the selectedModelFormat state set to the model format we want to download.

Inside the downloadModel function we use the RNFS module, part of the react-native-fs library, to access the device's file system. It allows developers to read, write, and manage files on the device's storage. In this case, the model is stored in the app's Documents folder using RNFS.DocumentDirectoryPath, ensuring that the downloaded file is accessible to the app. The progress bar is updated accordingly to reflect the current download status and the progress bar component is defined in the components folder.

handleDownloadAndNavigate is a simple function that will download the selected GGUF file by calling handleDownloadModel (implemented in the previous sections) and navigate to the conversation screen after the download is complete.

Industry observers note that congratulations you've just built the core functionality of your first AI chatbot, the code is available here ! You can now start adding more features to the app to make it more user friendly and efficient.

Sources indicate that the app is now fully functional, you can download a model, select a GGUF file, and chat with the model, but the user experience is not the best. In the EdgeLLMPlus repo, I've added some other features, like on the fly generation, automatic scrolling, the inference speed tracking, the thought process of the model like deepseek-qwen-1.5B,... we will not go into details here as it will make the blog too long, we will go through some of the ideas and how to implement them but the whole code is available in the repo.

In a recent development, the app generates responses incrementally, producing one token at a time rather than delivering the entire response in a single batch. This approach enhances the user experience, allowing users to begin reading the response as it is being formed. We achieve this by utilizing a callback function within context.completion, which is triggered after each token is generated, enabling us to update the conversation state accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that auto Scrolling ensures that the latest messages or tokens are always visible to the user by automatically scrolling the chat view to the bottom as fresh content is added. To implement that we need we use a reference to the ScrollView to allow programatic control over the scroll position, and we use the scrollToEnd method to scroll to the bottom of the ScrollView when a new message is added to the conversation state. We also define an autoScrollEnabled state variable that will be set to false when the user scrolls up more than 100px from the bottom of the ScrollView.

Inference Speed Tracking is a feature that tracks the time taken to generate each token and displays under each message generated by the model. This feature is easy to implement because the CompletionResult object returned by the context.completion function contains a timings property which is a dictionary containing many metrics about the inference process. We can use the predicted_per_second metric to track the speed of the model.

Recent findings suggest that the thought process is a feature that displays the thought process of the model like deepseek-qwen-1.5B. The app identifies special tokens like and to handle the model's internal reasoning or "thoughts." When a token is encountered, the app enters a "thought block" where it accumulates tokens that represent the model's reasoning. Once the closing token is detected, the accumulated thought is extracted and associated with the message, allowing users to toggle the visibility of the model's reasoning. To implement this we need to add a thought and showThought property to the Message type. message.thought will store the reasoning of the model and message.showThought will be a boolean that will be set to true when the user clicks on the message to toggle the visibility of the thought.

In a recent development, the app uses the react-native-markdown-display package to render markdown in the conversation. This package allows us to render code in a better format.

We added a checkDownloadedModels function to the App.tsx file that will check if the model is already downloaded on the device, if it's not we will download it, if it is we will load it into the context directly, and we added some elements in the UI to show if a model is already downloaded or not.

According to recent reports, we added two vital buttons in the UI, the stop button and the back button. The stop button will stop the generation of the response and the back button will navigate to the model selection screen. For that, We added a handleStopGeneration function to the App.tsx file that will stop the generation of the response by calling context.stop and set the isGenerating state to false. We also added a handleBack function to the App.tsx file that will navigate to the model selection screen by setting the currentPage state to modelSelection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily.

In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”.

Recent findings suggest that aware of an older source? Please comment!

The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY, “don’t repeat yourself”, in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition.

So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule:.

The outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how major file size savings are.

If you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today?

When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work.

In a recent development, to save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition.

In a recent development, skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works). This, then, gives us some data:.

Recent findings suggest that for the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings.

According to recent reports, I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance.

According to recent reports, important note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality—they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. Also note that this leaves out changes after compression—this was not part of the experiment but would be fair to test, too.

According to recent reports, for the question whether UDJO still works today, this should be a yes. It works as well as to even come with file size savings.

Recent findings suggest that maybe you’re curious, too, about what the situation looks like in our field, among web developers. Let’s take some samples on this, too.

It would be valuable to expand this analysis to take more samples and investigate the differences across samples, but there may be something to web professionals using shorter selectors so as to be able to benefit more from UDJO.

As mentioned at the beginning, UDJO’s effectiveness generally depends on the kind of repetition as well as on the length of selectors.

This can be managed, however: While tools like CSS Dedup make no difference between declaration use cases (and are therefore blunt), it is possible to configure them so as to reap the performance benefits.

In a recent development, as the data taken for this article suggest, file size savings may be achieved in most cases. Considering that this is based on safe changes, this means a low-cost performance optimization vector — especially when applied to minified output. It’s still a good idea to couch that against the use of further compression (e.g. gzip/Brotli), but at face value, deduplication indicates how it can reduce the size of CSS.

Sources indicate that for anyone generally interested in CSS optimization, maintainability, and performance, UDJO should probably be part of the overall approach to CSS. But since the technique has been niche and since tooling is latest, I invite you to review, test, and explore this vector. It seems hard to argue that we have reached the ceiling of how far we can take CSS optimization.

Industry observers note that A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

Sources indicate that retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

In a recent development, an idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

We'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

According to recent reports, the client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:.

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:.

To tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only shows up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:.

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:.

Two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

According to recent reports, the draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:.

In a recent development, the fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:.

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

In a recent development, the tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

Sources indicate that instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:.

The ENHANCEMENT in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Sources indicate that set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

It has been revealed that once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still says in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:.

According to recent reports, releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

It has been revealed that the route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:.

The server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a new key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:.

According to recent reports, the catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

In a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a new key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

It has been revealed that keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but claims it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:.

In a recent development, run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a new request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:.

Recent findings suggest that the second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Recent findings suggest that now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:.

To see the concurrent case, add await upcoming Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:.

It has been revealed that one request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

According to recent reports, this design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:.

In a recent development, idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

According to recent reports, with one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

It has been revealed that the same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped.
  • According to recent reports, pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record.
  • Industry observers note that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

According to recent reports, pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

Industry observers note that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

According to recent reports, two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

Recent findings suggest that october was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

Industry observers note that the October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

Sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split showed up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

The record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

House Bill 2801 would make operating or promoting online sweepstakes games illegal in Pennsylvania. Fines would range from $50,000 to $500,000 per violation.

It has been revealed that the bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state at the moment taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

According to recent reports, the bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.

LeRobot goes to driving school: World’s largest open-source self-driving dataset

📅 11 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR of L2D, the world's largest self-driving dataset!
  • State-of-the art Vision Language Models and Large Language Models are trained on open-source image-text corpora sourced from the internet, which spearheaded the recent acceleration of open-source AI.
  • Table 1: Open source self-driving datasets (*excluding lidar and radar).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR of L2D, the world's largest self-driving dataset!

State-of-the art Vision Language Models and Large Language Models are trained on open-source image-text corpora sourced from the internet, which spearheaded the recent acceleration of open-source AI. Despite these breakthroughs, the adoption of end-to-end AI within the robotics and automotive community remains low, primarily due to a lack of high quality, large scale multimodal datasets like OXE. To unlock the potential for robotics AI, Yaak teamed up with the LeRobot team at 🤗 and is excited to announce Learning to Drive (L2D) to the robotics AI community. L2D is the world’s largest multimodal dataset aimed at building an open-sourced spatial intelligence for the automotive domain with first class support for 🤗’s LeRobot training pipeline and models. Drawing inspiration from the best practices of source version control, Yaak also invites the AI community to search and discover novel episodes in our entire dataset (> 1 PetaBytes), and queue their collection for review to be merged into future release (R5+).

Table 1: Open source self-driving datasets (*excluding lidar and radar). Source.

L2D was collected with identical sensor suites installed on 60 EVs operated by driving schools in 30 German cities over the span of 3 years. The policies in L2D are divided into two groups — expert policies executed by driving instructors and student policies by learner drivers. Both the policy groups include natural language instructions for the driving task. For example, “When you have the right of way, take the third exit from the roundabout, carefully driving over the pedestrian crossing”.

Fig 1: Visualization: Nutron (3 of 6 cameras shown for clarity) Instructions: “When you have the right of way, drive through the roundabout and take the third exit”.

Expert policies have zero driving mistakes and are considered as optimal, whereas student policies have known sub optimality (Fig 2).

Fig 2: Student policy with jerky steering to prevent going into lane of the incoming truck.

Recent findings suggest that both groups cover all driving scenarios that are mandatory for completion to obtain a driving license within the EU (German version), for example, overtaking, roundabouts and train tracks. In the release (See below R3+), for suboptimal student policies, a natural language reasoning for sub-optimality will be included. F.ex “incorrect/jerky handling of the steering wheel in the proximity of in-coming traffic ” (Fig 2).

Sources indicate that L2D (R2+) aims to be the largest open-source self-driving dataset that empowers the AI community with unique and diverse ‘episodes’ for training end-to-end spatial intelligence. With the inclusion of a full spectrum of driving policies (student and experts), L2D captures the intricacies of safely operating a vehicle. To fully represent an operational self-driving fleet, we include episodes with diverse environment conditions, sensor failures, construction zones and non-functioning traffic signals.

Both the expert and student policy groups are captured with the identical sensor setup detailed in the table below. Six RGB cameras capture the vehicle’s context in 360o, and on-board GPS captures the vehicle location and heading. An IMU collects the vehicle dynamics, and we read speed, gas/brake pedal, steering angle, turn signal and gear from the vehicle’s CAN interface. We synchronized all modality types with the front left camera (observation.images.front_left) using their respective unix epoch timestamps. We also interpolated data points where feasible to enhance precision (See Table 2.) and finally reduced the sampling rate to 10 hz.

Fig 3: Multimodal data visualization with Visualization: Nutron (only 3 of 6 cameras shown for clarity).

Table 2: Modality types, LeRobot v3.0 key, shape and interpolation strategy.

It has been revealed that L2D follows the official German driving task catalog (detailed version) definition of driving tasks, driving sub-tasks and task definition. We assign a unique Task ID and natural language instructions to all episodes. The LeRobot:task for all episodes is set to “Follow the waypoints while adhering to traffic rules and regulations”. The table below shows a few sample episodes, their natural language instruction, driving tasks and subtasks. Both expert and student policies have an identical Task ID for similar scenarios, whereas the instructions vary with the episode.

Table 3: Sample episodes in L2D, their instructions and Task ID derived from EU driving task catalog.

According to recent reports, we automate the construction of the instructions and waypoints using the vehicle position (GPS), Open-Source Routing Machine, OpenStreetMap and a Large Language Model (LLM) (See below). The natural language queries are constructed to closely follow the turn-by-turn navigation available in most GPS navigation devices. The waypoints (Fig 4) are computed by map-matching the raw GPS trace to the OSM graph and sampling 10 equidistant points (orange) spanning 100 meters from the vehicles current location (green), and serve as drive-by-waypoints.

Fig 4: L2D 6x RGB cameras, waypoints (orange) and vehicle location (green) Instructions: drive straight up to the stop stop sign and then when you have right of way, merge with the moving traffic from the left.

According to recent reports, we collected the expert and student policies with a fleet of 60 KIA E-niro driving school vehicles operating in 30 German cities, with an identical sensor suite. The multimodal logs collected with the fleet are unstructured and void of any task or instructions information. To search and curate for episodes we enrich the raw multimodal logs with information extracted through map matching the GPS traces with OSRM and assigning node and way tags from OSM (See next section). Coupled with a LLM, this enrichment step enables searching for episodes through the natural language description of the task.

According to recent reports, for efficiently searching relevant episodes, we enrich the GPS traces with turn information obtained by map-matching the traces using OSRM. We additionally use the map-matched route and assign route features, route restrictions and route maneuvers, collectively referred to as route tasks, to the trajectory using OSM (See sample Map). Appendix A1-A2 provides for more details on the route tasks we assign to GPS traces.

Fig 5: Driving tasks assigned to raw GPS trace (View map).

The route tasks which get assigned to the map-matched route, are assigned the beginning and end timestamps (unix epoch), which equates to the time when the vehicle enters and exits the geospatial linestring or point defined by the task (Fig 6).

Fig 6: Pink: GNSS trace, Blue: Matched route, tasks: Yield, Train crossing and Roundabout (View Map).

In a recent development, we perform semantic spatiotemporal indexing of our multimodal data with the route tasks as described in Fig 5. This step provides a rich semantic overview of our multimodal data. To search within the semantic space for representative episodes by instructions, for example, “drive up to the roundabout and when you have the right of way turn right”, we built a LLM-powered multimodal natural language search, to search within all our drive data (> 1 PetaBytes) and retrieve matching episodes.

We structured the natural language queries (instructions) to closely resemble turn-by-turn navigation available in GPS navigation devices. To translate instructions to route tasks, we prompt the LLM with the instructions and steer its output to a list of route features, route restrictions, route maneuvers and retrieve episodes assigned to these route tasks. We perform a strict validation of the output from the LLM with a pydantic model to minimize hallucinations. Specifically we use llama-3.3-70b and steer the output to the schema defined by the pydantic model. To further improve the quality of the structured output, we used approx 30 pairs of known natural language queries and route tasks for in-context learning. Appendix A. 2 provides details on the in-context learning pairs we used.

Instructions: Drive up to the roundabout and when you have the right of way turn right.

L2D on 🤗 is converted to LeRobotDataset v2.1 and LeRobotDataset v3.0 format to fully leverage the current and future models supported within LeRobot. The AI community can now build end-to-end self-driving models leveraging the state-of-the-art imitation learning and reinforcement learning models for real world robotics like ACT, Diffusion Policy, and Pi0.

Recent findings suggest that existing self-driving datasets (table below) focus on intermediate perception and planning tasks like 2D/3D object detection, tracking, segmentation and motion planning, which require high quality annotations making them difficult to scale. Instead L2D is focused on the development of end-to-end learning which learns to predict actions (policy) directly from sensor input (Table 1.). These models leverage internet pre-trained VLM and VLAM.

Robotics AI models’ performances are bounded by the quality of the episodes within the training set. To ensure the highest quality episodes, we strategy a phased release for L2D. With each fresh release we add additional information about the episodes. Each release R1+ is a superset of the previous releases to ensure clean episode history.

In a recent development, 1. instructions: Natural language instruction of the driving task 2. task_id: Mapping of episodes to EU mandated driving tasks Task ID 3. observation.state.route : Information about lane count, turn lanes from OSM 4. suboptimal: Natural language description for the cause of sub-optimal policies.

Industry observers note that the entire multimodal dataset collected by Yaak with the driving school fleet is 5x larger than the planned release. To further the growth of L2D beyond R4, we invite the AI community to search and uncover scenarios within our entire data collection and build a community powered open-source L2D. The AI community can now search for episodes through our natural language search and queue their collection for review by the community for merging them into the upcoming releases. With L2D, we hope to unlock an ImageNet moment for spatial intelligence.

Fig 7: Searching episodes by natural language instructions.

For R0, R1 we recommend using LeRobotDataset, with revision=[R0|R1], which can be used directly from the pypi release of LeRobot. For R2+, please follow installation outlined here or install from main as below, as we recommend using StreamingLeRobotDataset as R3 is is Dataset v3.0 format.

In a recent development, for real world testing of the AI models trained with L2D and LeRobot, we invite the AI community to submit models for closed loop testing with a safety driver, starting summer of 2025. The AI community will be able to queue their models for closed loop testing, on our fleet and choose the tasks they’d like the model to be evaluated on and, for example, navigating roundabouts or parking. The model would run in inference mode (Jetson AGX or similar) on-board the vehicle. The models will drive the vehicle with LeRobot driver in two modes.

List of route restrictions. We consider route tags from OSM a restriction if it imposes restrictions on the policy, for example speed limit, yield or construction. Route features are physical structures along the route, for example inclines, tunnels and pedestrian crossing. Route maneuvers are different scenarios which a driver encounters during a normal operation of the vehicle in an urban environment, for example, multilane left turns and roundabouts.

OSM = Openstreetmap, VLM= Vision Language Model, derived: Hand crafted rules with OSM data.

It has been revealed that prompt template and pseudo code for configuring the LLM using groq to parse natural language queries into structured prediction for route features, restrictions and maneuvers with a pydantic model. The natural language queries are constructed to closely follow the turn-by-turn navigation available in most GPS navigation devices.

Example pairs (showing 3 / 30) for in-context learning to steer the structured prediction of LLM, where ParsedInstructionModel is a pydantic model.

Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • Recent findings suggest that when CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.
  • Industry observers note that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

Recent findings suggest that when CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

Industry observers note that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

Frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

Sources indicate that CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the company I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

Recent findings suggest that before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the organization I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

These questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional organization I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

According to recent reports, wheelman isn’t an ordinary tech giant, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the tech giant, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

Industry observers note that let’s imagine I’m designing a latest landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Sources indicate that before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

In a recent development, only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

Sources indicate that I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

Wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

It has been revealed that I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

It has been revealed that using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

In a recent development, the modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

According to recent reports, the result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

One thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

It has been revealed that wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

In a recent development, A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Recent findings suggest that combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

The point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same firm.

In a recent development, twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

Wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

In a recent development, and this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.

Open R1: Upgrade #3

📅 11 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last few weeks, we have focused our efforts on reproducing the competitive programming (code reasoning) aspects of the DeepSeek-R1 recipe.
  • Here’s an overview of how the OlympicCoder models stack up against various instruction fine-tuned and reasoning models.
  • Read on to learn how we built the dataset, benchmark and models!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last few weeks, we have focused our efforts on reproducing the competitive programming (code reasoning) aspects of the DeepSeek-R1 recipe.

In this post, we are excited to share:.

Here’s an overview of how the OlympicCoder models stack up against various instruction fine-tuned and reasoning models. We find that training models on CodeForces-CoTs produces top-tier performance, with OlympicCoder-32B outperforming all open-weight models we tested, including some that are over 100x larger 🤯.

Read on to learn how we built the dataset, benchmark and models!

International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI).

CodeForces is one of the most popular websites among competitive programmers, hosting regular contests where participants must solve challenging algorithmic optimization problems. The challenging nature of these problems makes them an interesting dataset to improve and test models’ code reasoning capabilities.

While previous efforts such as DeepMind’s CodeContests dataset have compiled a large number of CodeForces problems, today we are releasing our own open-r1/codeforces dataset, with more than 10k problems covering the very first contests all the way to 2025, ~3k of which were not included in DeepMind’s dataset. Additionally, for around 60% of the problems, we have included the editorial, which is an explanation, written by the contest organizers, explaining the correct solution. You will also find 3 correct solutions per problem extracted from the official website.

Furthermore, we are releasing open-r1/codeforces-cots, which contains chain of thought generations produced by DeepSeek-R1 on these problems, where we asked the model to produce solutions in C++ (the main language used in competitive programming) and Python, totaling close to 100k samples.

We fine-tuned Qwen2.5 Coder Instruct 7B and 32B on this dataset, resulting in our OlympicCoder-7B and OlympicCoder-32B models. You will find more details on these models further along in the blogpost.

While datasets like DeepMind’s contests and others containing competitive programming problems include test cases and claim to be verifiable, these test cases are often a small subset of the full suite used on contest websites. CodeForces, in particular, caps displayed test cases at ~500 characters, which means that these datasets only contain the shorter, easier test cases that fit into this limit.

As an example, we took 7 problems for which the R1 generated solution passed all the public test cases and tried submitting them to the CodeForces platform:.

Although they passed the shorter tests, every single one of these solutions failed on the full test set. This underscores the need for new fully verifiable competitive programming dataset. While we initiative to try model-based solutions to generate and validate additional challenging tests that may be added to our CodeForces dataset in the future, for now we went looking for fully available problem data elsewhere.

The International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) is one of five international science olympiads (if you are familiar with AIME, IOI is the programming equivalent of IMO, for which the very best students who take part in AIME are invited) and tests a very select group of high school students (4 per country) in complex algorithmic problems.

The problems are extremely challenging, and the full test sets are available and released under a permissive (CC-BY) license. This means that IOI is the perfect dataset to test a model's code reasoning capabilities.

In IOI, each problem has several subtasks, each with different input constraints. To solve a subtask, a submission needs to pass all of its test cases within the (strict) time limits. While the final subtask is usually the “full problem”, some subtasks effectively describe a much easier (more constrained) problem, and contestants very often target specific subtasks to get partial scores instead of just trying to solve the full problem (perfect scores are relatively rare).

Recent findings suggest that following a recent OpenAI paper where o1 live competed at IOI’2024 (the last iteration), we similarly processed all problems from IOI’2024 (as well as previous IOIs up until 2020), and split them into their subtasks, such that each prompt would ask models to solve one specific subtask. We release the processed problem statements, as well as all grading/checker files required to run them and test cases in open-r1/ioi and open-r1/ioi-test-cases.

We created custom code to run solutions (many problems have complicated setups, requiring a “manager” process communicating with several processes running the user submission and special checkers to validate solutions) and to grade according to IOI rules, which is available at https://github.com/huggingface/ioi, and evaluated over 40 leading reasoning models on IOI’2024.

At IOI, contestants have a 50 submission limit per problem. We generated 50 submissions for each subtask and then applied a selection strategy similar to the one used by OpenAI to get scores under contest conditions for each problem. Results can be found below, where the horizontal lines represent the threshold for bronze, silver and gold models from real contest data. While o1 comes very close to bronze, ultimately no model would reach the medal threshold (50th percentile of contestants).

Our OlympicCoder models (in red), do fairly well compared to other frontier models, even surpassing some closed source models (in gold) such as claude-3.7-sonnet-thinking, and OlympicCoder-32B even outperforms o1-mini and DeepSeek-R1, the model we distilled from, on the 50 submission limit setting.

It has been revealed that an key note is that our submission strategy may penalize non reasoning models, such as Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, OlympicCoder-32B’s base model. To simulate real contest conditions, in which a submission’s score is only known after it is actually submitted, we employed a round robin submission strategy similar to the one employed by OpenAI for o1-ioi: we start by submitting a solution that targets the last subtask of the problem, then one targeting the second to last, and so on, only evaluating a solution when it is picked for submission. We skip over submissions targeting subtasks that have already been solved by previously selected submissions, and within each targeted subtask we prefer submissions from longer generations — which is a criteria that makes sense for reasoning models, but less so for other models.

If we remove the 50 submission limit (which would place us outside the contest conditions), and evaluate all submissions we generated (50 per subtask), we obtain the following results:.

While creating the OlympicCoder models, we ran a large number of SFT experiments to understand the role of various filters applied to the CodeForces dataset. We found the following subsets of open-r1/codeforces-cots gave the best overall performance:.

Note that we only focused on the C++ solutions, but blending in the Python solutions would likely boost performance even further.

According to recent reports, we used LiveCodeBench as a test bed for our models and then ran the best performing checkpoints through the much harder IOI benchmark. We tested various hyperparameter configurations to train our models and settled on the following:.

Below we share some lessons we learned from tuning the Qwen2.5 Coder models on R1 reasoning traces.

In a recent development, sample packing is a widely used method to efficiently process variable-length sequences and accelerate training. As shown in the figure below, the way this works concatenating training samples (coloured) into equal sized chunks that removes the need to use padding tokens (gray) across batches:.

With packing, samples can overlap across the boundaries of each chunk, but in practice this doesn’t matter too much if most of the samples are much smaller than the chunk size.

However, for the reasoning traces we distilled from R1, we wondered whether packing could hurt performance because many traces are long and the fraction of clipped answers could be high. This means it may be difficult to train the model to attend to long context information, particularly when the question and answer have been packed into different chunks.

As shown in the striking figure below, we found that packing substantially hurts the model’s performance: with packing, the model is barely able to solve problems from LiveCodebench, but without packing, the performance improves over several epochs before plateauing out:.

We suspect this stark difference is accentuated by the fact that our training sets only consist of C++ solutions, while LiveCodeBench only evaluates performance on Python. Nevertheless, we found that across all datasets we ablated, packing was consistently worse.

For most SFT experiments that we’ve run with Qwen models, a learning rate of 2e-5 is typically good enough to get strong performance. However, when applying SFT with reasoning data to an existing instruct model, we found that significant performance gains could be had by using a much larger learning rate of 4e-5. As shown in the figure below, the difference across each doubling of the learning rate amounted to almost 10 points improvement on LiveCodeBench!

When we created the solutions_w_editorials subset of open-r1/codeforces-cots, our intuition was that by providing R1 with the problem and solution, we would obtain better reasoning traces. Surprisingly, this intuition was not borne out during evaluation, with the naive sampling from problem statements giving a modest, yet consistent boost during training:.

In a recent development, while vibe testing some of our models, we encountered a peculiar phenomenon: if prompted with in-domain queries (like competitive coding), the model would emit the expected long CoT within and tokens, followed by the final answer. However, for out-of-domain queries like “What is the capital of Switzerland”, the model would revert back to the behaviour of the original instruct model!

Here’s an example of a simple query failing to return the long CoT:.

Assistant: 2. It is one of the simplest mathematical addition problems. 1 + 1 equals 2. This problem is often used as a riddle or puzzle, particularly in job interviews or online tests to determine a candidate's ability to solve problems swiftly. While it may seem obvious to most people, it can be a useful question for employers to assess critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Additionally, it is an vital concept in mathematics and forms the basis for more complex arithmetic operations. So next time someone asks you what 1+1 is, you can confidently state that it is 2!

Recent findings suggest that in this solution, we define a function add_numbers that takes two parameters a and b and returns their sum. We then call this function with 1 and 1, storing the result in the variable result, which is then printed. This demonstrates a straightforward way to compute and display the sum of two integers. The example serves as a simple yet effective illustration of basic arithmetic operations in Python.

However, if we prefill the assistant's response with the desired behaviour emerges:.

According to recent reports, assistant: Okay, I need to answer the question "What is 1+1?" Let's see. Oh right, 1 plus 1 equals 2. But wait, maybe there's more to it. Like, what if someone asks in a different way? Or perhaps considering other number bases? Like in base 10 it's 2, but in binary it's 10. Hmm, but the question is straightforward. The user probably expects the simple answer. So the correct answer here is 2. Should I just state that? Yes, 1 + 1 is equal to 2. Is there anything else you'd like to know about this calculation?

Recent findings suggest that this suggests that when distilling reasoning traces into an existing post-trained model, one should enforce prefilling by default in the final model’s chat template. Incidentally, this is also what DeepSeek does with their distilled models and the behaviour above may be the reason why. (It is also amusing to speculate whether hitting the “think” button on popular chat UIs is simply prefilling the assistant response 🙂).

Combining all these lessons produced OlympicCoder-7B, which matches the performance of DeepSeek’s distilled model and significantly improves on the base Qwen2.5-Coder one:.

Sources indicate that throughout the training of OlympicCoder-7B, we found DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 was sufficient to train each model with 32k context on a single node of 8 x H100s. However, when we tried scaling up our recipe to 32B, we ran into a host of memory complications. In particular, our runs would OOM once the context was scaled beyond 20k tokens, even on 16 nodes 😢. This wasn’t ideal as 20% of the CodeForces-CoTs traces are larger than 20k tokens, which means they would get truncated during training.

The root of the problem is that transformers and trl do not yet support context parallelism, although see this problem to track progress.

In the meantime, we explored a variety of memory saving techniques and found that combining FSDP with the paged_adamw_8bit optimizer allowed us to scale the context to 22,528 tokens: still not ideal, but only 9% of the data was truncated.

Recent progress has been made to improve the implementation of GRPO in TRL, bringing enhancements that further boost efficiency, scalability, and resource utilization. Here’s a summary of the most vital changes since the last update:.

One of the main bottlenecks of GRPO is the same as for any online method: generation takes time. A key way to make GRPO more sample-efficient is to reuse generated samples multiple times during optimization instead of discarding them after a single use. This technique was actually introduced a long time ago with PPO.

For GRPO, the number of times a sample is reused is denoted as μ.

It is now possible to reuse generated samples multiple times, significantly speeding up the process.

However, be cautious—if μ is too large, it can negatively impact learning. Based on our experience, a good balance is between 2 and 4.

Recent findings suggest that when training a model, not all rewards are equally key. For example, we may want the model to prioritize correctness over formatting, rather than treating both aspects equally.

According to recent reports, to address this, it is now possible to assign different weights to different rewards, allowing finer control over the optimization process. By adjusting these weights, we can guide the model to focus more on the aspects that matter most for a given task.

Several smaller but impactful improvements have been made to GRPO:.

Starting with a randomly selected pool of 200k samples, we created six distinct SFT datasets based on the following filtering rules:.

Industry observers note that for filtering in data-constrained settings, both precision and recall are vital considerations. Therefore, we didn't run each experiment with the same token budget but rather trained on single epoch over all data. For the model, we chose Qwen7B-Instruct and fine-tuned it with RoPE extension to a 32k context length and cosine schedule. To track performance progression, we evaluated the models at every 40th step on AIME-24, AIME-25, and MATH-500 using lighteval. The results are summarized below:.

Based on our findings, the optimal filtering method depends heavily on the training token budget. For shorter runs, stricter verification methods offer significant advantages. As a general recommendation, we recommend combining llama verification with math_verify—as done in the LorMV dataset.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges. The vote would turn regulatory discretion into a statutory ban just as the CFTC proposes looser rules, and the House has only weeks to act.

Sens. Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act. It is the first prediction-market bill the Senate has passed this Congress. The measure now heads to the House.

It has been revealed that under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations. Sports contracts are not covered.

In a recent development, curtis made a moral case for the bill on the Senate floor. “There should be no financial incentive to profit from terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” he said.

In a recent development, whether such contracts can trade right now rests on the CFTC’s discretion. The bill would replace that discretion with a prohibition written into statute.

Industry observers note that the timing puts lawmakers and the regulator on different tracks. CFTC Chair Selig prepares to rewrite the prediction-market rules. The agency’s proposed rule would amend Regulation 40.11 and add Appendix F to Part 40. The agency would use that framework to decide when a contract linked to war, terrorism, assassination, gaming or illegal conduct is against the public interest.

In a recent development, that framework would give the agency more room, not less. The proposal would say only that the CFTC may find such contracts contrary to the public interest, dropping the categorical prohibitions in the current rule, according to the Congressional Research Service. The agency withdrew a stricter 2024 proposal in February 2026.

For exchanges, the difference is significant. An agency can revise a rule through its own process. A ban in statute would keep those categories off the table regardless of how the CFTC’s rules change.

Sources indicate that the DEATH BETS Act targets a specific set of contracts. Sports is a different matter for operators. Schiff and Curtis have also introduced the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act. That bill would bar sports-betting and casino-style contracts on these exchanges.

In a recent development, A unanimous vote on death and war contracts does not prove the same support exists for a sports ban. It does show that senators are willing to legislate directly on what prediction markets can list, rather than leave the question to the CFTC.

That makes the vote an early sign of how much support Congress has for limiting these platforms. It comes while the exchanges are fighting state gambling regulators in court. Operators now face pressure from state regulators, the CFTC’s rulemaking and Congress at the same time.

The House now has a short window. So far, the chamber’s leadership has given no word on putting the bill to a floor vote, FinanceFeeds reported.

Industry observers note that carving has a cost. Because file system information is ignored, names and folder structure are usually lost, which is why scan results often show generic names. That detail matters because a JPEG can contain an embedded thumbnail with its own markers, so stopping at the first end marker would cut a file short.

The distinction matters. Recovery retrieves missing or inaccessible data, while repair tries to fix damage that affects a file’s usability. Some cases need one, the other or both.
