#173759. Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1505 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks ↗ Open Full Page

Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”.
  • When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills.
  • In a recent development, don’t get me wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”.

I’ll agree with Ashutosh there.

When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills. Nevertheless, after reading Ashutosh’s article a few times, here’s a meme showing how I’d feel using such an elaborate algorithm for something as mundane as staggering the animations of some characters as they scroll into view.

In a recent development, don’t get me wrong. I know the complexity is because Ashutosh is going for a generic solution in which we can connect a “progress value to an animation, scroll progress, or any other input to drive the staggering.”.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, I can dream up a scenario in which this might be what we want: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on the user’s progress through the vocals measured via speech recognition. Running that kind of animation “not as a collection of independently timed objects, but as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value” might be exactly what the doctor ordered. This would be true because the staggered animations could be interrelated, and the overall animation would be driven by a custom input that’s not built into the browser.

But unlike this hypothetical scenario, replacing the passage of time with scroll progress to control animations is already built into modern CSS. I contend that we’d need a better reason to roll our own implementation than the examples Ashutosh gives.

Ashutosh showcases a scroll-driven use case as “one of those ideal scenarios where the stagger formula shines.” But a red flag that we’re in danger of reinventing something we can get for free is that the spec for scroll-driven animations is cognizant that if we opt to base an animation on scroll progress rather than on time, then, as Ashutosh notes, “the animation we are going to achieve is different from traditional ones because we don’t include time in our considerations.” This is no surprise to the creators of scroll timeline, and the MDN docs make Ashutosh’s point in different words when introducing scroll timeline.

Recent findings suggest that the docs also point out that animation-delay is only meaningful when we are using the default time-based document timeline. Therefore, animation-delay does not affect scroll-driven animations. But this is why CSS introduced animation-range-start, which allows us to delay a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress and not time.

So, as esoteric and trippy as the math-heavy approach appears, that could be because we are doing something that should be simple in an unusual way.

Let’s see if I’m right by rewriting Ashutosh’s demo to remove reliance on custom CSS functions and use animation-range-start instead.

Ashutosh’s rework of Frontend Masters’ animated tally of donations in the site footer is a nifty, subtle use of scrollytelling that makes the user feel invested in revealing that number.

According to recent reports, sidenote: The only qualm I have about this use of scroll-driven animations for the donation tally is that it might be too subtle — if the user scrolls too rapidly, the animated entrance of each digit might occur too quickly to notice. Therefore, the donation tally could be a good case study for comparing the merits of scroll-driven versus scroll-triggered animations as design options. However, that story will have to wait for another day, as the focus of this article is only to show that the staggered scrolling CSS animations can be greatly simplified.

According to recent reports, in the video below, my eight-year-old narrates, as a reminder that simplicity is key to the web we’re choosing to leave to the next generation. He compares the complex math in the original demo source code with my animation-range-start fork. He shows the two versions working side by side, demonstrating that sometimes the only thing we lose by judiciously deleting complex code is a headache.

Sources indicate that and for those using a Chromium-based browser, my fork of the Pen is below. You can peruse the CSS to see how it does away with the grand unified theory of staggered scrolling animations, and instead deals only with the problem at hand. Since I preserved the original functionality, you’ll need to scroll gradually to appreciate the staggered animations.

I once tackled a related problem with a mathematical formula in a previous article, which touched on how we can use sibling-index() to “increment animation-range-start to stagger the delay before characters fade in as the user scrolls.”.

The truth is, if we refuse to fall into the coding trap of possibly abstracting the wrong thing, we can use one line of CSS to replace a formula that took 1.3k words in the Frontend Masters article for me to still not fully grasp:.

The 2.5% increment for each sibling is because there are eight characters to stagger, and I wanted to choreograph the animations such that they are delayed in evenly-spaced increments till the last character makes its animated entrance when it reaches 30% of the containment range (10% + 20%).

It was inadvertently apt to describe the original post as “CSS on drugs.” Once you reinvent one built-in CSS feature, you can’t stop there. You find yourself having to recreate more stuff that CSS should be able to do by itself. Sure enough, even after we get through the custom formulas that make scroll timelines do what they already do, Ashutosh confirms, “Unfortunately, we can’t use easing keywords or cubic-bezier() or linear() functions here. We are left on our own to create easing functions.”.

We shouldn’t have to because, despite the word “timing” in the name of the animation-timing-function property, MDN is clear that “animation-timing-function has the same effect when creating CSS scroll-driven animations as it does for regular time-based animations.” I know from experience that scroll-driven animations work with animation-timing-function because I used scroll-driven animations with steps() to animate a sprite climbing a ladder in my CSS scrollytelling game.

The problem in the land of CSS on drugs is that after merging all the staggered animations into one, the easing applies to the entire master timeline rather than to each element. It’s not a flaw in CSS, but a logical consequence of the “holistic effect driven by one progress value.” Be careful what you wish for.

To be fair, over the years I have seen impressive results from developers reinventing things the browsers already do, usually because the reinvention gives us control we couldn’t obtain otherwise.

I mention this to show that reinventing something like scroll timelines isn’t an inherently bad idea if we know why we’re doing it. After all, scroll timelines are only a reinvention of what developers were doing for decades prior in JavaScript. Having stated that, I believe my rewrite of the staggered scroll-driven tally demo indicates that the original approach was overkill for that example. Do let me know in the comments if you see any advantage to the custom CSS functions version over using animation-range-start.

And yet the thought that stuck with me about the Frontend Masters post is that it opens the door to linking the progress of a CSS animation to any arbitrary input value that could be used in a conceptually similar way to scroll timelines.

It has been revealed that this really appeals to me, because even when I first started writing about scroll timelines in 2024, I mentioned that “I would love to see other input controls that can manipulate animation timelines. Imagine text fields progressing animations as you fill them out.” Or how about an animation driven by how closely the new password you are typing matches a password scheme?

Sidenote: Adam Argyle’s Prop For That library, which Geoff recently wrote up, makes it more convenient than ever to expose validation information about a field via CSS custom properties.

I can add my hypothetical karaoke machine scenario to the wishlist of custom progress inputs for controlling animations. How about an animation driven by the user’s progress through a quiz or a shopping cart?

Custom animation timelines would open the door to all sorts of engaging user experiences—but the code Ashutosh has shared may be the closest we are likely to get to driving CSS animations using values other than time or scroll progress.

Let me know in the comments if you can think of other types of progress inputs that could drive CSS animations to create immersive, interactive experiences.

Try out Gemma 3 now 👉🏻 Gemma 3 Space.

Gemma 3 is Google's latest iteration of open weight LLMs. It comes in four sizes, 1 billion, 4 billion, 12 billion, and 27 billion parameters with base (pre-trained) and instruction-tuned versions. Gemma 3 goes multimodal! The 4, 12, and 27 billion parameter models can process both images and text, while the 1B variant is text only.

The input context window length has been increased from Gemma 2’s 8k to 32k for the 1B variants, and 128k for all others. As is the case with other VLMs (vision-language models), Gemma 3 generates text in response to the user inputs, which may consist of text and, optionally, images. Example uses include question answering, analyzing image content, summarizing documents, etc.

Industry observers note that while these are multimodal models, one can use it as a text only model (as an LLM) without loading the vision encoder in memory. We will talk about this in more detail later in the inference section.

The three core enhancements in Gemma 3 over Gemma 2 are:.

In this section, we will cover the technical details that lead to these enhancements. It is interesting to start with the knowledge of Gemma 2 and explore what was necessary to make these models even better. This exercise will help you think like the Gemma team and appreciate the details!

Recent findings suggest that scaling context length to 128k tokens could be achieved efficiently without training models from scratch. Instead, models are pretrained with 32k sequences, and only the 4B, 12B, and 27B models are scaled to 128k tokens at the end of pretraining, saving significant compute. Positional embeddings, like RoPE, are adjusted—upgraded from a 10k base frequency in Gemma 2 to 1M in Gemma 3—and scaled by a factor of 8 for longer contexts.

KV Cache management is optimized using Gemma 2’s sliding window interleaved attention. Hyperparameters are tuned to interleave 5 local layers with 1 global layer (previously 1:1) and reduce the window size to 1024 tokens (down from 4096). Crucially, memory savings are achieved without degrading perplexity.

Gemma 3 models use SigLIP as an image encoder, which encodes images into tokens that are ingested into the language model. The vision encoder takes as input square images resized to 896x896. Fixed input resolution makes it more difficult to process non-square aspect ratios and high-resolution images. To address these limitations during inference, the images can be adaptively cropped, and each crop is then resized to 896x896 and encoded by the image encoder. This algorithm, called pan and scan, effectively enables the model to zoom in on smaller details in the image.

In a recent development, similar to PaliGemma, attention in Gemma 3 works differently for text and image inputs. Text is handled with one-way attention, where the model focuses only on previous words in a sequence. Images, on the other hand, get full attention with no masks, allowing the model to look at every part of the image in a bidirectional manner, giving it a complete, unrestricted understanding of the visual input.

One can see in the figure below that the image tokens are provided with bi-directional attention (the entire square is lit up) while the text tokens have causal attention. It also shows how attention works with the sliding window algorithm.

In a recent development, to make a LLM multilingual, the pretraining dataset incorporates more languages. The dataset of Gemma 3 has double the amount of multilingual data to improve language coverage.

It has been revealed that to account for the changes, the tokenizer is the same as that of Gemini 2.0. It is a SentencePiece tokenizer with 262K entries. The latest tokenizer significantly improves the encoding of Chinese, Japanese and Korean text, at the expense of a slight increase of the token counts for English and Code.

For the curious mind, here is the technical report on Gemma 3, to dive deep into the enhancements.

According to recent reports, the LMSys Elo score is a number that ranks language models based on how well they perform in head-to-head competitions, judged by human preferences. On LMSys Chatbot Arena, Gemma 3 27B IT reports an Elo score of 1339, and ranks among the top 10 best models, including leading closed ones. The Elo is comparable to o1-preview and is above other non-thinking open models. This score is achieved with Gemma 3 working on text-only inputs, like the other LLMs in the table.

Gemma 3 has been evaluated across benchmarks like MMLU-Pro (27B: 67.5), LiveCodeBench (27B: 29.7), and Bird-SQL (27B: 54.4), showing competitive performance compared to closed Gemini models. Tests like GPQA Diamond (27B: 42.4) and MATH (27B: 69.0) highlight its reasoning and math skills, while FACTS Grounding (27B: 74.9) and MMMU (27B: 64.9) demonstrate strong factual accuracy and multimodal abilities. However, it lags in SimpleQA (27B: 10.0) for basic facts. When compared to Gemini 1.5 models, Gemma 3 is often close—and sometimes better—proving its value as an accessible, high-performing option.

According to recent reports, gemma 3 comes with day zero support in transformers. All you need to do is install transformers from the stable release of Gemma 3.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A bill now sponsored by Wyoming's Legislative Management Council would make running a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a felony. The draft also targets the vendors behind these sites, which raises the legal risk for payment processors and B2B suppliers.

Sources indicate that wyoming is moving to outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos. Its bill reaches past operators to the companies that keep them running. The draft reached the Legislative Management Council through Sen. John Kolb, co-chair of the Select Committee on Gaming. The council also agreed to sponsor two other gaming bills, one on pari-mutuel wagering breakage and one on background checks.

The gaming committee claims casino-style sweepstakes games are already available in Wyoming. These games let players wager with currency redeemable for money or prizes. The draft would state that the state’s prize-promotion laws do not authorize them. People who take part only as players are exempt.

Sources indicate that working draft 0.4 widens the definition of professional gambling. It covers anyone who knowingly provides services to an online sweepstakes game. Those services include geolocation, payment processing, hosting, game content and advertising. Vendors and processors would carry legal risk, not only the brands that face players.

The approach follows Oklahoma. Under SB 1589, companies that provide geolocation or payment services to a sweepstakes operator after November 1 face the same felony charges as the operator. Oklahoma lawmakers overrode Gov. Kevin Stitt’s veto of that bill. The votes were 34-10 in the Senate and 68-19 in the House.

Recent findings suggest that complaints to the regulator help explain the push. Wyoming Gaming Commission Executive Director Nick Larramendy described his office’s complaint load to lawmakers. Sweepstakes complaints arrive each week in greater numbers than complaints about any regulated form of gaming. Most come from players whose accounts were shut down when they tried to cash out a jackpot. The operators are often offshore, where the commission cannot reach them.

Taking such sites down would be easier with the ban in place, in Larramendy’s view, because the commission would have firmer ground for working with the Department of Justice and internet service providers. His testimony also pointed to a well-known payment processor. It serves offshore sweepstakes sites while holding a Wyoming online sports betting permit.

The bill has drawn broad support at each step. At its October 5-6 meeting, the gaming committee voted 6-0 in a roll call to recommend the amended draft. It also renamed the bill ‘Online sweepstakes prohibited.’ Lawmakers weighed a rival draft, 27LSO-0200, which would have regulated sweepstakes rather than banned them. Only the prohibition draft went to the council.

Recent findings suggest that A sweepstakes ban bill in Pennsylvania has stalled. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced HB 2801 on September 24. The bill has had no hearing or vote in the House Gaming Oversight Committee. The state’s legislative session ends November 30.

In a recent development, wyoming’s draft is written as a Senate File. It now goes to the 2027 General Session, which is scheduled to begin January 12, 2027. A general session can last no more than 40 legislative days. If passed, the ban would take effect July 1, 2027.

What an AI Marketing Agent Actually Does, and How to Build a Guarded One

It has been revealed that an AI marketing agent is a system that pairs a language model with access to real tools, such as a CRM, an ad platform API or a CMS, and lets it work toward a goal instead of following a fixed script. That is the core idea. Much of what gets labeled agentic marketing is either a wrapper around that loop or a scheduled job with a newly introduced name.

It has been revealed that this article breaks down the mechanics in code terms, walks through a minimal guarded agent loop with tests, and gives a framework for deciding what to build, what to buy and what to keep away from any autonomous system. Product capabilities change swiftly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

In a recent development, ● An agent is a goal, a tool set and a loop. The model chooses the next action at runtime instead of following branches you wrote in advance.

● Guardrails belong in code. Spend caps, allow-lists and approval thresholds should never depend on the prompt.

It has been revealed that ● The prototype is the easy part. Validation, retries, logging and evaluation are where the weeks go.

According to recent reports, ● Match autonomy to reversibility. Let agents do reversible, measurable work and keep irreversible actions supervised.

● Treat vendor claims as claims. Ask for logs and test on your own data.

Many marketing features have been renamed in the last couple of years. Email sequencing, lead scoring and campaign tools are now often described as agents. The honest question is whether a given product is a real architecture shift or marketing automation with a chat box added. Both exist: some systems run a perceive-reason-act loop with dynamic tool selection, while others are if/else branches with a model writing the subject line.

Strip away the marketing language and an agent has three parts:.

● A goal, expressed in natural language or as a measurable target.

● A tool set: functions the model is allowed to call, each described by a schema.

● A loop that runs until the goal is met, a limit is hit or a human steps in.

Industry observers note that the reasoning step is a model call. You pass it the current state, the goal and the available tools, and it responds with text or a structured request to call a tool. Your code runs the call, feeds the result back and asks again. OpenAI's function calling guide describes this as a conversation between your application and the model, which is the primitive underneath most agent frameworks.

Compare that with a cron job. A cron job runs a rule such as pausing ads below a click-through threshold every morning. It cannot decide that cost per acquisition matters more than click-through this week. An agent can, because the branching is chosen at runtime by a model rather than at write time by you. A useful test: if you can draw the full decision tree before the system runs, it is automation. If the path depends on what the model decides after seeing the data, it is an agent.

● Perceive. Read current state from an ad platform's reporting endpoint, a CRM webhook or a database. Ordinary code, no model involved.

● Reason. One model call containing the goal, the state, a summary of past actions and the schemas of every tool the agent may use.

● Act. The model returns a structured tool call. Your code validates the arguments against the schema and your guardrails, then executes.

● Observe. Capture the result, including failures. A rate-limit error or validation error is information for the next step.

Sources indicate that ● Upgrade memory. Record the action and outcome so the agent does not repeat itself.

According to recent reports, ● Repeat or stop. Loop until the goal is met, an iteration cap is reached or a guardrail escalates to a human.

Steps two and three rely on function calling, where tools are declared with typed parameters and the model returns matching arguments. The Hugging Face function calling guide highlights the same pattern. For connecting tools across systems, the Model Context Protocol is an open protocol for integrating LLM applications with external data sources and tools. Instead of writing an adapter for every CRM and ad account, you point an MCP client at a server that exposes those tools with discoverable schemas.

Lead scoring and routing. The agent reads CRM state, enriches it with lookups, scores the lead and writes back an owner and next action. It is agentic when it chooses which enrichment tools to call based on what is missing, and not agentic when the score is a fixed model output piped into a rule.

In a recent development, ad creative generation and testing. The agent produces variations from brand inputs, launches a structured test, reads performance data and shifts budget toward what works. This is among the clearest closed feedback loops because the outcome signal is numeric and fast.

It has been revealed that IBM's overview of AI agents in marketing frames a similar progression, from scripted chatbots at one end to agents that decide, design workflows and use function calling at the other. Most products sit somewhere in between.

Vendors sometimes blur this line. Four criteria help even from the outside:.

Practical tests: give it a goal it has no preset workflow for and see whether it composes a path or returns an apology. Change the data mid-run and check whether the next step differs. Ask for the tool call log, because a real agent produces one. Ask what happens when a tool call fails; a script throws, while an agent should retry or re-plan.

Three questions decide this, and none are about how clever the model is: can errors be detected quickly, can the action be reversed, and what does one bad decision cost?

● Reasonable to hand over: drafting copy variations, summarizing campaign performance, flagging data mismatches, writing internal briefs, pausing clearly underperforming ads.

● Keep supervised: budget reallocation across accounts, legal, medical or financial claims, pricing and discount changes, messages to named customers and final brand-voice sign-off.

A human approval step costs minutes. An unsupervised mistake in those areas can cost far more.

In a recent development, for many teams the practical answer is to build the orchestration that touches proprietary data and internal systems, and to evaluate off-the-shelf tools for narrow, high-volume tasks that other teams have already solved. What people underestimate when building is not the prototype, which can take an afternoon, but everything after: schema validation, retries, idempotency, rate-limit handling, prompt versioning, cost controls, an audit log and an evaluation harness.

In a recent development, ad creative is a common candidate for the existing-tool route because volume is high and the loop is similar across businesses. Vendors in this space describe their products differently, so compare scope, integrations and pricing. As one example, Larven describes an AI marketing agent that runs Meta ads, pulls products and copy from a store such as Shopify, and connects to your own ad account. Treat any such description as the vendor's own, and verify it with a trial on your data before committing.

The goal: keep spend inside a daily cap while letting a model propose budget changes. The model is injected as a function, so you can wire in any provider's function-calling API or a stub for tests. The notable part is that every limit is enforced in code. The model proposes, and your code decides.

"""A minimal guarded agent loop. The model is injected as a function, so you can swap in any provider's function-calling API, or a stub for tests.""" from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Guardrails:     allowed_campaigns: set     daily_cap: float            # max total daily budget across campaigns     max_change_pct: float = 0.2 # larger single changes need a human     max_actions: int = 5        # per run @dataclass class State:     budgets: dict               # campaign_id -> daily budget     log: list = field(default_factory=list)     pending: list = field(default_factory=list) def check(call, state, g):     """Return 'run', 'approve' or ('deny', reason). Enforced in code, never by the prompt."""     if call["name"] != "adjust_budget":         return ("deny", "unknown tool")     cid, fresh = call["args"]["campaign_id"], call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]     if cid not in g.allowed_campaigns or cid not in state.budgets:         return ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     if new < 0:         return ("deny", "negative budget")     others = sum(v for k, v in state.budgets.items() if k != cid)     if others + new > g.daily_cap:         return ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     old = state.budgets[cid]     if old and abs(new - old) / old > g.max_change_pct:         return "approve"     return "run" def run(model, state, g):     """model(state) -> a tool call dict, or None when it has nothing to do."""     for in range(g.maxactions):         call = model(state)         if call is None:             break         verdict = check(call, state, g)         state.log.append({"call": call, "verdict": verdict})         if verdict == "run":             state.budgets[call["args"]["campaign_id"]] = call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]         elif verdict == "approve":             state.pending.append(call)     return state.

The tests use a stub in place of a model. They confirm that small changes run, large changes wait for approval, the daily cap and allow-list are enforced, an unknown tool is denied, and a model that never stops is halted by the action limit with everything logged:.

from agent_loop import Guardrails, State, check, run G = Guardrails(allowed_campaigns={"a", "b"}, daily_cap=200) def call(cid, newly introduced): return {"name": "adjust_budget", "args": {"campaign_id": cid, "new_daily_budget": new}} def test_small_change_runs():     assert check(call("a", 105), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "run" def test_large_change_needs_approval():     assert check(call("a", 150), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "approve" def test_cap_and_allow_list_are_enforced():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 90, "c": 10})     assert check(call("a", 115), s, G) == ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     assert check(call("c", 11), s, G) == ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     assert check({"name": "delete_account", "args": {}}, s, G) == ("deny", "unknown tool") def test_loop_stops_at_action_limit_and_logs_everything():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500, max_actions=3)     run(lambda st: call("a", st.budgets["a"] + 1), s, g)   # a model that never stops     assert len(s.log) == 3 and s.budgets["a"] == 103 def test_denied_and_pending_actions_do_not_change_budgets():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500)     seq = iter([call("a", 150), call("a", 600), None])   # needs approval, then breaks the cap     run(lambda st: next(seq), s, g)     assert s.budgets["a"] == 100 and len(s.pending) == 1.

Run them with pytest. In a real deployment, the model function would call your provider with the state, the goal and the tool schemas, then return the parsed tool call.

In a recent development, ● It handles one tool. A real agent needs several, such as reporting, pausing ads and requesting approval.

Sources indicate that ● It keeps state in memory. Production systems need a durable store and idempotent actions so a retry cannot apply a change twice.

According to recent reports, ● The thresholds are placeholders. Set your own caps and percentages from your spend and risk tolerance.

Industry observers note that ● It validates the call but not the data. If upstream numbers are wrong, the agent will act on them.

According to recent reports, runaway spend. Budget APIs act instantly and changes compound. Without a hard ceiling in your own code, a reasoning error becomes a billing event.

Dirty upstream data. Stale CRM records, a broken product feed or a misattributed conversion. The agent can act confidently on wrong inputs and leave a tidy audit trail of well-reasoned bad decisions.

Recent findings suggest that missing audit trails. If you cannot reconstruct why an agent acted, you cannot fix or defend it. Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise reports that close to three-quarters of companies proposal to deploy agentic AI within two years, and that only 21% of those companies report having a mature model for agent governance.

Sources indicate that ● Least-privilege credentials. A separate API key per agent, scoped to exactly what it needs, never a shared admin token.

● Hard caps in code. Daily spend ceilings and a maximum percentage change per adjustment, enforced outside the model.

Sources indicate that ● Human-in-the-loop thresholds. Define which actions always need approval.

Recent findings suggest that ● Log every tool call. Inputs, outputs, errors, model and prompt version, with timestamps you can query.

● Start read-only. Run in suggest mode and compare recommendations with what your team would have done.

It has been revealed that A system that pairs a language model with real tools and lets it pursue a goal. It reads state, decides on an action, executes it, observes the result and decides again.

Automation starts from a trigger and follows branches defined in advance. An agent starts from a goal and selects tools at runtime.

Not on current evidence. They handle high-volume, measurable, reversible work well. Strategy, positioning and final brand approval still sit with people.

Function calling, where tools are declared by schema and the model returns matching arguments, and increasingly the Model Context Protocol for connecting tools.

In a recent development, it depends on how promptly errors are detected, whether actions are reversible and what a bad decision costs. Automate the cheap and reversible; supervise the rest.

Wrong tool calls, runaway spend, confident action on dirty data and brand drift at scale. Missing audit trails make all of them harder to diagnose.

Sources indicate that an AI marketing agent is less magic than it sounds: a goal, a set of tools and a loop with limits. The model's intelligence matters, but the system around it decides whether it is safe to run. Define the tools narrowly, enforce limits in code, log everything, start read-only and widen autonomy only as the evidence supports it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).

Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.

Industry observers note that this marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets. If you're interested in deeper dives on the technology itself, check out the following posts:.

It has been revealed that but this post isn't about the core technology. It's a behind-the-scenes view of getting Xet on the Hub; taking you through our proof-of-concept to the first migration of repositories.

Industry observers note that the migration shifted ~6% of the Hub’s download traffic onto Xet infrastructure, validating several integral components and testing integrations with the myriad of ways repositories are accessed (e.g., via local development environments, different libraries, CI systems, cloud platforms, etc.). With nearly two million developers working on over two million public repositories, it’s real-world usage that’s the ultimate proving ground. Engineering a complex system like Xet storage is a balancing act. You plan for scale, performance, and reliability, but once bytes start moving, challenges emerge. The trick is knowing when to move from design and theory to practice.

It has been revealed that LFS, the storage system behind repositories today, stores large files in a separate object storage outside of the repository. LFS deduplicates at the file level. Even tiny edits create a new revision to upload in full; painful for the multi-gigabyte files found in many Hub repositories.

It has been revealed that in contrast, Xet storage uses content-defined chunking (CDC), to deduplicate at the level of bytes (~64KB chunks of data). If you edit one row in a Parquet file or tweak a small piece of metadata in a GGUF model, only those changed chunks are sent over the wire.

Industry observers note that this provides significant benefits to large file transfers. For example, the Xet team keeps an internal ~5 GB SQLite database that powers a metrics dashboard. With LFS, appending 1 MB (around the average update currently) requires re-uploading the entire 5 GB file. With Xet storage, we push only the fresh data.

This means uploads for the dashboard take a tenth of a second (at 50Mb/s) instead of the 13 minutes if the database were backed by LFS.

Making this work requires coordination between the following components:.

Before moving to production, the system was introduced into an ephemeral environment, where we built a steel thread of functionality to enable uploading and downloading via the huggingface_hub. The video below highlights our progress one month in:.

After the heady highs of a quick proof-of-concept, the team settled into battling gnarly integration points (privacy, backward compatibility, fragmentation, etc) with the complex ecosystem that is the Hub. Eventually, the infrastructure moved into production for Hugging Face team members. With real usage now rolling in, we moved forward with the first large-scale migration.

On February 20th at 10 a.m., it was all hands on deck. In the weeks prior the team had built the internal tooling to migrate files from LFS to Xet and, just as importantly, roll back a repository to LFS if necessary. Now it was time to put it to the test. Grafana and Kibana lit up with fresh logs and metrics, showing the load shift in real time.

The picture is the same in Kibana, only here you can tell when we took a lunch break:.

In a recent development, by the end of the day, we had successfully migrated all target repositories for a total of 4.5 TB into Xet storage. Downloads from each repository were now served by our infrastructure.

Sources indicate that no launch is without its lessons. The system handled the load smoothly and migrations went off without any major disruptions, but as the bytes flowed through various components we began to see some trends.

Reviewing network throughput post-migration, we saw that CAS was downloading four times more data than it was returning to clients:.

According to recent reports, upon further investigation we found the vast majority of requests to CAS were for 10MB ranges of data within files. These requests come from people that are using hf_transfer to accelerate their downloads of large files. The requested ranges do not align on block boundaries and the block format doesn’t provide uncompressed chunk lengths to facilitate skipping directly to the data within the block. Instead, CAS streams the block starting at the beginning and reads until it finds the requested data.

Given a block with an average size of 60MB and multiple partial requests to ranges within that block, the overhead accumulates. CAS reads 210MB for just 60MB delivered, a ratio of 3.5 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent to the client. At scale across blocks of irregular sizes and ranges that can span several blocks, the 4 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent ratio is matched.

As usual, an image is worth a thousand words:.

Industry observers note that to fix this, we updated the block format to store chunk-length metadata, enabling CAS to download only what each request actually needs. This format change required coordinated updates across:.

Recent findings suggest that all of which were undertaken without downtime. Not only did this result in a balanced ratio in CAS downloads to returned data, but also reduced GET latency by ~35% across the board.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, we also saw an unexpected load imbalance across our CAS cluster. One pod would spike to hundreds of active uploads while other pods chugged along at single digits. Swapping the load balancer’s routing algorithm (from round-robin to least outstanding requests) and adding more nodes made little difference in the moment.

It has been revealed that digging deeper we realized that during uploads, CAS writes to a temporary file for validation before uploading without calling fsync, allowing the OS to buffer writes in the page cache. When a spike of uploads comes in, the unflushed page cache leads to increased memory pressure.

In a recent development, as the OS tries to flush the page cache to disk, the pod experiences throughput throttling from block storage, causing increased latency on uploads. While uploads slowly process, new requests continue to come in, pushing more to the disk. This creates a vicious cycle, leading to a backlog of uploads and the imbalance that we saw during the migration:.

Industry observers note that to keep a pod from getting in this state, we put a limit to the number of concurrent uploads each machine accepts before rejecting requests that, when reached, pushes requests on to other pods in the cluster. If all pods in the cluster get in this state, then our autoscaling policies kick in. Longer-term solutions might include forcing disk syncs, removing the on-disk buffering, or switching to ephemeral storage with better throughput.

According to recent reports, these two issues led to crucial architectural improvements, but they weren’t the only challenges the team tackled in the weeks following the migration. We also addressed other performance issues, a memory leak (which we fixed but still can't definitively root cause), and on advice from AWS to migrate the LFS Bridge from an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to improve scalability during bursts of traffic.

Industry observers note that in short, real-world load was essential for exposing these challenges, and incremental migrations let us tackle them safely. That’s how we’re ensuring Xet-backed repositories scale reliably for the entire Hugging Face community with faster uploads, fewer bottlenecks, and minimal disruption all the way.

With the initial migration complete, Xet is now on the Hugging Face Hub.

We’re finalizing an official integration with the huggingface_hub that will mean you get the benefits of Xet without any significant changes to your current workflow. To get going:.

If you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇 or open a discussion on the Xet team page. And stay tuned as we roll out more pieces (faster web uploads, faster Git workflows), bringing faster big-file collaboration to every AI builder on Hugging Face!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks.
  • Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Android’s source code is major – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

In a recent development, we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 indicates the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

#173753. When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s been a… year, huh?
  • Industry observers note that technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do.
  • It has been revealed that it’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that indicates a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first….

Industry observers note that technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI. I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity.

It has been revealed that it’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop, somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children. The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry.

In a recent development, the technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now. In the space between that piece being published and now, we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes.

In a recent development, the mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume, regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either.

This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least.

Recent findings suggest that the sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide, devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers. It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing.

Industry observers note that some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them. Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is increasingly difficult.

Recent findings suggest that as the numbers go up in the AI world, the numbers very much go down for independent educators, publishers and community conferences. There’s a developing and worrying culture of “I don’t need to skill up now because I can use AI for work”, so allow me to break down why that reductive view of your work and your career is harmful in the long term.

And don’t ever forget that! Let’s have a think for a second about what actually makes you a good developer, because typing characters in a text editor certainly isn’t it. What makes us good is experience, knowledge, nuance and above all else, creativity.

Recent findings suggest that look, I get it, AI really can feel like it’s a miracle machine, but it’s key to take a wider view. Along with the published studies on cognitive decline and the widening skills gap, it’s more important than ever to invest in your brain to keep your skills sharp because you’re not getting that repetitive reinforcement that writing code every day gives you anymore if AI tools do everything for you. There’s a reason that I often build most of my teaching around a linear build-along because the tangible nature of repeating patterns you’ve learned really helps that knowledge to sink in.

As always, this article is addressed to everyone, but I want to talk directly to founders (like me), decision makers, and managers for a second. A big part of our job, in fact, the most notable part, is to ensure that our workers are looked after. I’m not just talking about compensation and perks here. I’m talking about our responsibility to ensure that our workers’ skills are kept sharp, their professional curiosities are satisfied and above all else that they are happy in the work they are doing. Our workers are much more than “number go up” vehicles.

You should be giving your developers more time to learn, rather than chasing endless volume. If AI enthusiasts are to be believed, there’s hours upon hours of time efficiencies created by this technology. Don’t fill that time with more volume. Instead, invest that time in developing your worker’s skills. It’s going to avoid burnout which yep, daily LLM use will likely cause in the long term.

One thing that is increasingly clear is that the health of the AI industry is not good. The bubble has already effectively burst in China and more worryingly for economy enjoyers, the “picks and shovels” — AKA the chips industry in Korea — has seen dramatic downturns. This is not how an “inevitable” outcome is supposed to happen!

It has been revealed that the U.S. AI industry is on very shaky ground too. Circular financing, unbelievable levels of debt and a data center build out that simply cannot keep up with the required power levels to turn profits for hyperscalers and startups, mixed with a genuine hatred of the technology by the general public, creates enough risk in itself. Recent events, such as the Democrats dominating the midterms causing AI stocks to drop and as well as Nvidia’s stock because of its CEO being caught up in a spying scandal shine a light on the fragility of the industry. A healthy industry doesn’t work like this.

With all that in mind, what would be a really silly thing to do? Yeh, you guessed it: put AI at the heart of everything in your business. Sure, there’s open source models — which I think is the logical destination of the technology — but how many companies are going to be willing to maintain their infrastructure needs? Not many. The low barrier of entry of commercial AI technology is the selling point, let’s be honest.

Sources indicate that above everything, people need to be invested in, not pushed aside by technology like AI. As I mentioned earlier, it’s experience, knowledge, nuance, and creativity that sets humans far apart from AI. That technology does indeed keep evolving, but even the most ardent of AI supporters will concede that the rate of frontier model improvement is very much levelling out.

There’s never been a more vital time to keep human skills sharp, so here’s some ideas on how to do that.

This is not just directed at individuals but also at founders, decision makers and managers. Our industry has been historically excellent at investing in skilling people up and we need to bring that back.

According to recent reports, give staff the time and budget to learn, to develop their skills and to engage with the community at conferences. You already know the positive outcomes that brings, so bring it back to your organization. At the absolute worst case, it’ll make the usage of AI in your organization more efficient and when the token subsidies inevitably end, more cost effective.

Again, token subsidies will inevitably end. So, getting thousands of dollars of worth from a $200 a month subscription will be something you’ll look fondly back on. When hallucinations from AI tools are suddenly costing thousands, does it make sense to force your staff to produce as much volume as possible? Of course not.

Sources indicate that my advice is to re-evaluate those prior decisions and invest saved costs back into developing your workers instead, while there’s still a hope of them not burning out completely. Make sure you include your workers in these decisions and discuss the impacts of mandates on them. It’s key for you to understand the impact of these sort of decisions.

This advice is more aimed at developers, but stay paying attention, managers. As I noted earlier, repetition (especially typing) reinforces upcoming learning and existing knowledge. The slower pace also allows your brain to think, which from a quality of output perspective, is imperative. Doing none of that atrophies skills over time.

According to recent reports, I recently read Jenn Schiffer’s great post. She did the Weird Web October challenge and wrote this:.

[…] i encourage anyone who uses ai and/or vibe codes to consider doing an exercise like this without those tools as a way to challenge your brain and you can continue doing your regular work the way you do your regular work.

I think that’s a very good idea, even if it’s messing around with a little side project — if you’ve got the energy from Producing Value all day, of course. Guess what bosses: this is another way you can make your staff happier, by giving them time to do this on the clock.

Sources indicate that at the end of the day, you’ll miss the soul when it’s gone. It’s not gone yet though. Far from it. Independents like CSS-Tricks, my publication, Piccalilli, and Smashing Magazine are trying hard to keep the soul of our industry alive by sharing high quality educational content with the community.

Recent findings suggest that most of this content is free at the point of entry, but it certainly isn’t free to produce. We all pay writers fairly to share their knowledge with the community and we are all tiny organizations. We’re certainly not in this game to make huge profits, that’s for sure.

In a recent development, all of us could do more though, but funding is the ultimate barrier. For both companies and individuals, purchase courses, join the membership programs, and purchase ad space. With the right financial support, publications like ours can be a real force in pushing the good stuff back into our industry and bringing everyone up with us. That’s what we do it for.

In a recent development, some course producers I recommend are Miriam, Sara, Mat, Scott, Brad and Ian, Josh, Ahmad, Christine, Vitaly, Ben and of course, myself! All of these will have generous Black Friday deals, so go ahead and ask your boss to invest in you.

Now, share this post with your boss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at its annual GTC conference, NVIDIA has unveiled a trio of groundbreaking open-source releases aimed at accelerating physical AI development. Release of a new suite of world foundation models (WFMs) with multicontrols called Cosmos Transfer, a highly curated Physical AI Dataset, and the first open model for general humanoid reasoning called NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1 - represent a significant leap forward in physical AI technology, offering developers powerful tools and resources to advance robotics systems, and enhance autonomous vehicle technology.

Cosmos Transfer, the latest addition to NVIDIA's Cosmos™ world foundation models (WFMs), introduces a fresh level of control and accuracy in generating virtual world scenes.

Available in 7 billion parameter size, the model utilizes multicontrols to guide the generation of high-fidelity world scenes from structural inputs, ensuring precise spatial alignment and scene composition.

The model is built by training individual ControlNets separately for each sensor modality used to capture the simulated world.

Input types include 3D bounding box map, Trajectory map, Depth map, Segmentation map.

Outputs from Cosmos Transfer varying environments and weather conditions.

Cosmos Transfer coupled with the NVIDIA Omniverse platform is driving controllable synthetic data generation for robotics and autonomous vehicle development at scale. Find more Cosmos Transfer Examples on GitHub.

Cosmos Transfer samples built using post-training base model are also available for autonomous vehicles.

NVIDIA has also released Physical AI Dataset, an open-source dataset on Hugging Face for developing physical AI. This commercial-grade, pre-validated dataset consists of 15 terabytes of data representing more than 320,000 trajectories for robotics training, plus up to 1,000 Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) assets, including a SimReady collection.

The dataset is designed for post-training foundation models like Cosmos Predict world foundation models, providing developers with high-quality, diverse data to enhance their AI models.

According to recent reports, another exciting announcement is the release of NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1, the world's first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model takes multimodal input, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks in diverse environments. The NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that isaac GR00T N1 was trained on an expansive humanoid dataset, consisting of real captured data, synthetic data generated using components of the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T Blueprint, and internet-scale video data. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks and environments.

Isaac GR00T N1 uses a single model and set of weights to enable manipulation behaviors on various humanoid robots, such as the Fourier GR-1 and 1X Neo. It demonstrates robust generalization across a range of tasks, including grasping and manipulating objects with one or both arms, as well as transferring items between arms. It can also execute complex, multi-step tasks that require sustained contextual understanding and the integration of diverse skills. These capabilities make it well-suited for applications in material handling, packaging, and inspection.

Isaac GR00T N1 features a dual-system architecture inspired by human cognition, consisting of the following complementary components:.

Post-training is the path forward to advancing autonomous systems, creating specialized models for downstream physical AI tasks.

In a recent development, check out GitHub for Cosmos Predict and Cosmos Transfer inference scripts. Explore the Cosmos Transfer research paper for more details.

The NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face. Sample datasets and PyTorch scripts for post-training using custom user datasets, which is compatible with the Hugging Face LeRobot format are available on GitHub. For more information about the Isaac GR00T N1 model, see the research paper.

Follow NVIDIA on Hugging Face for more updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Average US wedding cost (national median is closer to $10,000-$15,000).

What $30K grows to in 30 years at 7% annual return.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

Sources indicate that the FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:.

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently demonstrates that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

Sources indicate that the golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:.

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

Recent findings suggest that for couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

Industry observers note that before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Sources indicate that any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Industry observers note that set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.
